title: Build TaskFlow Lite in JavaScript
subtitle: Hands-on track project
text: f02-javascript f02-javascript Build TaskFlow Lite in JavaScript Turn the static page into a working task manager using only browser JavaScript so the language fundamentals are visible. Create task Toggle complete Delete task Search/filter localStorage persistence One async fetch exercise Model one task as a plain object, then create an array of tasks. Write pure functions for creating, updating, filtering, and deleting tasks. Render the array into the DOM and keep rendering separate from state-changing functions. Files, Programs, Processes, and the Terminal Why this matters A source file is data; a program is executable instructions; a process is a running instance with memory and operating-system resources. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction. Mental model • A source file is data; a program is executable instructions; a process is a running instance with memory and operating-system resources. • The terminal is a text interface to the operating system. The shell parses commands, resolves executables through PATH, sets environment variables, and starts processes. • The working directory changes how relative paths resolve. Many 'file not found' errors are simply the right command from the wrong directory. • Ports identify network endpoints owned by processes. localhost means the current machine, not 'the frontend'. Step-by-step walkthrough 1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level. 2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise. 3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment. 4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes. 5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic. 6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill. title: Full Stack Mental Model
subtitle: Full-Stack Architecture & Orientation
text: full-stack-mental-model Full Stack Mental Model Phase 00 How Modern Full- Stack Applications Work A visual mental model for browsers, frontend rendering, APIs, business logic, persistence, authentication and state ownership. Book 1 · Full-stack mental model Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented Contents 1. A request is a journey 7. The API boundary 2. Browser responsibilities 8. State ownership 3. Frontend responsibilities 9. Failure paths 4. Backend responsibilities 10. The complete request lifecycle 5. Database responsibilities 11. Knowledge checks 6. Authentication vs authorization Phase 00 | Page 2 of 10 A request is a journey through responsibilities When a user clicks Create Task, no single framework “does the feature.” Multiple layers cooperate. Becoming a full-stack developer means understanding that journey well enough to diagnose it when something goes wrong. Browser Next.js frontend HTTP API request NestJS controller + service Prisma data access Supabase PostgreSQL Figure 1 - Core application request path - This is the central diagram we will repeatedly expand throughout the course. Layer 1: the browser The browser renders HTML and CSS, runs client-side JavaScript, stores limited client state, sends network requests, receives responses, enforces web security rules such as CORS, and reports failures in developer tools. It does not decide authoritative business rules just because it can run code. Layer 2: Next.js Next.js is the presentation application. It owns routes, pages, layouts, rendering choices, UI composition, navigation and interaction. Later it also coordinates client-side server state through TanStack Query. The course deliberately prevents Next.js from becoming a second backend full of duplicated business rules. Phase 00 | Page 3 of 10 Layer 3: HTTP HTTP is the contract boundary between independently running applications. A request carries a method, URL, headers and optional body. A response carries a status code, headers and optional body. This boundary is valuable because the frontend and backend can evolve independently as long as they honor the contract. Method Path Headers Body POST /tasks Auth, Content-Type JSON NestJS route receives the request Figure 2 - HTTP request anatomy - The API boundary is explicit; it is not a function call disguised as networking. Layer 4: NestJS + Fastify NestJS provides the application architecture for controllers, providers, dependency injection, guards, interceptors and modules. Fastify is the HTTP platform underneath NestJS in this course. Controllers translate HTTP into application calls; services own business behavior. Phase 00 | Page 4 of 10 HTTP request Controller Validation / auth boundary Service business logic PrismaService Database Figure 3 - Backend responsibility chain - Keep controllers thin enough that business rules remain reusable and testable. ASP.NET CORE BRIDGE If you know ASP.NET Core: a Nest controller is conceptually similar to a controller, providers/ services use dependency injection, guards/interceptors overlap with filter/middleware concerns, and PrismaService loosely occupies the “database access gateway” role that DbContext often plays. The mapping is useful, but the frameworks are not identical. Layer 5: Prisma Prisma is not PostgreSQL. It is the application-facing ORM/data-access layer. It turns model definitions into typed database operations and manages schema changes through migrations. In our architecture, Prisma stays behind NestJS so browser code never receives database credentials. Layer 6: PostgreSQL PostgreSQL is authoritative persistent storage for application data: users, memberships, projects, tasks, comments, audit history and other relational records. Supabase hosts PostgreSQL for the course, but the relational concepts remain standard PostgreSQL concepts. Phase 00 | Page 5 of 10 Authentication is not authorization Authentication answers “who are you?” Authorization answers “are you allowed to perform this action on this resource?” Those questions happen at different points and should remain conceptually separate. User signs in Supabase Auth Access token (JWT) Next.js sends Bearer token NestJS validates token Service receives trusted identity Figure 4 - Future authentication flow - Authentication establishes a trustworthy identity before business logic evaluates permissions. Later, authorization adds another decision: Phase 00 | Page 6 of 10 Verified user Requested action Membership / role / ownership check Allowed? Execute business operation Figure 5 - Authorization decision - A valid identity is necessary but not sufficient; permissions and resource ownership still matter. State ownership Many frontend applications become difficult because every kind of state is placed in one global store. The course teaches state by ownership instead. Server-owned state Client-owned state TanStack Query Local / URL / Form state tasks · projects · users · API results dialogs · filters · inputs · navigation Persistent truth Domain behavior PostgreSQL Services / optional stores authoritative business data rules and interaction logic Figure 6 - State ownership map - Different categories of state deserve different tools and lifecycles. Phase 00 | Page 7 of 10 Failure paths are part of the architecture A professional mental model includes failure. Network requests time out. Validation rejects input. Authentication expires. Authorization denies access. Database constraints conflict. Bugs throw exceptions. The goal is not to pretend failures are rare; the goal is to know which layer should detect, translate, log and present them. Database Prisma Service HTTP constraint error decision 409 UI message “Already exists” Figure 7 - Failure translation - Errors should become more meaningful as they travel toward the user. Phase 00 | Page 8 of 10 The full lifecycle User interaction React / Next.js UI TanStack Query or API client HTTP + JWT NestJS controller Guard / validation Service Prisma PostgreSQL Response + cache update UI re-renders Figure 8 - Complete vertical slice - This is the mental model you should be able to narrate from memory by the end of Phase 00. Knowledge checks 1. Why should Next.js not receive a PostgreSQL password? 2. What responsibility would be lost if all business logic lived in controllers? 3. What is the difference between authentication and authorization? Phase 00 | Page 9 of 10 4. Where does durable business data live? 5. Why is HTTP useful even when frontend and backend are in one monorepo? 6. Give one example of server state and one example of local UI state. YOU ARE READY WHEN You can narrate the request path without memorizing framework slogans: user → UI → HTTP → controller → service → Prisma → PostgreSQL → response → UI. Book 4 · Workflow, discipline and development habits Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented Contents 1. The engineering loop 7. Environment variables and secrets 2. Windows and PowerShell conventions 8. Git workflow 3. Repository discipline 9. Definition of done 4. Working-directory awareness 10. Documentation habits 5. Small verified changes 11. AI-assisted development rules 6. Debugging by layer Phase 00 | Page 2 of 6 The engineering loop matters more than typing speed requirement, locate the responsible layer, make the smallest coherent change, verify behavior, and preserve a clean history. Requirement / bug report Locate responsibility Plan smallest vertical change Implement Run checks Inspect runtime behavior Commit coherent change Figure 1 - Professional change loop - This loop is repeated from the first health endpoint to production deployment. Windows-first command discipline The course uses ordinary Windows PowerShell as the primary shell. Every command will say where it runs. Paths containing spaces are quoted. Bash-only syntax is never silently mixed into PowerShell instructions. cd "C:\Projects\TaskFlow\apps\api" Get-Location pnpm run start:dev Phase 00 | Page 3 of 6 THE WORKING DIRECTORY IS PART OF THE COMMAND A correct command executed from the wrong workspace can produce a misleading package, script or configuration error. Always include location in your debugging model. User-profile tooling instead of unnecessary admin rights On restricted Windows machines, global package setup should prefer user-owned locations rather than assuming Administrator privileges. The course will document permission failures such as Corepack attempting writes under C:\Program Files\nodejs , then teach a user-profile installation strategy when appropriate. Repository discipline • One responsibility per new file. • No “utils” dumping ground when a specific module owns the behavior. • Do not create a package simply because a packages/ directory exists. • Commit the lockfile. • Keep secrets out of Git. • Run lint/typecheck/tests/build at meaningful checkpoints. taskflow/ workspace apps/web apps/api Next.js NestJS + Fastify packages/* only when justified Figure 2 - Repository responsibility map - The monorepo is a container for independently owned applications and later shared packages. Phase 00 | Page 4 of 6 Debugging by layer When an error appears, avoid replacing whole files. First determine which layer can actually produce the observed symptom. Symptom First layer to inspect Example evidence Button does nothing Browser/UI Console, event handler, disabled state. Request blocked before API Browser/network DevTools Network, CORS message. 404/405 HTTP/controller routing Method/path mismatch. 401/403 Authentication/authorization Token/guard/permission logs. 400/422 Validation boundary DTO/schema error details. 409 Business rule/database constraint Unique conflict or domain rule. 500 Backend runtime/data access Server logs and stack trace. Reproduce reliably Inspect browser console/network Confirm HTTP route and status Inspect server log/request id Inspect service decision Inspect database query/constraint Figure 3 - Debug from the outside inward - Evidence narrows the search area before code changes begin. Environment variables and secrets Configuration enters the course when a layer first needs it. Secrets never appear in screenshots, example repositories or PDF source snippets. Public browser variables and server-only secrets are treated differently. Phase 00 | Page 5 of 6 # Example documentation only DATABASE_URL="postgresql://..." NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL="http://localhost:4000" Git workflow for learning and real projects 1. Start from a known-green main branch. 2. Create a focused branch for a coherent change. 3. Make small, verifiable commits. 4. Keep generated artifacts and secrets out of commits unless intentionally versioned. 5. Before merge: lint, typecheck, tests and production build. 6. Review the diff for accidental files and architecture drift. Definition of done □ Requirement is satisfied. □ Expected behavior was manually verified. □ Error/failure path is understood. □ Lint passes. □ Typecheck passes. □ Relevant tests pass. □ Production build passes when applicable. □ No secret or debug artifact leaked. □ Architecture documentation still matches reality. AI-assisted development rules AI can accelerate explanation, search, refactoring and test design, but it should not erase your mental model. The course treats AI like a pair programmer: it may propose changes, but you should be able to explain what layer changed, why the change is correct, and how you verified it. RULE FOR THIS COURSE Never accept a large generated patch as “correct” because it compiles. Read the diff, identify the responsibility of every new file, and verify the behavior at the boundary that matters. text: guided-build-lab Guided Build Lab Purpose Explain the complete TaskFlow request path and identify which layer owns presentation, transport, business rules, persistence, identity, and operations. Guided Build Lab — Phase 00: Full-Stack Architecture & Orientation Purpose Explain the complete TaskFlow request path and identify which layer owns presentation, transport, business rules, persistence, identity, and operations. Deliverable A one-page architecture map plus an ADR-style note describing the responsibilities of Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and supporting infrastructure. Before you touch the code Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything. Architecture trace Browser interaction -> Next.js presentation boundary -> HTTP request -> NestJS controller/guard -> Service/business rules -> Prisma persistence -> PostgreSQL -> HTTP response -> UI update Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization. Step 1 — Draw TaskFlow as boxes and arrows before opening an IDE. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption. Step 2 — Label every arrow with what crosses it: props, HTTP JSON, verified identity, Prisma calls, SQL results. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 00: Full-Stack Architecture & Orientation Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk Browser interaction -> Next.js presentation boundary -> HTTP request -> NestJS controller/guard -> Service/business rules -> Prisma persistence -> PostgreSQL -> HTTP response -> UI update Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. text: powershell-and-windows-mental-model PowerShell and Windows Mental Model Phase 01 PowerShell & the Windows Developer Mental Model Learn the shell, paths, PATH lookup, environment variables, working directories, and failure evidence before frameworks enter the picture. Book 1 · Windows & terminal foundations Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented Contents 1. The shell mental model 6. Exit codes 2. Working directories 7. PowerShell vs Bash 3. Navigation 8. Mini lab 4. PATH lookup 9. Common failures 5. Environment variables 10. Knowledge check Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6 Your terminal is an engineering instrument Many learners treat a terminal as a place where tutorials tell them to paste commands. A full-stack developer needs a better model: the shell is a programmable interface to the operating system. It has a current working directory, environment variables, executable lookup rules, command parsing rules, and an exit status. You type a command → PowerShell parses it → Windows locates executable → Program runs → Exit/output returns Figure 1 - What happens when you press Enter Step 1 - Observe where you are Get-Location Get-ChildItem Get-ChildItem -Force Get-Location answers one of the most important debugging questions in this entire course: where is this command running? Get-ChildItem lists directory contents; -Force also reveals hidden items such as .git . MENTAL MODEL A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. If the current directory is wrong, a perfectly valid command can appear broken. Step 2 - Navigate without fear Set-Location $HOME New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "$HOME\Developer" -Force Set-Location "$HOME\Developer" Get-Location PowerShell aliases such as cd and ls are convenient, but the course sometimes shows the full cmdlet name so you understand what PowerShell is actually doing. Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6 Paths with spaces Set-Location "C:\Users\YourName\Desktop\Full Stack Learning" Quotes are not decoration. They tell the shell that spaces belong to one path argument. Step 3 - Inspect commands instead of guessing Get-Command node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-Command git -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-Command pnpm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue $env:Path -split ';' Get-Command tells you which executable PowerShell will run. This becomes crucial when two Node installations exist and the wrong one appears first on PATH. PowerShell receives: node Search PATH entries from left to right First matching node.exe wins That executable starts Figure 2 - PATH lookup - Version mismatches often come from executable lookup, not from the project. Environment variables Environment variables are named values inherited by processes. They are how shells and applications discover paths, configuration, and later secrets. Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6 $env:Path $env:USERPROFILE $env:APPDATA $env:LOCALAPPDATA TEMPORARY VS PERSISTENT $env:Path += ";C:\something" changes PATH for the current PowerShell process. It does not automatically rewrite the user's persistent environment settings. This distinction prevents the classic “it worked until I opened a new terminal” confusion. Exit codes and evidence git --version $LASTEXITCODE Human-readable output is useful, but programs also communicate success or failure through exit codes. Later, CI/CD systems rely on exactly this behavior. PowerShell vs Bash Intent PowerShell Bash equivalent Environment value $env:NAME $NAME Set environment value $env:NAME="x" export NAME=x Delete file tree Remove-Item -Recurse rm -rf Home $HOME $HOME Mini lab 1. Create $HOME\Developer\full-stack-2026-lab . 2. Move into it. 3. Create notes.txt with New-Item . 4. List normal and hidden files. 5. Print your PATH one entry per line. 6. Use Get-Command for PowerShell itself. Phase 01 | Page 5 of 6 Common failures “The term ... is not recognized” PowerShell could not resolve the command. Check whether the tool is installed, then Get-Command , then PATH. Do not reinstall the entire project. Path not found Check Get-Location , spelling, quoting, and whether the directory actually exists. Knowledge check 1. Why can the same command work in one terminal and fail in another? 2. What does PATH control? 3. Why does a working directory matter to project tools? 4. What is the difference between shell output and an exit code? Book 2 · Node runtime Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented Contents 1. Why Node comes first 6. PowerShell shell setup 2. LTS vs Current 7. Install Node 24.21.0 3. Why version managers matter 8. npm mental model 4. Inspect first 9. Common errors 5. Install fnm 10. Checkpoint Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6 Node.js is the runtime beneath our JavaScript tooling Next.js, NestJS, pnpm, Prisma tooling, test runners, build systems, and many developer utilities ultimately run on Node.js. If the runtime is wrong, every layer above it can become confusing. Windows process Node.js runtime 24.21.0 LTS Package manager and CLIs Next.js / NestJS / tooling Figure 1 - Why Node comes before frameworks - Framework commands are programs running on a specific Node runtime, not independent magic. Why use LTS instead of Current? As of September 17, 2026, Node 24.21.0 is an LTS release while Node 26 is the Current line. This course chooses the LTS line because a long multi-phase curriculum benefits from stability and ecosystem compatibility more than early access to the newest runtime features. Why use a version manager? Installing one global Node version seems simpler until project A requires Node 24 and a future experiment requires Node 26. A version manager turns runtime selection into an explicit action. Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6 Project requirements → fnm → Selected Node version → node.exe Figure 2 - Runtime selection instead of global guesswork Step 1 - Inspect the machine first node -v npm -v Get-Command node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-Command npm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue If Node already exists, do not immediately uninstall it. First learn where it came from. Step 2 - Install fnm on Windows The official fnm documentation supports WinGet on Windows: winget install Schniz.fnm After installation, open a new PowerShell and verify: fnm --version Step 3 - Configure fnm for PowerShell fnm works by updating environment variables for the shell. The official project recommends evaluating fnm env for the current shell. For a PowerShell profile, a common setup is: if (-not (Test-Path $PROFILE)) { New-Item -ItemType File -Path $PROFILE -Force } notepad $PROFILE Add the shell-initialization line appropriate to the installed fnm version, based on fnm env --shell powershell . Reopen PowerShell and verify fnm --version . WHY WE DO NOT BLINDLY OVERWRITE THE PROFILE PowerShell profiles are personal configuration files. Inspect them before editing. A course should never erase existing developer configuration just to add one tool. Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6 Step 4 - Install the locked Node runtime fnm install 24.21.0 fnm use 24.21.0 node -v npm -v Expected baseline: v24.21.0 11.19.0 Step 5 - Make the choice reproducible Later we can place a runtime version file in the repository. For now, the important skill is being able to select and verify the runtime explicitly. What npm is npm ships with Node and serves two roles: package registry client and project/package command tool. In this course we will use pnpm as the primary package manager, but npm remains useful for bootstrapping pnpm into the user profile when needed. Common errors fnm works, but node does not change The shell environment probably has not loaded fnm's environment changes. Inspect fnm env --shell powershell , your PowerShell profile, and Get-Command node . Wrong Node after opening a new terminal Check whether fnm initialization loads in that new shell and whether another Node path appears earlier on PATH. Company machine blocks WinGet Use an approved installer mechanism from IT or the fnm release binary. The engineering principle stays the same: install in user-accessible locations and make PATH explicit. Corepack EPERM Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6 pnpm is the package manager for this course A package manager resolves dependencies, downloads packages, records exact versions, creates executable shims, and runs project scripts. pnpm adds a content-addressable store and workspace features that make it a strong fit for the monorepo we will build in Phase 02. Read package.json Resolve dependency graph Read/write lockfile Use pnpm content-addressable store Link project node_modules Expose package executables Figure 1 - Package installation lifecycle - A package manager is performing dependency graph and filesystem work, not merely downloading ZIP files. Why pnpm 12.4.2? Phase 00 froze the course baseline. pnpm 12.4.2 was released September 15, 2026 and includes current security and Windows installation fixes. We keep that exact version throughout the generated course unless an explicit migration is approved. odejs for package-manager shims. npm config set prefix "$env:APPDATA
pm" npm install -g pnpm@12.4.2 $env:Path += ";$env:APPDATA
pm" pnpm -v The temporary PATH append makes the current shell see the user-profile npm bin directory. If your persistent user PATH does not already contain it, add that directory through Windows user environment settings or an approved PowerShell profile mechanism. WHY THIS SOLVES EPERM Global npm packages are written under the current user profile instead of a protected Program Files directory. The principle is least privilege: use administrator rights only when the operation actually requires them. Corepack and the permission trap On some Windows installations, corepack enable attempts to create or update shims beside Node in C:\Program Files
odejs\ . A standard user may receive EPERM: operation not permitted . That does not mean pnpm is broken; it means the requested filesystem location is protected. corepack enable → tries protected Node directory → Windows access check → EPERM Figure 2 - Permission failure path Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6 pnpm commands you should understand now Command Meaning pnpm -v Verify the package-manager executable selected by PATH. pnpm install Resolve/install dependencies using the lockfile and manifest. pnpm add package Add a runtime dependency to the current package. pnpm add -D package Add a development-only dependency. pnpm remove package Remove a dependency cleanly. pnpm exec tool Run a locally installed project executable. pnpm run script Run a script defined in package.json. Why local executables matter Later, Prisma is intentionally local. We will run pnpm exec prisma so the project controls the exact Prisma version. This is a general professional principle: project tools should usually be versioned with the project. Build-script approval Modern pnpm may refuse unapproved dependency build scripts and report ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS . Treat that as a security signal, not an invitation to disable protection globally. pnpm approve-builds Approve only packages the project genuinely requires, and understand why their install scripts execute. text: git-and-professional-version-control Git and Professional Version Control Phase 01 Git & Professional Version Control Build a correct mental model of working tree, staging, commits, diffs, identity, repository hygiene, and safe engineering history. Book 4 · Version control Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented Contents 1. Git mental model 7. .gitignore 2. Install Git for Windows 8. Commit design 3. Configure identity 9. Branches 4. Practice repository 10. What not to do 5. Stage and commit 11. Checkpoint 6. Understand diffs Phase 01 | Page 2 of 5 Git is the memory of the engineering process Git is not merely a cloud backup mechanism. It records intentional snapshots of a project's state so developers can compare, review, branch, integrate, and recover changes. Working tree - files you edit Staging area - changes selected for next snapshot Commit - named project snapshot Remote - shared repository history Figure 1 - Git mental model - The staging area lets you decide exactly what belongs in a commit instead of committing every modified file by accident. Step 1 - Install Git for Windows The official Git install page lists Git 2.55.0(5) as the maintained Windows build as of the Phase 01 baseline. WinGet is supported: winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget Open a new PowerShell and verify: git --version Get-Command git Phase 01 | Page 3 of 5 Step 2 - Configure identity git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@example.com" git config --global init.defaultBranch main git config --global --list Your Git identity becomes metadata on commits. It is not the same thing as logging in to GitHub. Step 3 - Create a disposable practice repository Set-Location "$HOME\Developer\full-stack-2026-lab" git init git status "Phase 01 Git practice" | Set-Content README.md git status Step 4 - Stage and commit intentionally git add README.md git status git commit -m "docs: add Phase 01 practice readme" git log --oneline --decorate -5 Professional habit: read git status before and after every important Git action. Step 5 - Learn the three diffs git diff git diff --staged git show HEAD Command Question it answers git diff What changed in the working tree but is not staged? git diff --staged What exactly will the next commit contain? git show HEAD What did the latest commit record? Phase 01 | Page 4 of 5 .gitignore is part of architecture hygiene Generated output, dependencies, logs, editor state, and secrets should not pollute version history. Later we will ignore node_modules , .env , build artifacts, and other generated files. Commit design A good commit is a coherent engineering statement. Avoid a week of unrelated changes under update stuff . Prefer messages such as feat: add health endpoint , fix: validate missing task title , or docs: document local setup . Make one coherent change → Review diff → Stage intentionally → Commit with useful message → Continue Figure 2 - Professional commit loop Branches - concept before workflow A branch is a movable name pointing at a commit. We will use branches more seriously when collaboration and CI/CD arrive. For now, understand that branches isolate lines of work without duplicating the entire project manually. What not to do • Do not commit .env secrets. • Do not delete .git because a command feels confusing. • Do not run destructive reset/clean commands copied from the internet before understanding what they remove. • Do not use GitHub Desktop or an IDE as a substitute for understanding Git state. Checkpoint □ git --version works. □ Name, email, and default branch are configured. □ You can explain working tree, staging area, commit, and remote. □ You can create a repository, stage one file, commit, inspect log, and inspect diffs. Install/verify VS Code 7. Workspace hygiene 3. Open current folder 8. Line endings 4. Important panels 9. Checkpoint 5. Extension discipline Phase 01 | Page 2 of 5 Your editor should reveal the system, not hide it A good editor improves navigation, feedback, refactoring, and inspection while keeping the project understandable outside the editor. The terminal and repository remain authoritative. VS Code installation If VS Code is already installed, verify rather than reinstall. If not, use the official installer or WinGet according to your organization's policy. After installation: code --version Get-Command code If code is not recognized but VS Code opens normally, the shell command may not yet be on PATH. Reopen the terminal after installation and inspect PATH before reinstalling the editor. Open the current folder Set-Location "$HOME\Developer\full-stack-2026-lab" code . The dot means “this directory.” This habit matters because the folder you open becomes the editor's workspace context. PowerShell working directory → code . → VS Code workspace root → Explorer / Search / Git / Terminal Figure 1 - One folder, multiple developer views Phase 01 | Page 3 of 5 The panels that matter Explorer Search File tree. Use it to understand structure, not Search across the repository. Essential for to create random folders. tracing usage and avoiding duplicate abstractions. Source Control Integrated Terminal Convenient view of Git changes. Still verify Useful, but remember that each terminal with git status and diffs. has its own process environment and working directory. Extensions: deliberately small set Do not install dozens of extensions before the project needs them. Start with language/editor support that provides clear value. JavaScript/TypeScript support is built in. Later phases can add ESLint, framework-specific helpers, database tooling, and formatting once the corresponding configuration exists. Formatting vs linting vs type checking Concern Main question Formatter How should code be laid out? Linter Does the code violate style or correctness rules? Type checker Are values used consistently with their types? Tests Does observable behavior meet expectations? These are different quality gates. Later CI will run them separately so failures are diagnosable. Workspace hygiene Use one project root. Avoid nesting accidental duplicate repositories such as taskflow/taskflow . Avoid placing projects inside folders aggressively synchronized by enterprise backup software if it causes file-locking or node_modules issues. Prefer a simple development path such as: Phase 01 | Page 4 of 5 $HOME\Developer\taskflow Line endings Windows commonly uses CRLF while many developer tools and servers use LF. Git can normalize line endings. We will add an explicit .gitattributes only when the repository exists in Phase 02 rather than generating configuration before there is a project to own it. text: path-permissions-and-troubleshooting PATH Permissions and Troubleshooting Phase 01 PATH, Permissions & Environment Troubleshooting Diagnose command lookup, EPERM, wrong versions, shell initialization, working-directory mistakes, and filesystem interference with evidence. Book 6 · Troubleshooting Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented Contents 1. Debugging ladder 7. Execution policy 2. EPERM 8. Synced folders 3. Command not recognized 9. Evidence bundle 4. Wrong versions 10. Troubleshooting matrix 5. Terminal environment inheritance 11. Professional rule 6. Wrong working directory Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6 When tooling fails, diagnose the operating-system layer first Environment failures are frustrating because they happen before application code exists. They become manageable when you classify them: command lookup, working directory, permission, version, shell initialization, or filesystem lock. 1. Read exact error text 2. Confirm current directory 3. Resolve command with Get-Command 4. Print tool version 5. Inspect PATH / environment 6. Inspect permissions and filesystem 7. Change the smallest thing Figure 1 - Environment debugging ladder - Debug from evidence. Reinstalling everything is not a diagnosis. Case 1 - EPERM in Program Files EPERM: operation not permitted, ... C:\Program Files\nodejs\... Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6 Layer: filesystem permissions. Hypothesis: a standard user is trying to modify a protected machine-wide directory. Smallest correction: install the user-owned tool under the user profile or use an approved installation route. Do not make “run everything as Administrator” your default workflow. Case 2 - command not recognized pnpm : The term 'pnpm' is not recognized... Layer: executable lookup. Run: Get-Command pnpm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue $env:Path -split ';' Test-Path "$env:APPDATA\npm\pnpm.cmd" If the file exists but PATH does not include its directory, fix lookup rather than reinstalling the package. Case 3 - wrong version node -v Get-Command node -All Multiple executables may exist. Identify which path wins and why. Version managers solve selection only if the shell loads their environment. Case 4 - command works only in one terminal Each terminal is a process with inherited environment state. A terminal opened before installation may not know about new persistent PATH entries. Close and reopen the shell before assuming installation failed. Case 5 - wrong working directory Symptoms include missing scripts, package manifests not found, Prisma config missing, or Git reporting that the directory is not a repository. Phase 01 | Page 4 of 6 Get-Location Get-ChildItem Test-Path package.json Test-Path .git Case 6 - execution policy confusion PowerShell execution policy can affect scripts. Do not globally weaken security as a reflex. First determine exactly which script is blocked and whether the tool offers a signed executable or .cmd shim. Follow organization policy on managed devices. Case 7 - synced/locked folders Cloud sync, antivirus, or corporate endpoint software can temporarily lock large dependency trees. If repeated filesystem errors occur under a synchronized Desktop/Documents directory, a dedicated user development folder can reduce interference. The evidence bundle Before asking for help, capture: Get-Location $PSVersionTable.PSVersion node -v npm -v pnpm -v git --version Get-Command node Get-Command pnpm Get-Command git This gives another engineer enough context to reason rather than guess. Troubleshooting matrix Symptom Likely layer First check Term not recognized PATH / install Get-Command Wrong version PATH / version manager Get-Command -All EPERM filesystem permissions target path and ownership No package.json working directory Get-Location Phase 01 | Page 5 of 6 Works only in old/new shell process environment reopen and compare PATH Intermittent file locks sync/AV/filesystem workspace location Professional rule Change one variable at a time. Knowledge assessment 3. Lab C - command resolution 8. Answer guide 4. Lab D - Git history 9. Exit checklist 5. Lab E - environment report 10. Next phase Phase 01 | Page 2 of 6 Phase 01 hands-on lab: prove the workstation This lab turns the phase from reading into observable skill. Complete it in an ordinary PowerShell session. If your organization prevents an installation step, record the constraint and verify everything that is permitted. Lab A - Create a clean learning workspace $DevRoot = "$HOME\Developer" New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $DevRoot -Force Set-Location $DevRoot New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "full-stack-2026-lab" -Force Set-Location "full-stack-2026-lab" Get-Location Verification The current path ends with Developer\full-stack-2026-lab . Lab B - Verify runtime and tooling fnm use 24.21.0 node -v npm -v pnpm -v git --version code --version Record the output in your notes. Do not continue until unexpected versions have an explanation. Lab C - Verify command resolution Get-Command node Get-Command npm Get-Command pnpm Get-Command git Get-Command code For every command, write one sentence explaining which directory owns the executable or shim. Phase 01 | Page 3 of 6 Lab D - Create the first Git history git init "# Full-Stack Developer 2026 - Environment Lab" | Set-Content README.md git add README.md git diff --staged git commit -m "docs: initialize environment lab" git status git log --oneline -3 Lab E - Build an environment report Create environment-report.txt using PowerShell output redirection: "Phase 01 Environment Report" | Set-Content environment-report.txt "Generated: $(Get-Date -Format o)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt "PowerShell: $($PSVersionTable.PSVersion)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt "Node: $(node -v)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt "npm: $(npm -v)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt "pnpm: $(pnpm -v)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt "Git: $(git --version)" | Add-Content environment-report.txt Get-Content environment-report.txt This is intentionally not an automated installer. Do not copy a complete solution from the book. Use if , command output, and exit . Your plan must avoid unnecessary administrator rights, preserve existing PowerShell configuration, verify PATH resolution, and produce an evidence report. Knowledge assessment 1. Why is Node treated as a project/runtime dependency rather than a permanent global assumption? 2. Why can corepack enable fail for a non-admin user even when Node itself works? 3. What does pnpm exec protect us from? 4. Why should Get-Location be one of the first commands when a project CLI cannot find its files? 5. What is the difference between Git identity and GitHub authentication? 6. Why is git diff --staged valuable before a commit? 7. What does PATH determine? 8. Why can a freshly installed command require a new terminal? Answer guide 1. Projects need reproducible runtime compatibility; version managers make selection explicit. 2. It may attempt to write shims into a protected machine-wide Node directory. 3. It resolves a tool from project dependencies, preserving the project's exact version. 4. Relative configuration and manifest discovery depends on the working directory. 5. Git identity is commit metadata; GitHub authentication authorizes access to a remote service. 6. It shows exactly what the next snapshot will contain. 7. Which executable directories the shell searches, in order. 8. The old process inherited environment values before installation changed persistent settings. subtitle: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation
text: monorepo-mental-model Monorepo Mental Model Phase 02 The Monorepo Mental Model Repository, workspace, package, application, dependency graph, and why TaskFlow uses one repository without becoming one giant process. Book 1 - Concepts Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented The Monorepo Mental Model Before we create files, we need precise language. Most monorepo confusion comes from using repository, workspace, project, application and package as if they mean the same thing. They do not. One repository, multiple projects A monorepo is one version-controlled repository that contains multiple related projects. pnpm calls the package-management layer a workspace. Git knows about files and commits; pnpm knows which package.json files belong to one dependency graph. Repository vs The .git directory makes taskflow a Git repository. pnpm-workspace.yaml makes workspace the same folder a pnpm workspace root. One folder can be both, but the responsibilities are different. Repository and workspace are overlapping concepts Git repository same root pnpm workspace declares Workspace packages contains contains apps/web apps/api Figure 1 - Git owns history; pnpm owns the multi-package dependency workspace Four words you must separate Term Meaning in this course Repository The entire taskflow folder tracked by Git. Workspace The pnpm-managed set of packages declared by pnpm-workspace.yaml. Application A deployable product such as apps/web or apps/api. Package A directory with its own package.json that participates in the workspace. An app is also a package from pnpm's perspective. Why one repository for TaskFlow? The frontend and backend are separate applications, but they evolve together. A single repository lets one commit represent a coherent system change: an API contract update, the matching frontend change, and any shared validation change can be reviewed together. • One version-control history for related full-stack changes. • One workspace lockfile for consistent dependency resolution. • One place for repository-wide scripts and policy. • Easy local linking when a real shared package appears later. • A clear boundary between deployable apps and reusable packages. Why not one giant application? A monorepo does not mean one runtime process. Next.js and NestJS will remain independent applications with different ports, build outputs, environment variables and deployment targets. They share a repository, not a process. Repository unity does not erase runtime boundaries taskflow repository contains contains apps/web - Next.js apps/api - NestJS build/deploy build/deploy frontend deployment API deployment Figure 2 - One Git history can contain multiple independently deployable applications The root is a control plane The root package.json should coordinate the workspace, not become a dumping ground for application dependencies. React belongs to the web package. NestJS belongs to the API package. A formatter or repository-wide build orchestrator may eventually belong at the root because it acts across packages. A useful ownership question Which package imports this dependency at runtime or build time? If the answer is apps/web, install it there. If the answer is apps/api, install it there. If the tool genuinely coordinates the entire repository, the root may own it. apps/ versus packages/ Directory Responsibility Examples later apps/ Deployable or runnable applications web, api, worker packages/ Reusable code/config used by more than one validators, shared types only when earned workspace package The dependency graph is the architecture you can compile Once packages depend on one another, the workspace becomes a graph. Healthy graphs point toward reusable foundations rather than creating cycles. GOOD apps/web ----> packages/validators <---- apps/api BAD apps/web ----> packages/shared ----> apps/api ----> apps/web Cycle warning pnpm can detect cyclic workspace dependencies. A cycle usually means responsibilities are mixed. Do not hide the warning; inspect which package should stop depending on which other package. Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation One lockfile, strict declarations pnpm workspaces use a shared lockfile by default. That gives the repository one exact dependency-resolution snapshot while still keeping each package honest: a package should only access dependencies it declares in its own package.json. This matters because a monorepo should make dependency boundaries more visible, not less visible. When a monorepo is the wrong tool • Projects have unrelated release cycles, ownership and security boundaries. • Teams cannot share repository access for compliance reasons. • The repository becomes a dumping ground for unrelated experiments. • Tooling complexity exceeds the coordination benefit. TaskFlow is a good fit because the web and API are parts of one product and will share contracts, versions and learning checkpoints. Mental-model checkpoint • Git repository != pnpm workspace, even when they share the same root folder. • A workspace package has its own package.json. • An application is a package with a deployable runtime responsibility. • The root coordinates; it should not absorb every dependency. • Shared packages are introduced by reuse pressure, not by folder aesthetics. text: create-the-taskflow-root-repository Create the TaskFlow Root Repository Phase 02 Create the TaskFlow Root Repository A clean PowerShell build of the Git repository, pnpm workspace root, version pins, lockfile, and structural directories. Book 2 - Hands-on foundation Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Create the TaskFlow Root Repository Now we build the repository from nothing. The lesson is intentionally small: create the root, make it a Git repository, establish package-manager metadata, and verify each file before frameworks enter the picture. Step 1 - Choose the parent directory Run repository-creation commands from the directory that should contain taskflow, not from inside another project. This avoids accidental nested repositories and confusing workspace roots. Get-Location Get-ChildItem -Force Example parent location: C:\Users\<you>\Desktop\Projects Step 2 - Create and enter the repository folder New-Item -ItemType Directory -Name taskflow Set-Location .\taskflow Get-Location Expected: the current path ends in taskflow. Do not continue until that is true. Step 3 - Initialize Git git init git status At this point Git knows the folder is a repository, but there are no committed files yet. The hidden .git directory contains repository metadata; never edit it manually during normal work. Step 4 - Create the minimal root package.json Use the editor and create package.json at the repository root: { "name": "taskflow", "version": "0.0.0", "private": true, "packageManager": "pnpm@12.4.2", "engines": { "node": ">=24.21.0 <25" }, "scripts": { "workspace:list": "pnpm list -r --depth -1" } } Why private: true? The root package exists to coordinate the repository. It is not a package we intend to publish to a registry, so marking it private protects against accidental publication. Step 5 - Pin Node for the repository Create a file named .node-version containing exactly: 24.21.0 fnm supports .node-version files. With automatic switching configured in Phase 01, entering the repository can select the course Node version without relying on memory. Step 6 - Create pnpm-workspace.yaml packages: - "apps/*" - "packages/*" pnpm requires pnpm-workspace.yaml at the workspace root. These patterns mean: any immediate child folder under apps/ or packages/ that contains a package.json can participate as a workspace package. Workspace globs describe where packages may live pnpm-workspace.yaml glob glob apps/* packages/* future match future match apps/web packages/validators Figure 1 - The workspace file declares locations; it does not create packages by itself Step 7 - Create the structural directories New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .\apps -Force New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .\packages -Force Get-ChildItem -Force Git and empty Git tracks files, not empty directories. If apps/ and packages/ are still empty at directories commit time, they will not appear in a clone. That is fine. Phase 03 and later will put real package files inside them. subtitle: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation
text: pnpm-workspaces-and-dependency-boundaries pnpm Workspaces and Dependency Boundaries Phase 02 pnpm Workspaces & Dependency Boundaries Workspace membership, the shared lockfile, strict dependencies, local package linking, and where dependencies belong. Book 3 - Workspace architecture Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented pnpm Workspaces and Dependency Boundaries The root now exists. Before we add frameworks, we need to understand how pnpm decides what belongs to the workspace and where dependencies should be installed. The workspace file is a membership rule pnpm-workspace.yaml sits at the root and defines package locations. The patterns apps/* and packages/* are intentionally shallow: they match immediate package folders such as apps/web or packages/validators without recursively pulling in arbitrary nested folders. Workspace membership requires a package A directory does not become a workspace package merely because it matches a glob. In practice it needs a package.json. This distinction explains why an empty apps/ directory does not appear in pnpm recursive listings. The shared lockfile pnpm uses a single pnpm-lock.yaml at the workspace root by default. That makes dependency resolution reviewable in one place and avoids one lockfile per application. The packages still declare their own dependencies; the lockfile simply records the resolved graph for the workspace. One workspace lockfile, separate dependency declarations pnpm-lock.yaml resolution resolution resolution content-addressed files packages/validators apps/web package.json apps/api package.json package.json pnpm store Figure 1 - The lockfile is shared; dependency ownership remains package-specific Root dependency or package dependency? Dependency type Where it belongs Example Frontend runtime/build apps/web react, next dependency Backend runtime/build apps/api @nestjs/core, fastify dependency Database dependency used by apps/api initially prisma, @prisma/client, pg API Shared library dependency the package that imports it zod inside validators, if that package exists Repository-wide developer tool root only when genuinely possible formatter/orchestrator later cross-workspace The -w flag is an explicit root decision pnpm protects workspace roots from accidental dependency installation. If you intentionally add a root dependency, use the workspace-root flag so the decision is visible: pnpm add -w -D <tool> Do not respond to an ERR_PNPM_ADDING_TO_ROOT warning by blindly adding -w. First ask whether the dependency actually belongs to the root. Package-specific installs later Once apps/web exists, a dependency can be targeted without changing directories: pnpm --filter <package-name> add <dependency> Filtering becomes powerful in larger workspaces, but directory-local installation is also fine when it is clearer. The goal is correct ownership, not clever commands. The workspace: protocol When one workspace package genuinely depends on another, pnpm supports the workspace: protocol. It guarantees the dependency resolves to a local workspace package instead of silently falling back to a registry package. { "dependencies": { "@taskflow/validators": "workspace:*" } } Not yet We do not create @taskflow/validators in Phase 02. This is a mental model for later. The package will be introduced only when both web and API have real validation reuse. Strict dependencies are a feature pnpm is intentionally strict about package access. A package should not rely on a dependency simply because another workspace package installed it. This prevents hidden dependencies that work on one machine and fail when isolated. Why we are not adding Turborepo yet Task orchestration tools become useful when several packages have real dev, build, lint and test scripts. Right now there are no applications to orchestrate. pnpm already gives us workspaces, recursive execution and filters, so introducing another tool would add vocabulary without solving a present problem. Future, not forbidden Turborepo may become useful later for task graphs, caching and coordinated builds. The teaching rule is not "never use Turbo"; it is "earn the abstraction when the repository has enough work to orchestrate." Version pins operate at different layers File/field What it communicates .node-version The exact Node version fnm should select for this repository. engines.node The Node compatibility range expected by the package. packageManager The pnpm version the repository expects. Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation File/field What it communicates pnpm-lock.yaml The exact resolved dependency graph. title: Root Scripts and Workspace Commands
subtitle: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation
text: root-scripts-and-workspace-commands Root Scripts and Workspace Commands Phase 02 Root Scripts & Workspace Commands Recursive execution, filters, command scope, and why the repository root coordinates work without becoming another application. Book 4 - Workspace operations Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Root Scripts and Workspace Commands The repository root is now a control plane. This book teaches the commands you will use to inspect and eventually orchestrate packages, while keeping Phase 02 intentionally small. Start with one script that has a job Our root package.json contains only one repository-level script: "scripts": { "workspace:list": "pnpm list -r --depth -1" } That script answers a real question: which packages does pnpm currently see in the workspace? It is useful now and remains useful later. Recursive execution The -r or --recursive flag runs a command across workspace packages. Once web and API exist, recursive commands let the root coordinate common scripts without changing directories repeatedly. pnpm -r --if-present run lint pnpm -r --if-present run typecheck pnpm -r --if-present run test Why --if-present? Different packages may not define every script at the same time while the course is evolving. --if-present lets a repository-level command skip packages that do not define the requested script instead of failing immediately. Later, when consistency matters, we may remove that leniency for specific checks. Filtering Filters target part of the workspace. After applications exist, you can run a command for a named package or dependency graph instead of the entire repository. pnpm --filter <package-name> run dev Do not memorize complicated filter syntax yet. Learn the idea: recursion means many packages; filtering means a selected subset. Three ways to reach workspace scripts root command many subset alternative -r / recursive --filter run inside package runs runs runs web api shared Figure 1 - Choose the clearest command for the scope of work Do not create future scripts before the packages exist It is tempting to add dev, build, lint, test and typecheck scripts now because we know we will eventually need them. Resist that urge. A root script should coordinate real package scripts. Phase 03 and 04 will create the applications, then the root can acquire orchestration scripts that we can actually run and verify. What the root package.json should look like now { "name": "taskflow", "version": "0.0.0", "private": true, "packageManager": "pnpm@12.4.2", "engines": { "node": ">=24.21.0 <25" }, "scripts": { "workspace:list": "pnpm list -r --depth -1" } } Future shape - not yet added { "scripts": { "dev": "pnpm -r --parallel --if-present run dev", "build": "pnpm -r --if-present run build", "lint": "pnpm -r --if-present run lint", "typecheck": "pnpm -r --if-present run typecheck", "test": "pnpm -r --if-present run test" } } This preview explains the destination. It is not an instruction to modify the Phase 02 root. We will add scripts only when there are packages behind them. Command scope is part of debugging Question Command Where am I? Get-Location What files exist, including dotfiles? Get-ChildItem -Force What packages does pnpm see? pnpm run workspace:list Which pnpm executable is running? Get-Command pnpm Which Node executable is running? Get-Command node What changed in Git? git status Checkpoint • You understand root scripts as orchestration, not application logic. • You know the difference between recursive and filtered execution. • You can explain why the root currently has only workspace:list. • You can identify the working directory before running a command. • You know that adding more tooling is not progress unless it solves an observed problem. title: Git Repository Hygiene
subtitle: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation
text: git-repository-hygiene Git Repository Hygiene Phase 02 Git Repository Hygiene Ignore rules, line-ending normalization, README discipline, lockfile policy, staged-diff review, and the first clean repository commit. Book 5 - Repository hygiene Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Git Repository Hygiene A professional repository is defined as much by what it refuses to track as by what it commits. This book establishes ignore rules, line-ending policy, documentation, the lockfile decision, and the first clean commit. Create .gitignore Use a repository-level .gitignore for files that every contributor should keep out of version control. # Dependencies node_modules/ .pnpm-store/ # Framework/build output .next/ dist/ coverage/ # Logs *.log # Environment secrets .env .env.* !.env.example # OS noise .DS_Store Thumbs.db Important Git rule Adding a path to .gitignore does not untrack a file that was already committed. Ignore rules affect intentionally untracked files. If a secret was committed, removing it from the working tree is not enough; treat it as exposed and rotate the secret. Create .gitattributes Windows and Linux use different conventional line endings. Git can normalize text in the repository so diffs do not become dominated by CRLF/LF noise. * text=auto *.sh text eol=lf *.bat text eol=crlf *.cmd text eol=crlf *.png binary *.jpg binary *.jpeg binary *.gif binary *.pdf binary Git documentation recommends text normalization and allows file-specific eol rules. We use a small policy: text is normalized automatically, Unix shell scripts stay LF, Windows batch scripts check out as CRLF, and obvious binary formats are marked binary. Git hygiene acts at different points in the file lifecycle Working tree git add Staging area git commit Commit history filters untracked normalizes text .gitignore .gitattributes Figure 1 - Ignore rules and attributes solve different problems Create README.md # TaskFlow TaskFlow is the production-style project used by the ## Course baseline - Node.js 24.21.0 - pnpm 12.4.2 - Windows-first development workflow ## Workspace - apps/ deployable applications - packages/ reusable packages introduced only when needed ## Current phase Phase 02 - Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces and Repository Foundation The README does not need to predict every future module. It records the repository purpose, baseline and current structure. It will evolve as the product evolves. Commit the lockfile pnpm-lock.yaml belongs in version control for this application repository. package.json expresses dependency intent; the lockfile records the exact resolved graph. Together they make installs reviewable and reproducible. Inspect before staging git status git diff Before git add, read the change set. This habit becomes more valuable as generated framework files appear in later phases. Stage intentionally and inspect again git add . git status git diff --staged Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation The staged diff is the exact content about to become history. If node_modules, a secret, or a generated build folder appears here, stop and correct the repository policy before committing. First repository checkpoint commit git commit -m "chore: initialize taskflow workspace" The commit message describes the outcome rather than the commands used. A future reader should understand why this point in history exists. Expected committed files .gitattributes .gitignore .node-version README.md package.json pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml Where are apps/ and They are empty, so Git may not show them. That is correct. Phase 03 and packages/? Phase 04 will create real packages inside apps/. Secret-management preview There is no .env file in Phase 02, but our ignore policy is already ready for later phases. We allow .env.example because it documents variable names without containing credentials. This is preventive engineering: establish the safe default before secrets arrive. Checkpoint • git status is clean after the checkpoint commit. • node_modules and build outputs are ignored. • .env and .env.* are ignored, but .env.example can be committed. • .gitattributes normalizes text and marks binary formats. • pnpm-lock.yaml is committed. • No empty-directory placeholder files were added only for appearance. title: Professional Monorepo Workflow and Troubleshooting
subtitle: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation
text: professional-monorepo-workflow-and-troubleshooting Professional Monorepo Workflow and Troubleshooting Phase 02 Professional Monorepo Workflow & Troubleshooting A layer-by-layer diagnostic playbook for workspace roots, dependency ownership, lockfiles, versions, line endings, Git state, and common setup failures. Book 6 - Debugging and workflow Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Professional Monorepo Workflow and Troubleshooting Most setup failures are not mysterious. They are scope errors: wrong directory, wrong executable, wrong workspace root, malformed configuration, or a file that Git is already tracking. This book gives you a repeatable diagnostic sequence. The six-question diagnostic loop Question Evidence 1. Where am I? Get-Location 2. What files does this directory Get-ChildItem -Force contain? 3. Which executable is actually Get-Command node / pnpm / git running? 4. Which versions are active? node --version / pnpm --version / git --version 5. Does pnpm see the expected pnpm run workspace:list workspace? 6. What does Git think changed? git status / git diff / git diff --staged Problem - command run from the wrong directory Symptom: pnpm cannot find the expected workspace, package.json, or script. Diagnosis: Get-Location Get-ChildItem -Force Correction: move to the directory containing the intended package.json or workspace root. Do not reinstall pnpm. Problem - ERR_PNPM_ADDING_TO_ROOT Symptom: pnpm warns that a dependency is being added to the workspace root. This warning is a decision checkpoint, not a failure to suppress. • If the dependency belongs to apps/web, install it in or target apps/web. • If it belongs to apps/api, install it there. • If it truly coordinates the entire repository, use -w deliberately. • If you cannot explain the owner, do not install it yet. Problem - multiple pnpm-lock.yaml files Symptom: a lockfile appears inside an application in addition to the workspace root. That often means a package was created or installed outside workspace awareness, or commands were run before the workspace root existed. Diagnosis: inspect the repository tree and determine which lockfile belongs to the actual workspace. Avoid deleting lockfiles blindly; understand how they were created first. Problem - Node changed after reopening PowerShell Check: node --version Get-Command node Get-Content .\.node-version If fnm automatic switching is configured, entering the repository should align Node with .node-version. If it does not, debug the fnm shell initialization from Phase 01 rather than changing the repository version pin. Problem - workspace package does not appear Check whether the folder actually contains a package.json and whether its path matches the pnpm-workspace.yaml glob. A folder name matching apps/* is not enough by itself. Problem - endless line-ending changes Symptom: Git shows files changed even though their text appears identical. Inspect .gitattributes and local Git line-ending settings. Repository attributes should provide a predictable project-level policy. Avoid solving line-ending noise by disabling normalization randomly per developer. Problem - .env is still tracked after adding it to .gitignore Git ignore rules do not stop tracking a file that is already in the index. If the file contained a real credential, rotate the credential. Then remove it from version control history/index using an appropriate remediation workflow. Do not assume adding .env to .gitignore makes an exposed secret safe. Problem - nested .git directory If git status inside a subfolder appears to show a completely different repository, someone may have run git init inside the monorepo. Inspect hidden files with: Get-ChildItem -Force -Recurse -Directory -Filter .git A normal TaskFlow course repository should have one .git directory at the root. Remove a nested repository only after confirming it is accidental and that no unique history is needed. Debug the layer that produced the symptom Observed symptom where/version json/yaml git/lockfile Check scope Check config Check state evidence evidence evidence Smallest correction Figure 1 - Evidence narrows the problem before you change anything A professional pre-commit rhythm git status git diff # edit or verify git add . git diff --staged # only then git commit -m "..." This rhythm is intentionally repetitive. It makes accidental secrets, generated output and unrelated changes visible before they become history. Volume 01 - Engineering Foundation Phase 02 operational checklist • I can identify the workspace root without guessing. • I know which package should own a dependency before installing it. • I inspect staged changes before committing. • I can distinguish a pnpm warning from a Git problem or Node-version problem. • I prefer one small evidence-based correction over deleting node_modules or reinstalling everything. text: workspace-command-reference-and-practical-patterns Workspace Command Reference and Practical Patterns Phase 02 Workspace Command Reference & Practical Patterns A compact, intent-driven reference for PowerShell orientation, pnpm workspace scope, dependency installation, recursive scripts, and Git inspection. Book 8 - Command reference Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Workspace Command Reference and Practical Patterns This reference book keeps the commands you will use most often in one place, but each command is grouped by intent rather than presented as a memorization list. The point is to choose the right scope deliberately. Repository orientation commands Intent PowerShell command What it proves Current directory Get-Location Which folder receives relative paths and local config lookup Visible and hidden items Get-ChildItem -Force Whether .git, dotfiles and root files actually exist Resolve Node executable Get-Command node Which node.exe PowerShell will launch Resolve pnpm executable Get-Command pnpm Which pnpm command PowerShell will launch Git repository state git status Tracked/untracked/staged state in the current repository Workspace inspection commands pnpm run workspace:list pnpm list -r --depth -1 pnpm root -w workspace:list is our repository script. pnpm list -r --depth -1 is the underlying recursive package view. pnpm root -w is useful later when diagnosing where the workspace-level node_modules is located. Dependency installation patterns Situation Pattern Reasoning Install in current package pnpm add Use when your shell is already inside the owning package Install in named package pnpm --filter add Useful from the root when ownership is already clear Install root dev tool pnpm add -w -D Explicitly states that the workspace root owns the tool Local workspace dependency workspace:* in package.json Guarantees local workspace resolution instead of registry fallback Recursive script patterns - for later phases pnpm -r --if-present run lint pnpm -r --if-present run typecheck pnpm -r --if-present run test pnpm -r --parallel --if-present run dev These become useful after packages define the corresponding scripts. --parallel makes sense for long-running development servers that should run together; build-like tasks often benefit from dependency-aware ordering instead. Git inspection patterns git status git diff git add <path> git diff --staged git restore --staged <path> git commit -m "message" The sequence matters more than the individual commands. Inspect -> stage intentionally -> inspect the staged snapshot -> commit. This is the workflow that protects the repository from accidental noise and secrets. The command-selection loop Orient where/which package Decide scope root/filter/local Run command next decision status/output Verify result Figure 1 - A professional workflow starts with scope, not with the command itself Commands we intentionally postpone • Framework generators - introduced only when the relevant app phase begins. • Turbo task graph commands - postponed until there are several real scripts worth orchestrating. • Prisma commands - database architecture begins in Volume 03, with Prisma 7.9.1 locked. • Docker and deployment commands - postponed until the application works locally and is testable. Quick reference checklist Before any workspace command, answer three questions: Where am I? Which package owns this change? How will I verify the result? If you cannot answer those questions, the command is premature. title: Repository Design Decisions and Anti Patterns
subtitle: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation
text: repository-design-decisions-and-anti-patterns Repository Design Decisions and Anti Patterns Phase 02 Repository Design Decisions & Anti-Patterns Why the TaskFlow root stays boring, which abstractions we rejected, and the evidence that would justify adding them later. Book 9 - Architecture decisions Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Repository Design Decisions and Anti-Patterns The strongest repository architecture is usually the one with the fewest unexplained moving parts. This book records the decisions Phase 02 made, the alternatives we rejected, and the signals that would justify changing those decisions later. Decision 1 - One monorepo for web and API Choice Why now Revisit when... One Git repository The applications form one product and access, compliance, ownership or change together release boundaries become truly independent pnpm workspace Built-in multi-package management already a future orchestrator must solve solves our current problem measurable task-graph/caching pain One shared lockfile Consistent resolution and easier review almost never for this single-product workspace without a concrete reason Decision 2 - Keep the root boring The root is policy and orchestration. A root package that accumulates React, NestJS, database libraries and application utilities has erased the very ownership boundaries the monorepo was meant to clarify. Smell If you cannot tell whether a dependency is frontend, backend, or repository tooling because everything is installed at the root, the package boundaries are already failing. Decision 3 - Do not create packages before reuse exists A folder named shared is not architecture. A shared package earns its existence when it owns one coherent responsibility that at least two consumers need and when keeping duplicate implementations would create real drift or risk. Good future package candidate A validators package can become reasonable after web and API both need the same task input schema and we intentionally want one authoritative contract. Weak package candidate A utils package that collects unrelated date helpers, string functions, API wrappers and business rules becomes a dependency magnet. Prefer colocating helpers with the feature or responsibility they support until a coherent reusable package emerges. Anti-pattern - the prebuilt enterprise tree packages/ common/ core/ domain/ infrastructure/ shared/ utils/ types/ config/ The problem is not the names themselves. The problem is creating them before the system contains responsibilities that require those boundaries. Empty architecture makes navigation harder while teaching nothing about why the abstraction exists. Anti-pattern - framework dependencies at root taskflow/package.json react next @nestjs/core prisma @prisma/client This makes the root look convenient while hiding which app truly depends on each technology. The correct default is package ownership: frontend libraries in apps/web, backend/database libraries in apps/api initially. Anti-pattern - multiple nested repositories Running git init inside apps/web or apps/api creates independent histories unless intentionally using submodules or another advanced strategy. That would undermine the course monorepo model. One .git directory at taskflow/ is the expected state. Anti-pattern - generated files without review Framework generators are useful, but generated output is still your codebase. Starting in Phase 03, every generator step must be followed by tree inspection and Git diff review before the generated code is accepted. How architecture should evolve Observed need problem first Smallest option implement/test Verify benefit no clear gain repeated pressure Keep simple Earn abstraction Figure 1 - Abstractions are responses to evidence, not decorations chosen in advance Decision record for future phases • Phase 03 creates apps/web and lets Next.js own frontend dependencies. • Phase 04 creates apps/api and lets NestJS/Fastify own backend dependencies. • Prisma remains inside apps/api when introduced; no packages/db is created by default. • A shared validators package is considered only when real cross-app schema reuse appears. • Turborepo is considered only when pnpm orchestration becomes measurably insufficient. • Deployment remains independent per app even though source history is shared. Engineering checkpoint A clean Phase 02 repository is intentionally unimpressive to look at. That is a strength. Every file at the root has a concrete responsibility, and there is almost nothing to delete. The sophistication will come from working software and earned boundaries, not from an elaborate empty tree. Debugging Workshop — Phase 02: Monorepo, pnpm Workspaces & Repository Foundation Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk Repository root -> pnpm-workspace.yaml -> apps/* -> packages/* -> workspace dependencies -> root scripts -> Turbo/task graph Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Installing app-only dependencies at workspace root Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.
