text: app-router-mental-model App Router Mental Model Phase 03 The App Router Mental Model Understand route segments, pages, layouts, special files, and the rendered route tree before building more UI. Book 2 - Routing concepts Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented The App Router Mental Model The App Router is not a list of magic filenames. It is a file-system model that turns directories into route segments and special files into pieces of the rendered route tree. Routes come from folders src/app/ |-- layout.tsx -> shared root layout |-- page.tsx -> / |-- projects/ | `-- page.tsx -> /projects `-- settings/ `-- page.tsx -> /settings A folder becomes a URL segment when a page exists beneath it. The route is not created by the folder name alone; page.tsx provides the route UI. Folders shape the route tree app root wraps route segment layout.tsx page.tsx -> / projects/ route page.tsx -> /projects Figure 1 - The filesystem describes both URL segments and layout composition page.tsx A page is the UI exposed at a route. In this course, pages should usually compose feature components rather than contain every visual element and behavior inline. layout.tsx A layout wraps child route content and persists across navigation within its segment. The root layout is required and owns the html/body shell. Nested layouts let areas share navigation or framing without duplicating markup. Why layouts matter beyond convenience • They encode shared UI structure into the route hierarchy. • They reduce duplicated navigation and shell markup. • They create stable boundaries where state can be preserved across navigation. • They make route ownership visible from the filesystem. Special files we will meet File Purpose in the mental model page.tsx Route UI layout.tsx Persistent shared UI around descendants loading.tsx Route-segment pending UI error.tsx Error boundary UI for a segment; requires client behavior not-found.tsx Not-found UI template.tsx Layout-like wrapper that remounts on navigation; use only when needed route.ts HTTP route handler; not our primary business API in this course Important boundary Next.js route handlers exist, but TaskFlow will use NestJS for the authoritative application API. We will not create duplicate business logic in route.ts just because the framework can host server code. Route groups and private folders Later, parentheses can group routes without adding URL segments, and underscore-prefixed private folders can organize implementation details without becoming routes. Do not introduce these until the file tree needs them. Dynamic routes - concept preview src/app/projects/[projectId]/page.tsx URL: /projects/42 projectId: "42" The brackets represent a dynamic segment. We will use them later when projects and tasks come from the API. Phase 03 only needs the mental model. Rendering tree versus URL The URL tells you which route segments are active. The rendered tree combines each active layout with the leaf page. This is why layout placement is an architectural choice, not only a styling decision. A route renders through nested layout layers RootLayout children Dashboard layout children Projects page Figure 2 - Each active layout contributes persistent structure around the leaf page Checkpoint questions • What makes /projects exist? text: server-and-client-components Server and Client Components Phase 03 Server and Client Components Learn the server/browser network boundary, choose Client Components for the right reasons, and avoid turning the entire frontend into a client island. Book 3 - Rendering boundary Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Server Components and Client Components The most important Next.js concept in Phase 03 is not routing. It is understanding that your component tree can cross a network boundary. Next.js uses Server Components by default in the App Router; Client Components are opt-in islands for browser capabilities and interaction. The network boundary inside a React component tree SERVER Server Components RSC payload network compose BROWSER Client Components render hydrate/interact rendered output interactive JS Figure 1 - Server and browser environments have different capabilities; use client marks where browser-side JavaScript is needed Server Component by default A component file under the App Router is a Server Component unless a Client Component boundary applies. This lets static and server-rendered UI avoid sending unnecessary component JavaScript to the browser. Good Server Component jobs • Compose mostly non-interactive UI. • Read server-side data later without exposing secrets to the browser. • Perform server-only work when appropriate. • Keep large dependencies or logic off the client bundle when no browser interaction is required. What makes a Client Component necessary? Use a Client Component when the component needs browser-only capabilities or interactive React state/effects. Need Client? Reason Static heading No No browser state or event needed Button with onClick Yes Event handler executes in browser useState/useEffect Yes Client hooks require browser-side React window/localStorage Yes Browser APIs do not exist on the server Pure presentational card Usually no Can remain server-rendered Later API server-state with TanStack Yes at Query client lives in browser context Query provider/query boundary The use client directive "use client"; import { useState } from "react"; export function DemoCounter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( <button onClick={() => setCount((value) => value + 1)}> Count: {count} </button> ); } The directive marks a client module boundary. It does not mean every component in the entire application must become client-rendered. Keep the boundary small A common beginner response to a hook error is to put "use client" at the top of the root layout. That makes the error disappear by widening the client boundary, but it throws away a core architectural advantage. Move only the interactive portion behind a client boundary. Prefer a small client island over a client application shell DashboardLayout Server compose Nav Server interactive island ThemeToggle Client children ProjectsPage Server Figure 2 - Only the component that needs browser interaction crosses the client boundary Serialization boundary Data passed from a Server Component into a Client Component must be serializable across the server/client boundary. This is another clue that the boundary is architectural, not just a syntax marker. Do not confuse rendering location with API architecture Server Components can fetch directly from a data source in some applications. TaskFlow deliberately routes authoritative business data through NestJS later so business rules live in one backend. The fact that Next.js can access server resources does not require us to put domain logic there. Mini exercise Create an interactive small button or disclosure control as a Client Component and import it into a Server Component page. Then explain why the page itself did not need use client. Checkpoint • Server Component is the default in the App Router. • Client Components are for interaction/browser APIs/client hooks. title: Routing Loading and Errors
subtitle: Next.js Fundamentals
text:
routing-loading-and-errors Routing Loading and Errors Phase 03 Routing, Loading and Error States Build navigation that accounts for shared layout, pending UI, failures, and not-found states instead of only the happy path. Book 4 - Navigation states Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Routing, Navigation, Loading, Errors and 404s A production frontend is not only successful page rendering. Users navigate, wait, hit missing resources, and encounter failures. The App Router gives these states explicit places in the route tree. Navigation with Link import Link from "next/link"; Projects Use Next.js Link for internal application navigation. It integrates with client-side navigation and prefetching behavior instead of forcing a full browser document request for every route transition. A simple TaskFlow route map / /projects /settings src/app/ |-- page.tsx |-- projects/page.tsx `-- settings/page.tsx Shared navigation belongs in layout structure If Home, Projects, and Settings share the same top navigation, render that navigation from a layout rather than copy it into every page. A component handles reusable markup; a layout controls where that reusable markup participates in routing. loading.tsx - pending UI A loading file provides route-segment fallback UI while content below the segment is waiting. It works with streaming and Suspense semantics. Use it to communicate progress, not to hide slow architecture indefinitely. export default function Loading() { return

Loading projects...

; } error.tsx - recoverable route UI An error boundary lets a route segment show fallback UI when a descendant throws during rendering. Error components need client-side behavior because reset/retry interaction happens in the browser. "use client"; export default function ErrorView({ reset }: { reset: () => void }) { return (

Something went wrong

); } Do not swallow errors An error boundary is presentation for failure, not permission to ignore the root cause. Production logging/observability enters later, but even now the developer should inspect the terminal and browser console. not-found.tsx Use a not-found UI for missing route resources. Later, a project detail page can call notFound() when the API says the project does not exist. This is different from a server crash or validation error. text: styling-assets-and-accessibility Styling Assets and Accessibility Phase 03 Styling, Assets and Accessibility Use CSS Modules and global CSS with clear ownership, then build an accessible application shell with semantic HTML and useful metadata. Book 5 - UI foundations Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Styling, Assets, Metadata and Accessibility TaskFlow needs enough design to feel like an application, but Phase 03 avoids turning into a CSS framework course. We use global CSS for global rules and CSS Modules for component-scoped styles. Global CSS has a global responsibility Use src/app/globals.css for document-wide rules such as box sizing, base body typography, background, and CSS variables. Avoid placing page-specific selectors there merely because it is convenient. CSS Modules for local ownership /* project-card.module.css */ .card { border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 12px; padding: 1rem; } /* project-card.tsx */ import styles from "./project-card.module.css"; export function ProjectCard() { return <article className={styles.card}>...</article>; } The filename communicates that the CSS is scoped to the component/module rather than intended as a site-wide API. A styling ownership rule Question Preferred home Does every page need it? globals.css or shared design token Does one component own it? Component CSS Module Is it an inline state-dependent value? Occasional style prop, used deliberately Is it a future design-system primitive? Earn a shared component/package when repeated patterns justify it Public assets Files in public/ are served from the site root. public/logo.svg is addressed as /logo.svg. Keep public for static assets, not application source code. Images Next.js provides Image for image optimization and layout behavior. In this early shell, learn the API but do not add images unless they communicate product context. Decorative images are not a requirement for good UI. Metadata export const metadata = { title: "TaskFlow", description: "Project and task management for focused teams", }; Metadata belongs with the route/layout structure because it describes the document the framework is producing. Later phases can refine per-route metadata. Semantic HTML first UI intent Prefer Primary site navigation nav Page content main Independent card/content item article when semantically appropriate Action button Navigation a / Link Section heading Correct heading level rather than styled div Accessibility is architecture, not polish • Use real buttons for actions so keyboard behavior exists automatically. • Use visible focus states rather than removing outlines. • Provide labels for controls and meaningful alt text for informative images. • Keep heading hierarchy meaningful. • Use aria-live sparingly for important asynchronous status updates. • Test keyboard navigation while the interface is still small. Responsive shell without a CSS framework Use modern CSS layout primitives directly. The goal is to understand the browser before adding another vocabulary. The TaskFlow shell can use a responsive grid or flex layout, sensible max width, and media queries where necessary. Design target TaskFlow -------------------------------------------------- Home Projects Settings Your work Organize projects and keep tasks moving. [ Active Projects ] [ Tasks Due ] [ Completed ] Recent projects [ Website refresh ] [ Inventory rollout ] The interface should feel intentional but remain small enough that routing and rendering concepts are visible. Checkpoint • Global styles stay global. • Component styles are locally owned through CSS Modules. • Public assets are addressed from /. • Semantic elements are chosen by meaning rather than appearance. • Keyboard and focus behavior are checked before the phase is complete. title: Environment DevTools and Debugging
subtitle: Next.js Fundamentals
text: environment-devtools-and-debugging Environment DevTools and Debugging Phase 03 Environment, DevTools and Debugging Learn frontend environment-variable boundaries, browser/terminal evidence, and a systematic Next.js debugging loop. Book 6 - Diagnostics Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Environment Variables, DevTools and Next.js Debugging Frontend bugs often sit at a boundary: server versus browser, build time versus runtime, route versus component, or workspace root versus package directory. Phase 03 teaches how to locate the failing layer before editing code. Environment variable boundary By default, environment variables are server-only. A variable exposed to browser JavaScript requires the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix. That prefix is a publication decision, not a naming style. Example Browser-visible? Use API_INTERNAL_SECRET No Never place secrets in frontend browser code DATABASE_URL No Later belongs to API/backend environment, not apps/web NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL Yes Later tells browser where public API is NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME Yes Harmless public configuration if needed Security rule If a value must remain secret, it must never depend on NEXT_PUBLIC_ protection. Anything delivered to browser JavaScript is inspectable by the user. Where errors appear Symptom First place to look Build/type error Terminal running next dev/build Client runtime error Browser console and Next error overlay Failed network request later Browser Network tab Server Component exception Terminal plus rendered error boundary Wrong route/404 Route tree and browser URL CSS not applied DOM class name, imported module, browser styles panel A layered debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure. 2. Identify the environment: terminal/server or browser/client. 3. Read the first useful error, not only the last stack frame. 4. Confirm the current route and file path. 5. Reduce the failing component or change. 6. Make the smallest correction. 7. Re-run the same verification. 8. Run lint/type/build before declaring victory. Common error: hook in Server Component Symptom: useState/useEffect or event-handler related error in a Server Component. Diagnosis: the component needs browser interactivity. Correction: move only the interactive portion into a Client Component; do not automatically convert the root layout. Common error: module not found Check the import alias, file casing, relative path, and whether the dependency belongs to apps/web. On Windows, case mistakes may remain hidden locally and fail on a case-sensitive production filesystem. Common error: command ran in wrong place Get-Location Get-Content .\package.json pnpm --filter web dev If you are inside apps/web, pnpm dev is fine. If you are at taskflow root, filter to the package. Make the location explicit rather than guessing. Common error: port 3000 already used Do not kill random processes. Identify which process owns the port, determine whether another dev server is already running, and either reuse/stop it intentionally or choose a different port. Production build is a different verification Fast Refresh success does not prove the application is production-buildable. At the phase exit, run the web package build from the workspace and fix type/lint/build failures before continuing. Browser DevTools habits • Elements: inspect actual DOM and computed styles. • Console: client errors and logs. • Network: later inspect API requests, status codes and timing. • Application/Storage: later inspect browser-managed storage only when the feature actually uses it. • Accessibility tree where available: verify semantic output instead of visual appearance alone. Debug by locating the failing boundary first Symptom locate Which environment? inspect Collect evidence hypothesis Small fix test Repeat verification Figure 1 - A disciplined loop is faster than rewriting code until the error disappears Checkpoint • You can explain why NEXT_PUBLIC_ means browser-visible. • You know whether to inspect terminal or browser first for a given symptom. • You can diagnose Server/Client boundary errors without widening use client unnecessarily. • You use the production build as a phase gate. text: exercises-and-phase-exit Exercises and Phase Exit Phase 03 Exercises and Phase Exit Practice Next.js independently, debug realistic failures, pass the architecture oral exam, and verify readiness for NestJS. Book 8 - Exercises Course baseline: September 17, 2026 - Windows-first - Project-driven - Production-oriented Exercises, Architecture Checks and Phase Exit The phase is complete only when you can reproduce the ideas without following every line. These exercises move from guided repetition toward independent engineering decisions. Level 1 - Follow • Create the /projects and /settings routes from memory. • Add primary navigation in the root layout using Link. • Create one CSS Module and apply it to a project card. • Run dev, lint and build from the workspace root using a filter. Level 2 - Modify • Add an /about route without changing the root layout API. • Add a descriptive empty state to /projects when the sample array is empty. • Improve visible keyboard focus for navigation links. • Add metadata appropriate for the application. Level 3 - Implement Create a small ProjectStatusFilter Client Component that switches between All, Active and Planning for static sample projects. Keep the page as a Server Component if possible. Explain what data had to move into the client island and why. Level 4 - Engineer Design a route structure for the future TaskFlow product without implementing backend data. Include dashboard, projects, a future project-detail route, and settings. Decide where a dashboard layout would live, which sections should share navigation, and where you would avoid route groups until the need is real. Debugging scenarios Scenario Your diagnosis should start with useState error in page.tsx Server/Client boundary; isolate interactive component /projects is 404 Filesystem route structure and page.tsx location CSS class undefined CSS Module import/name mismatch pnpm --filter web says no package matched Check apps/web package name and workspace membership Works in dev, fails build Read build/type error; do not assume Fast Refresh proved correctness Secret appears in browser bundle Treat as exposure; remove public prefix and redesign ownership Architecture oral exam • Why can Next.js be called full-stack while this course still uses NestJS? • What is the difference between a route layout and a reusable UI component? • Why are Server Components the default? • What capabilities force a Client Component? • Why is use client at the root layout usually a poor first fix? • Why is NEXT_PUBLIC_ a security boundary? • Why do we build with static data before inventing an API that does not exist yet? Expected answers - concise • Next.js vs NestJS: Next.js has server capabilities, but TaskFlow centralizes authoritative domain rules in NestJS so there is one business API. • Layout vs component: a layout participates in the route tree and persists around descendant routes; a component is reusable UI independent of route semantics. • Server default: non-interactive UI can render without shipping component JavaScript to the browser and can use server capabilities. • Client requirement: browser event handlers, client hooks, browser APIs, or client-only libraries. • NEXT_PUBLIC_: it declares that a value may be included in browser-visible code; therefore secrets never belong there. text: guided-build-lab Guided Build Lab Purpose Build the Next.js application shell while understanding App Router routing, layouts, Server Components, Client Components, environment boundaries, and rendering behavior. Guided Build Lab — Phase 03: Next.js Fundamentals Purpose Build the Next.js application shell while understanding App Router routing, layouts, Server Components, Client Components, environment boundaries, and rendering behavior. Deliverable A navigable TaskFlow web shell with route groups/layouts, server-first composition, selective client interactivity, and verified environment handling. Before you touch the code Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything. Architecture trace Route request -> App Router match -> layout/page Server Component -> optional server fetch -> Client Component island -> browser interaction Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization. Step 1 — Generate the web app in the monorepo and verify the development server from the correct workspace. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption. Step 2 — Create nested routes and a shared layout, then predict which layouts persist across navigation. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption. Step 3 — Build one component as a Server Component and identify exactly why it can remain server-only. Do the smallest version of this step first. Debugging Workshop — Phase 03: Next.js Fundamentals Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk Route request -> App Router match -> layout/page Server Component -> optional server fetch -> Client Component island -> browser interaction Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Adding 'use client' too high in the tree Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Book 2 of Phase 04 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04 Bootstrap and the Fastify Adapter NestJS and Fastify solve different problems Layer What it contributes NestJS Modules, dependency injection, controllers, providers, guards, pipes, interceptors and application structure. Fastify The concrete HTTP server/runtime that accepts requests and sends responses. @nestjs/platform-fastify The adapter that lets Nest run on Fastify while keeping Nest abstractions. main.ts application entry point NestFactory.create(...) starts Nest runtime FastifyAdapter selects HTTP platform AppModule root dependency graph listen(4000) opens local HTTP port Figure - Bootstrap flow: main.ts chooses the platform, provides the root module, then starts listening. Step 1 - Install the Nest Fastify platform adapter From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm add @nestjs/platform-fastify@12.0.3 pnpm remove @nestjs/platform-express The course chooses Fastify intentionally, so keeping the Express platform package after the migration would create ambiguity. Nest remains the application framework; only the concrete HTTP platform changes. Fastify version policy The course is locked to Fastify 5.x. The September 17, 2026 stable patch reference is 5.12.5. Fastify 6 is still an alpha line and is not used in this course. Step 2 - Change main.ts apps/api/src/main.ts import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core'; import { FastifyAdapter, NestFastifyApplication, } from '@nestjs/platform-fastify'; import { AppModule } from './app.module.js'; async function bootstrap() { FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04 Bootstrap and the Fastify Adapter const app = await NestFactory.create<NestFastifyApplication>( AppModule, new FastifyAdapter(), ); const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 4000); await app.listen(port, '127.0.0.1'); } void bootstrap(); Read the file as an architectural sentence ● NestFactory.create starts the Nest runtime. ● AppModule is the root of the dependency graph. ● FastifyAdapter selects Fastify as the HTTP platform implementation. ● NestFastifyApplication gives TypeScript the correct application type for this platform. ● listen opens the local port only after Nest has created and wired the application graph. Why port 4000? The frontend already uses the common Next.js development port 3000. The backend uses 4000 so both applications can run simultaneously without fighting for the same port. In a second PowerShell window (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/' -UseBasicParsing).Content Checkpoint B NestJS boots successfully using Fastify, and an HTTP request reaches the generated controller. The controller and service do not become available merely because their files exist; the module registers them into the graph. Book 4 of Phase 04 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04 Dependency Injection and the Application Graph Dependency injection is object wiring The phrase dependency injection can sound abstract, but the practical question is simple: when HealthController needs HealthService, who creates the service instance and gives it to the controller? In Nest, the IoC container performs that wiring based on the providers registered in modules. HealthController HealthService declares dependency @Injectable provider constructor type metadata Nest IoC Container creates + wires instances Figure - Dependency injection: the controller asks for a service; Nest resolves and supplies the registered provider. Constructor injection health.controller.ts - the consumer @Controller('health') export class HealthController { constructor(private readonly healthService: HealthService) {} } health.service.ts - the provider @Injectable() export class HealthService { getStatus() { return { status: 'ok' }; } } health.module.ts - the registration @Module({ controllers: [HealthController], providers: [HealthService], }) export class HealthModule {} These three snippets form one relationship: consumer, dependency, registration. If any side is missing, Nest cannot complete the graph. What Nest resolves at startup 1 Read AppModule and all imported modules. 2 Collect controller/provider metadata. 3 Create provider instances according to their registration and scope. 4 Inspect constructor dependencies and resolve each required provider. 5 Instantiate controllers with their dependencies already supplied. 6 Fail startup if the graph cannot be resolved. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04 Dependency Injection and the Application Graph Important default Providers are generally singleton-scoped by default for the application lifecycle. Request scope exists, but using it everywhere would increase complexity and overhead. This phase stays with the default scope. Classic failure: Nest cannot resolve dependencies Representative startup error Nest can't resolve dependencies of the HealthController (?). Please make sure that the argument HealthService ... is av Do not reinstall Nest. Read the dependency graph. Is HealthService decorated with @Injectable()? Is it listed in providers? Is it exported/imported if consumed across module boundaries? Is the constructor asking for a runtime-resolvable class/token? Interfaces are erased at runtime TypeScript interfaces do not exist after compilation. Nest cannot inject an interface by type alone. Later, when we need abstraction tokens, we will use explicit injection tokens. Do not introduce tokens early merely to imitate enterprise architecture. Book 5 of Phase 04 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04 Request Lifecycle, Routes and Decorators Follow one request instead of memorizing decorators HTTP Client browser / curl / API tool Fastify accepts socket + HTTP request Nest Platform Adapter maps Fastify into Nest abstractions Controller Route matches method + path Provider / Service performs application work Response serialized back to HTTP client Figure - Phase 04 request lifecycle. Guards, pipes, interceptors, validation and database access are intentionally postponed to later phases. Controller decorators form an HTTP routing boundary apps/api/src/health/health.controller.ts import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common'; import { HealthService } from './health.service.js'; @Controller('health') export class HealthController { constructor(private readonly healthService: HealthService) {} @Get() getHealth() { return this.healthService.getStatus(); } } @Controller('health') establishes the route prefix. @Get() registers an HTTP GET handler at that prefix. The method name is for your code; the decorators determine the HTTP route. Method and path are a pair Decorator Example route Meaning @Get() GET /health Read a resource/status. @Post() POST /todos Create - introduced later. @Patch(':id') PATCH /todos/:id Partial update - introduced later. @Delete(':id') DELETE /todos/:id Delete - introduced later. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04 Request Lifecycle, Routes and Decorators Phase 05 will teach HTTP and REST in depth. Here we only need enough routing knowledge to understand how a request reaches a controller. Return values become HTTP responses Controller/service return value return { status: 'ok', service: 'taskflow-api', }; Nest serializes ordinary JavaScript objects to JSON through the platform integration. Later phases add explicit status handling, DTO validation, exception filters and richer response behavior. Avoid solving future problems in Phase 04. Boundary discipline A controller should remain an HTTP boundary. Once business behavior becomes meaningful, delegate it to a service instead of putting database queries and rules directly inside route methods. What is NOT in this lifecycle yet ● No validation pipe. ● No authentication guard. ● No authorization policy. ● No Prisma query. ● No interceptor-based logging architecture. ● No global exception strategy. Those omissions are intentional. A clean mental model is easier to extend than a crowded diagram full of tools the learner has not earned yet. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. text: independent-challenge Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge Mission Rebuild the capability of Phase 04 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes? Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — NestJS + Fastify Fundamentals Mission Rebuild the capability of Phase 04 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes? Required outcome Build a NestJS 12 API on Fastify and understand modules, controllers, providers, dependency injection, configuration, and request lifecycle. Required artifact A modular API with health endpoint and a small feature module whose controller and service responsibilities are separate. Constraints • Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch. • Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt. • Keep changes scoped to the capability. • Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases. • Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable. Acceptance criteria • Can explain provider resolution. • Can create a feature module from scratch. • Can distinguish adapter and framework responsibilities. • Can debug a dependency injection error. Independent build sequence 1. Generate the API workspace and replace the default HTTP adapter with Fastify deliberately. 2. Create a HealthModule with controller and service instead of putting everything in AppController. 3. Inject the service through the constructor and explain how Nest resolves it. 4. Add configuration through Nest Config rather than reading process.env everywhere. 5. Trace one request with logs through bootstrap, controller, and service. 6. Break provider registration intentionally, read the dependency-resolution error, and repair the module graph. Self-review Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence. Stretch challenge Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Book 1 of Phase 05 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Mental Model HTTP is a contract, not a framework feature NestJS did not invent GET, status 200 or JSON. Next.js will not invent them either. Both applications participate in an HTTP contract defined independently of either framework. That separation is useful: if you later replace Next.js with a mobile app, or NestJS with another backend, the HTTP concepts remain recognizable. HTTP is the contract between independent programs. REQUEST HTTP Client TaskFlow API PowerShell / browser / later Next.js NestJS + Fastify RESPONSE method + target + headers + optional body status + headers + optional body Figure - HTTP request/response exchange. Phase 05 studies the protocol before Phase 06 introduces a browser cross-origin call. The roles Role Meaning in TaskFlow Client A program that initiates a request. In this phase: PowerShell. Later: Next.js/browser. Server The TaskFlow NestJS + Fastify process listening on port 4000. Resource The thing addressed by the request, such as the Todo collection or a specific Todo. Representation A transferable form of resource state, commonly JSON in our API. Contract The agreed method, URL, headers, body shape, status and response shape. One request has one primary direction The client decides when to initiate an ordinary HTTP request. The server receives it, processes it, and sends a response. This is different from realtime push architectures, which appear much later. Understanding ordinary request/response behavior first makes later realtime technology easier to justify. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Mental Model Resource identity and request semantics are separate Todo Collection /todos Todo 1 Todo 2 Todo 3 /todos/1 /todos/2 /todos/3 URLs identify resources. HTTP methods express what the client asks to do with them. Figure - REST-oriented resource modeling separates resource identity from method semantics. The URL identifies what the request targets. The HTTP method contributes what kind of operation the client is requesting. This is why GET /todos/3 and DELETE /todos/3 can target the same resource while expressing different semantics. Mental model Think: resource + method + representation + outcome. Do not think: "controller function name somehow became an API." The controller is only the server-side implementation of a protocol contract. HTTP version vs HTTP semantics HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ in framing, multiplexing and transport behavior. For application development, the course first focuses on the shared semantics: methods, target URIs, fields/headers, representations and status codes. That knowledge transfers across protocol versions. What the server can and cannot infer ● A server receives the request the client actually sent, not the request the developer intended to send. ● If the path is wrong, routing may fail even if the JSON body is perfect. ● If the method is wrong, the correct path may still not match the intended handler. ● If JSON is malformed or the content type is incorrect, the server may not obtain the expected representation. ● If a request succeeds but the status code is misleading, client code can still behave incorrectly. A strong API contract reduces coupling between those clients and the backend implementation. Official source notes Primary protocol reference: RFC 9110 - HTTP Semantics (RFC Editor). Book 2 of Phase 05 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Request and Response Anatomy Anatomy of an HTTP request POST /todos HTTP/1.1 request line: method + target + protocol Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json headers: metadata about the request {"title":"Learn HTTP"} body: representation sent to the server Figure - Simplified HTTP request anatomy. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode messages differently on the wire, but the semantic concepts remain method, target, headers and content. Method The method communicates the request semantics. GET asks for a representation; POST commonly submits content for processing or creation; PUT requests replacement; PATCH requests a partial modification; DELETE requests removal. Target The request target identifies the addressed resource. In TaskFlow, /todos identifies the collection while /todos/3 identifies one member. Query parameters can refine a request later, such as /todos?completed=true. Headers Header Why it matters Content-Type: application/json Describes the media type of request content being sent. Accept: application/json Expresses a representation preference for the response. Authorization: Bearer ... Carries credentials later when authentication is introduced. Cache-Control Influences caching behavior when relevant. Body / content A request may carry content. For a Todo creation request, JSON can represent the new data. GET normally retrieves data and should not depend on a request body for ordinary API design. JSON is a representation format, not HTTP itself HTTP can carry many media types. TaskFlow uses JSON because it maps naturally to JavaScript data and is widely supported. The protocol and the representation format remain separate concepts. Example JSON representation FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Request and Response Anatomy { "title": "Learn HTTP", "completed": false } Anatomy of an HTTP response HTTP/1.1 201 Created status line: protocol + status code + reason phrase Content-Type: application/json Location: /todos/3 response headers: metadata and controls {"id":3,"title":"Learn HTTP","completed":false} response body: selected representation Figure - Simplified HTTP response anatomy. The status code is part of the contract, not decoration around JSON. The status code summarizes the outcome at the protocol level. Headers provide metadata or controls. The response content carries a representation when one is appropriate. A well-designed client uses all three instead of parsing a JSON message string to guess whether the request succeeded. Representation vs database row Later, Prisma returns database records, but an API response does not have to expose a database row exactly as stored. A representation is part of the API contract. This distinction becomes important when hiding internal fields, combining data or versioning an API. Boundary rule Do not let the fact that JavaScript objects serialize easily to JSON trick you into thinking every internal object should automatically become a public API response. Public representations are contracts. Official source notes Primary protocol reference: RFC 9110 - HTTP Semantics (RFC Editor). text: http-methods-status-codes-and-idempotency HTTP Methods Status Codes and Idempotency FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Methods, Status Codes and Idempotency VOLUME 02 - FRONTEND + BACKEND FOUNDATIONS HTTP Methods, Status Codes and Idempotency Choose protocol semantics deliberately instead of by habit HTTP is the contract between independent programs. REQUEST HTTP Client TaskFlow API PowerShell / browser / later Next.js NestJS + Fastify RESPONSE method + target + headers + optional body status + headers + optional body Figure - HTTP request/response exchange. Book 3 of Phase 05 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Methods, Status Codes and Idempotency Method semantics matter GET read safe + idempotent POST create/action normally not idempotent PUT replace idempotent PATCH partial change not guaranteed idempotent DELETE remove idempotent semantics Figure - Common method semantics. Safe and idempotent are protocol properties; they are not synonyms for "nothing happened" or "same response". RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as safe methods. Safe means the client is not requesting a state-changing action. The server may still log the request or perform incidental work. Idempotent means multiple identical requests have the same intended effect on the server as one request. Safe methods, PUT and DELETE are defined as idempotent. Safe is not the same as "zero side effects" Logging a GET request changes a log file, but that does not make GET unsafe in HTTP semantics because the client did not request that state change. The distinction is about the requested action. Idempotent is not the same as "same response" DELETE /todos/3 might return 204 the first time and 404 the second time. Those responses differ, yet the intended resource-removal effect after repeated identical requests is still the same: Todo 3 is absent. Common TaskFlow method choices Operation Method Route Reasoning List Todos GET /todos Read collection representation. Read Todo GET /todos/:id Read one identified resource. Create Todo POST /todos Server assigns a new member identity. Replace Todo PUT /todos/:id Full replacement semantics; not used in our first implementation. Modify Todo PATCH /todos/:id Partial update of selected fields. Delete Todo DELETE /todos/:id Request removal of identified resource. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Methods, Status Codes and Idempotency Status code classes 1xx Information request processing / protocol info 2xx Success request understood and handled 3xx Redirection further action or alternate representation 4xx Client-side request problem request cannot be fulfilled as sent 5xx Server-side failure server failed while handling a valid-looking request Figure - HTTP status codes are grouped by first digit. Application APIs mostly use 2xx, 4xx and 5xx in ordinary workflows. Status codes used in this phase Code Meaning in TaskFlow Typical use 200 OK Successful request with a response representation. GET and PATCH here. 201 Created A new resource was created. POST /todos. 204 No Content Successful request intentionally returns no DELETE /todos/:id. response content. 400 Bad Request Request cannot be processed as sent. Malformed/basic unusable input in examples. 404 Not Found Target resource is not available. Unknown Todo id. 409 Conflict Request conflicts with current resource/application Later useful for uniqueness/state conflicts. state. 500 Internal Server Unexpected server failure. Do not intentionally use for client mistakes. Error Do not return 200 for everything A response body such as {"success": false} with HTTP 200 forces every client to reinvent outcome detection. Use the protocol status code accurately, then add structured error content when useful. Official source notes Primary protocol reference: RFC 9110 - HTTP Semantics (RFC Editor). REQUEST HTTP Client TaskFlow API PowerShell / browser / later Next.js NestJS + Fastify RESPONSE method + target + headers + optional body status + headers + optional body Figure - HTTP request/response exchange. Book 4 of Phase 05 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 REST Resource and Route Design Design APIs around resources Todo Collection /todos Todo 1 Todo 2 Todo 3 /todos/1 /todos/2 /todos/3 URLs identify resources. HTTP methods express what the client asks to do with them. Figure - REST-oriented resource modeling separates resource identity from method semantics. REST is often taught as a rigid list of URL rules. A more useful starting point is resource-oriented thinking: identify the domain concepts the client manipulates, give them stable resource identifiers, and use standard HTTP semantics to interact with them. Prefer nouns in resource paths Avoid action-shaped route Prefer resource-oriented route GET /getTodos GET /todos GET /getTodo?id=3 GET /todos/3 POST /createTodo POST /todos POST /completeTodo/3 PATCH /todos/3 with { completed: true } POST /deleteTodo/3 DELETE /todos/3 This is not because verbs are forbidden in URLs. It is because HTTP already provides method semantics. Resource-oriented contracts tend to be easier to predict and compose. Some domain actions genuinely do not map cleanly to CRUD; later systems may use action endpoints when the domain warrants them. Collections and members Target Examples of reasonable operations /todos GET list; POST create /todos/:id GET one; PATCH change; DELETE remove /projects/:projectId/tasks Later: nested collection when project context is meaningful Path parameters vs query parameters Use path parameters to identify a resource or hierarchical context. Use query parameters to modify how a representation is selected, filtered, sorted or paged. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 REST Resource and Route Design Resource identity vs query refinement GET /todos/42 GET /todos?completed=true GET /todos?sort=createdAt&order=desc Do not leak UI button names into the API A frontend button might say Mark complete, but the API contract does not need a /markComplete route. The underlying resource change is a Todo update. This keeps the API useful to clients that have completely different interfaces. REAL-WORLD NOTE A payroll or procurement API often includes operations that are more than CRUD, such as approve, post or close. Resource-oriented design is a default mental model, not a command to distort domain workflows. Introduce explicit actions when the domain operation is genuinely meaningful and cannot be represented clearly as ordinary resource state. Contract checklist before implementing a route ● What resource is being targeted? ● Which HTTP method best expresses the requested semantics? ● Where is resource identity carried: path or query? ● Does the request need content? What media type? ● What success status should the client expect? ● What happens if the resource does not exist? ● Is retrying the operation safe or idempotent? ● What representation should a successful response expose? Step 1 - Generate the Todo feature From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm exec nest generate module todos pnpm exec nest generate controller todos --no-spec pnpm exec nest generate service todos --no-spec Step 2 - Give the service temporary state apps/api/src/todos/todos.service.ts - first read operations FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 Build the In-Memory Todo API import { Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common'; interface Todo { id: number; title: string; completed: boolean; } @Injectable() export class TodosService { private nextId = 3; private readonly todos: Todo[] = [ { id: 1, title: 'Learn HTTP', completed: false }, { id: 2, title: 'Build the API contract', completed: false }, ]; findAll() { return this.todos; } findOne(id: number) { const todo = this.todos.find((item) => item.id === id); if (!todo) throw new NotFoundException('Todo not found'); return todo; } } The service owns temporary application state. The controller should not own an array just because it receives HTTP requests. Later, Prisma replaces this in-memory persistence without changing the conceptual controller responsibility. Step 3 - Add read routes apps/api/src/todos/todos.controller.ts - read routes @Controller('todos') export class TodosController { constructor(private readonly todosService: TodosService) {} @Get() findAll() { return this.todosService.findAll(); } @Get(':id') findOne(@Param('id') id: string) { return this.todosService.findOne(Number(id)); } } We convert the route parameter to a number for this protocol exercise. Formal validation and typed DTO boundaries are deliberately deferred. The book should make that technical debt visible rather than pretend raw input is trustworthy. Step 4 - Add creation todos.service.ts - temporary creation behavior create(title: string) { const todo = { id: this.nextId++, title, completed: false, }; this.todos.push(todo); return todo; } todos.controller.ts - POST /todos FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 Build the In-Memory Todo API @Post() create(@Body() body: { title?: string }) { if (!body.title?.trim()) { throw new BadRequestException('title is required'); } return this.todosService.create(body.title.trim()); } Nest defaults successful POST handlers to 201 Created. We use only a tiny manual guard here so the protocol example is usable; this is not the validation architecture taught later. Step 5 - Add partial update todos.service.ts - patch behavior update(id: number, changes: { title?: string; completed?: boolean }) { const todo = this.findOne(id); if (changes.title !== undefined) todo.title = changes.title; if (changes.completed !== undefined) todo.completed = changes.completed; return todo; } todos.controller.ts - PATCH /todos/:id @Patch(':id') update( @Param('id') id: string, @Body() body: { title?: string; completed?: boolean }, ) { return this.todosService.update(Number(id), body); } Step 6 - Add deletion with 204 todos.service.ts - removal behavior remove(id: number) { const todo = this.findOne(id); const index = this.todos.indexOf(todo); this.todos.splice(index, 1); } todos.controller.ts - DELETE /todos/:id @Delete(':id') @HttpCode(204) remove(@Param('id') id: string) { this.todosService.remove(Number(id)); } A 204 response intentionally has no content. Returning a JSON success object would conflict with the meaning we are teaching. Nest allows explicit status selection through @HttpCode(204). Temporary limitation The array disappears when the server stops. That is useful right now because the learner can focus on request/response semantics. Do not add Prisma early to "fix" it. Book 7 of Phase 05 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Error Semantics and Debugging Treat error responses as part of the API contract Can the TCP request reach port 4000? process + port Did a route match? method + path Was the request representation usable? headers + JSON shape Did application logic succeed? controller / service What status and body came back? observe exact response Figure - HTTP debugging from the outside in. Preserve the request and response as evidence before editing code. An API is not defined only by happy-path JSON. Clients must also know what happens when a route does not exist, a resource is absent, the request content is unusable or the server fails unexpectedly. 404 can mean different things operationally Observation Likely meaning 404 for GET /todos/999 Route matched; application says that resource does not exist. 404 for GET /todo/1 Likely route mismatch: collection path is /todos. 404 for POST /todos/1 when no route exists Method/path combination does not match a handler. 400 is for a request problem, not every business rejection In this phase, a missing Todo title produces a basic 400 response. Later, formal DTO validation will give consistent field-level errors. A state conflict such as creating a duplicate unique value may be better represented by 409. Status selection should describe the kind of failure, not merely "something went wrong." 5xx means the server failed Do not deliberately convert expected client mistakes into 500 responses. A 500-class response tells the client the server could not fulfill the request because of a server-side failure. Production systems should log the internal details without leaking secrets or stack traces into public responses. Inspect what you actually sent 1 Record the exact method. 2 Record the exact URL, including port and query string. 3 Record request headers that affect representation, especially Content-Type. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 HTTP Error Semantics and Debugging 4 Record the JSON content exactly as serialized. 5 Observe the numeric status code. 6 Observe response headers and body. 7 Only then decide which application layer to inspect. Book 8 of Phase 05 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05 API Design Decisions and Anti-Patterns API design decisions that age well Decision Prefer Avoid Resource naming Plural nouns such as /todos Verb-heavy routes such as /getTodos Outcome signaling Meaningful HTTP status Always 200 + success boolean Representation Stable public shape Blindly expose every internal object Deletion DELETE /todos/:id POST /deleteTodo Partial edit PATCH /todos/:id One endpoint per field/button Errors Consistent status + structured body Random strings and stack traces Testing Independent API client first Only test through UI clicks Anti-pattern: controller as the entire application The controller should not gradually accumulate arrays, database queries, permission rules and business workflows. Phase 05 keeps the in-memory array in TodosService so that when persistence changes later, the HTTP boundary remains conceptually stable. Anti-pattern: status code as decoration If a client must inspect { success: false } to discover that a request failed while the HTTP status is 200, intermediaries, monitoring tools and generic client behavior lose useful protocol information. Use HTTP semantics rather than hiding them inside JSON. Anti-pattern: design from screens instead of domain resources A UI might have buttons named Add, Finish, Archive, Restore and Delete. If every button becomes an endpoint name, the API becomes tightly coupled to one interface. Start from the resource and its state transitions, then introduce explicit action endpoints only when the domain operation itself deserves an action concept. Anti-pattern: pretending Phase 05 input handling is production validation The manual title check in POST /todos is intentionally minimal. It does not give reusable schemas, transformation, field-specific validation or consistent DTO behavior. Later phases introduce a real validation boundary. A professional course should label temporary scaffolding honestly. API contract review checklist ● Is the resource name meaningful without seeing the frontend? ● Does the method match the intended semantics? ● Can a client predict common success and failure statuses? ● Is the response shape stable and intentional? ● Is resource identity in the correct part of the URL? ● Are query parameters used for selection/filter/sort rather than hidden actions? ● Is the endpoint independently testable? The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Variable Available where? Purpose API_BASE_URL Server runtime only Server Components and server-only code NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL Browser bundle + server Browser/client code that must know the public API URL Next.js only exposes environment values to browser code when they are explicitly prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_. Those public values are inlined into browser JavaScript at build time, so they must never contain secrets. SECURITY BOUNDARY A value being called an environment variable does not make it secret. NEXT_PUBLIC_* means the value is intentionally public to the browser. API URLs are normally fine; database passwords and service-role keys are not. Browsers treat origin as scheme + host + port. http://localhost:3000 and http://127.0.0.1:3000 are different origins even though both reach the same machine. Our Nest CORS example allows both to reduce accidental local friction, but consistency remains a good habit. Browser Origin GET /todos API Origin http://localhost:3000 http://localhost:4000 different port = different origin Browser checks Nest CORS config response CORS headers allowed origins If the server does not grant the browser origin, JavaScript cannot read the cross-origin response. Figure - CORS is permission communicated through HTTP headers and enforced by browsers. It is not a replacement for authentication or authorization. What counts as an origin? Origin mental model origin = scheme + host + port http://localhost:3000 http://localhost:4000 <- different port, different origin http://127.0.0.1:3000 <- different host from localhost Enable only the frontend origins we need apps/api/src/main.ts - before app.listen(...) app.enableCors({ origin: [ 'http://localhost:3000', 'http://127.0.0.1:3000', ], }); NestJS exposes enableCors() on the application object. With the Fastify platform, Nest uses the platform-appropriate CORS integration under the hood. The important part for the learner is the policy: the API tells browsers which origins may read cross-origin responses. CORS IS NOT AUTH FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06 Browser Fetch and CORS Allowing http://localhost:3000 through CORS does not prove who the user is, does not protect a Todo from another authenticated user, and does not make the API private. Book 5 of Phase 06 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06 CORS Preflight and Fetch Error Semantics Why GET may work while POST suddenly shows OPTIONS A simple cross-origin GET can often proceed without an OPTIONS preflight. A browser POST that sends Content-Type: application/json is different: application/json is not a CORS-safelisted content type, so the browser commonly checks permission first. Browser wants POST /todos Content-Type: application/json OPTIONS /todos CORS preflight NestJS CORS response Access-Control-Allow-* POST /todos actual JSON request 201 Created Todo representation Figure - A JSON cross-origin POST commonly triggers an automatic browser preflight. The frontend normally does not hand-code the OPTIONS request. Create helper Add to apps/web/src/lib/api/todos.ts export async function createTodo(baseUrl: string, title: string): Promise<Todo> { const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/todos`, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ title }), }); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`POST /todos failed: ${response.status}`); } return response.json() as Promise<Todo>; } The browser owns the preflight The frontend normally does not write an OPTIONS request manually. The browser decides that a cross-origin request requires preflight, sends OPTIONS with the intended method/headers, inspects the server CORS response, and only then sends the actual request if policy allows it. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06 CORS Preflight and Fetch Error Semantics Network error vs HTTP error Situation fetch promise Response available? What to inspect API process stopped Rejects No catch / network error DNS or malformed URL Rejects No URL/configuration CORS blocked browser Typically rejects to JS as a No usable response Console + Network + CORS headers access network-style failure 404 Not Found Resolves Yes, ok=false status + response body 500 Server Error Resolves Yes, ok=false status + server logs IMPORTANT FETCH RULE A try/catch around fetch is not enough to detect HTTP failures. Check response.ok or response.status because 404 and 500 are still valid HTTP responses. Preflight debugging checklist ● Was the browser request actually cross-origin? ● Did the Network panel show OPTIONS before the actual method? ● What Origin header did the browser send? ● Did the API return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that exact origin? ● Did Access-Control-Allow-Methods include the intended method? ● Did Access-Control-Allow-Headers permit non-safelisted headers? ● Did the actual request run after OPTIONS? Do not "fix" CORS with no-cors Setting fetch mode to no-cors is not a general solution. It produces an opaque response whose useful status/body are not available to application JavaScript. The correct fix is an intentional server CORS policy when the browser should be allowed to call the API. End-to-end development becomes manageable when every failure is located on the actual request path. Is Next.js running? port 3000 Is NestJS running? port 4000 What exact URL did fetch use? environment variable Did the request leave the browser? Network tab Was there OPTIONS first? preflight What status + headers returned? HTTP evidence Did fetch code check response.ok? application handling Figure - Phase 06 debugging follows the network path instead of guessing from the UI symptom. Browser Network panel workflow 1 Open DevTools -> Network. 2 Clear previous entries. 3 Trigger exactly one operation. 4 Select the request to port 4000. 5 Inspect Request URL and Request Method. 6 Inspect Status Code. 7 Inspect Request Headers, especially Origin and Content-Type. 8 Inspect Response Headers, especially Access-Control-Allow-* when cross-origin. 9 Inspect Response/Preview body. 10 If OPTIONS exists, inspect it separately from the actual request. Terminal evidence still matters A Server Component fetch runs in the Next.js server process, so its stack trace and fetch error appear in the Next.js terminal. A NestJS handler failure appears in the API terminal. A browser Client Component failure can appear in browser Console/Network. Good debugging follows the process that executed the failing code. Preserve one failing request, make one hypothesis, change one layer, rerun the same request, then observe whether the evidence changed. A powerful test: bypass the browser If a browser call fails, repeat the equivalent request with PowerShell. If PowerShell succeeds while browser JavaScript fails, that strongly narrows the problem toward browser-only policy/configuration such as CORS. Book 1 of Phase 07 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Relational Database Mental Model A database is durable application state Our in-memory Todo array is useful for teaching HTTP, but it is not durable application state. A relational database gives the application a separate system whose job is to store facts, enforce rules around those facts, answer queries and coordinate concurrent changes. Relationships are data rules, not drawing decorations. projects tasks comments id PK id PK id PK name project_id FK task_id FK one project many tasks many comments Relational database tables + constraints + relationships + transactions Figure - A relational schema stores facts in tables and uses keys/constraints to preserve valid relationships. Database, schema, table, row and column tasks table id title completed project_id 1 Learn SQL false 10 2 Design API true 10 3 Add persistence false 11 column = attribute/type/rule row = one stored record Figure - Tables organize typed columns; each row stores one record that must satisfy table constraints. Term Practical meaning Database A PostgreSQL database that contains application schemas and objects. Schema A namespace that groups database objects. PostgreSQL commonly starts with the public schema. Table A relation used to store records with a defined set of columns and constraints. Column A named attribute with a data type and possibly rules/defaults. Row One stored record satisfying the table definition. Constraint A database-enforced rule that prevents invalid states. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Relational Database Mental Model The database should protect invariants An invariant is a condition that must remain true for valid persistent data. For example, a task title may be required; an email may need to be unique; a task may reference only an existing project. Application code can validate these conditions, but durable database constraints provide a final line of defense when multiple clients, scripts, background jobs or future services write to the same database. Incoming row candidate data Type checks is the value compatible? NOT NULL / CHECK does the value satisfy local rules? UNIQUE / PRIMARY KEY does identity remain valid? FOREIGN KEY does the referenced row exist? Accepted row database invariant preserved Figure - Database constraints reject invalid states before they become persistent application data. Rows are not objects A TypeScript object and a database row can describe the same business concept, but they are not the same thing. Objects live in process memory and can contain methods, derived values or temporary state. Database rows are persisted values governed by database types and constraints. Prisma later maps between these worlds; understanding the difference makes ORM behavior less surprising. Set-oriented thinking SQL is designed to describe sets of rows. Instead of looping through every task in JavaScript to find incomplete items, a query asks the database for the set matching a condition. This becomes increasingly important as data grows beyond what can be loaded into application memory safely. Think in sets SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE completed = false ORDER BY created_at DESC; REAL-WORLD NOTE In an HRIS, Payroll, Inventory or Procurement system, the same mental model applies: tables persist facts, constraints protect valid relationships, and application services orchestrate workflows around that durable state. sql Explain Relational Database Mental Model in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Book 2 of Phase 07 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Data Types, NULL and Constraints Data types are part of the contract Choosing a column type tells PostgreSQL what values can be represented and what operations make sense. Good types reduce ambiguity and make invalid states harder to store. Application value Useful PostgreSQL type Why Task title / description text Variable-length text without an arbitrary storage limit. Completed flag boolean Represents true/false directly. Priority number smallint / integer Numeric ordering; pair with CHECK for allowed range. Money numeric(p,s) Exact decimal arithmetic when a monetary amount is truly needed. Created timestamp timestamptz Timestamp with time-zone semantics normalized by PostgreSQL. Identifier bigint identity or uuid Choice depends on system boundaries and identity strategy. Structured flexible metadata jsonb Useful when structure is genuinely variable; not a substitute for normal columns. Prefer modern identity columns for generated numeric IDs Generated identity example CREATE TABLE practice_tasks ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL ); PostgreSQL supports identity columns as the SQL-standard way to generate values. The course uses them for fundamentals. Later, TaskFlow may use UUIDs where that better matches authentication or distributed identity requirements. NULL means missing/unknown, not empty NULL is not the same as an empty string, zero or false. Comparisons involving NULL require special reasoning. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, not = NULL. Correct NULL check SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE due_at IS NULL; Three-valued logic SQL conditions can evaluate to TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. A comparison such as due_at = NULL does not mean what JavaScript developers often expect. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Data Types, NULL and Constraints Constraints encode durable rules Incoming row candidate data Type checks is the value compatible? NOT NULL / CHECK does the value satisfy local rules? UNIQUE / PRIMARY KEY does identity remain valid? FOREIGN KEY does the referenced row exist? Accepted row database invariant preserved Figure - Database constraints reject invalid states before they become persistent application data. Constraint Protects NOT NULL A required value cannot be absent. CHECK A value or combination of values must satisfy an expression. UNIQUE No two rows may share the constrained value combination. PRIMARY KEY The table has one chosen unique non-null row identity. FOREIGN KEY A relationship must point to a valid referenced row (unless nullable by design). A small constraint-rich table CREATE TABLE practice_tasks ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL, completed boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false, priority smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 2, due_at timestamptz, CONSTRAINT practice_tasks_priority_check CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 3) ); Defaults are convenience, constraints are rules A default supplies a value when an INSERT omits that column. It does not make arbitrary incoming values valid. A CHECK or other constraint is what rejects invalid persisted values. Keep those responsibilities separate. Do not use JSON for everything PostgreSQL has excellent jsonb support, but a flexible JSON document is not automatically the best model for strongly related business data. If the application routinely filters, joins or constrains a field, a normal typed column is usually easier to validate, query and index. JSON is useful when the domain is genuinely document-like or extensible. sql Explain Data Types NULL and Constraints in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Application SQL / ORM PostgreSQL NestJS business logic database commands durable relational state… FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Keys, Relationships and Joins VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Keys, Relationships and Joins Identity, referential integrity and relational reads Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic. Application SQL / ORM PostgreSQL NestJS business logic database commands durable relational state Phase 07 focus understand the database before Prisma Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning. Book 3 of Phase 07 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Keys, Relationships and Joins Primary keys answer: which row? A primary key identifies each row uniquely and cannot be NULL. PostgreSQL automatically creates a unique B-tree index for the primary-key columns. The key is both a data-integrity rule and an efficient lookup path. Primary key CREATE TABLE projects ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL ); Foreign keys answer: does this relationship exist? A foreign key requires values in the referencing column to match a key in another table. This prevents a task from claiming to belong to a project that does not exist. Foreign key CREATE TABLE tasks ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, project_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id), title text NOT NULL ); Relationships are data rules, not drawing decorations. projects tasks comments id PK id PK id PK name project_id FK task_id FK one project many tasks many comments Relational database tables + constraints + relationships + transactions Figure - A relational schema stores facts in tables and uses keys/constraints to preserve valid relationships. Foreign-key actions are domain decisions Action Meaning Typical question NO ACTION / RESTRICT Prevent parent change/delete when Should a project be deletable while tasks still exist? dependent rows would be invalid. CASCADE Propagate parent delete/update to Are child rows meaningless without the parent? related rows. SET NULL Remove the relationship while Can a task exist without a project? preserving the child row. Do not cargo-cult CASCADE Cascade behavior can be correct, but it can also turn one delete into a large irreversible data change. Choose referential actions from business meaning, not convenience. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Keys, Relationships and Joins One-to-many and many-to-many A project has many tasks when tasks.project_id references projects.id. A many-to-many relationship usually becomes an explicit join table containing two foreign keys, often with a composite primary key or unique constraint. Many-to-many join table CREATE TABLE task_labels ( task_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES tasks(id), label_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES labels(id), PRIMARY KEY (task_id, label_id) ); JOIN reads related facts Inner join SELECT t.id, t.title, p.name AS project_name FROM tasks AS t JOIN projects AS p ON p.id = t.project_id ORDER BY t.id; The join condition states how rows relate. An INNER JOIN returns rows that have matches on both sides. A LEFT JOIN keeps rows from the left side even when no right-side match exists. Choosing a join is therefore part of the question being asked, not merely SQL syntax. Question Useful join Show tasks only when their project exists INNER JOIN Show every project, including projects with zero tasks LEFT JOIN from projects to tasks Show every task and optional assignee details LEFT JOIN when assignee is nullable Foreign keys and indexes are different responsibilities The referenced primary/unique key is indexed, but PostgreSQL does not automatically create an index on the referencing foreign-key column. If the application frequently joins, filters, updates or deletes through that foreign key, an index on the referencing column is often useful. We justify it from query patterns rather than from habit. sql Explain Keys Relationships and Joins in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Book 4 of Phase 07 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 SQL CRUD, Filtering and Aggregates CRUD in SQL is explicit data manipulation Our HTTP API uses GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE. The database has a different language. SQL commands describe data retrieval and changes. Prisma later translates typed method calls into SQL concepts like these. INSERT - create persistent rows INSERT with RETURNING INSERT INTO projects (name) VALUES ('Full Stack Course') RETURNING id, name; RETURNING lets PostgreSQL return the inserted or modified rows without a second SELECT. This is useful for generated IDs and server-side defaults. SELECT - ask a question Filtered and ordered query SELECT id, title, completed FROM tasks WHERE project_id = 10 AND completed = false ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; FROM / JOIN which rows and relationships participate? WHERE which rows survive filtering? GROUP BY which rows become groups? HAVING which groups survive? SELECT which expressions are returned? ORDER BY / LIMIT how is the final result shaped? Figure - A useful conceptual order for reasoning about SELECT queries. SQL syntax is written in a different order, but this mental pipeline helps debugging. UPDATE - change selected rows Targeted update UPDATE tasks SET completed = true, completed_at = now() WHERE id = 42 RETURNING id, completed, completed_at; DELETE - remove selected rows Targeted delete FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 SQL CRUD, Filtering and Aggregates DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = 42 RETURNING id; DANGEROUS DIFFERENCE UPDATE tasks SET completed = true; affects every row. DELETE FROM tasks; deletes every row. The absence of WHERE is valid SQL, which is why query review and transactions matter. Filtering operators you will use constantly Pattern Example Equality status = 'OPEN' Range priority >= 2 Set membership status IN ('OPEN', 'BLOCKED') Pattern matching title ILIKE '%postgres%' Null test due_at IS NULL Date/time comparison created_at >= now() - interval '7 days' Aggregates answer questions across rows Aggregate query SELECT project_id, count(*) AS open_task_count FROM tasks WHERE completed = false GROUP BY project_id HAVING count(*) >= 5 ORDER BY open_task_count DESC; WHERE filters rows before grouping. GROUP BY creates groups. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. This distinction becomes important for dashboards and reports. Select only what the caller needs During learning it is tempting to write SELECT * everywhere. Production queries are often clearer and more stable when they select the columns the caller actually needs. Explicit projections also make API contracts and performance tradeoffs more visible. sql Explain SQL CRUD Filtering and Aggregates in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence.
