Book 5 of Phase 07 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Transactions, Indexes and Concurrency Transactions protect multi-step invariants Many application workflows require several database changes to succeed together. If one succeeds and another fails, the database can end up representing a business state that should never exist. A transaction groups the changes into one unit of work. A transaction groups related changes into one unit of work. BEGIN start transaction UPDATE task INSERT activity mark complete record event COMMIT ROLLBACK all changes become durable discard transaction changes Figure - COMMIT makes the unit succeed; ROLLBACK abandons it when the workflow cannot be completed safely. Successful transaction BEGIN; UPDATE tasks SET completed = true WHERE id = 42; INSERT INTO activity_log (task_id, action) VALUES (42, 'completed'); COMMIT; Abandon changes BEGIN; -- perform several related changes -- something fails or business rule is not satisfied ROLLBACK; ACID as an application developer Property Practical meaning Atomicity The transaction commits as one unit or rolls back as one unit. Consistency Constraints and application rules move the database between valid states. Isolation Concurrent transactions are controlled so their interaction has defined behavior. Durability Committed changes survive normal process/server failures according to PostgreSQL durability mechanisms. FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Transactions, Indexes and Concurrency Concurrency means other users exist A single-user tutorial can pretend no one else changes data between your read and write. Production systems cannot. PostgreSQL uses MVCC and transaction isolation to coordinate concurrent access. You do not need deep database-internals knowledge yet, but you must stop assuming that a value you read will remain unchanged until your later UPDATE. Later application pattern Optimistic concurrency checks, row locks and carefully scoped transactions exist because multiple requests can race. We introduce advanced patterns only when TaskFlow has workflows that actually need them. Indexes are access paths Indexes are access paths - not free speed buttons. Without useful index With useful B-tree scan many table rows navigate matching key range Trade-off faster reads can mean more storage and write work Figure - An index can reduce lookup work when it matches the query pattern, but it has storage and maintenance cost. By default, CREATE INDEX creates a B-tree index, which is appropriate for many equality and range searches. An index helps only when it matches how the application searches or orders data. It also consumes storage and must be maintained when rows are inserted, updated or deleted. Example indexes CREATE INDEX tasks_project_id_idx ON tasks (project_id); CREATE INDEX tasks_project_open_idx ON tasks (project_id, completed); Why foreign-key columns often need deliberate indexes A foreign-key declaration does not automatically index the referencing column in PostgreSQL. If TaskFlow frequently finds tasks by project_id or PostgreSQL must locate child rows while checking a parent change/delete, an index can reduce the work. The correct index still depends on the actual workload. Composite index order matters An index on (project_id, completed) is not equivalent to one on (completed, project_id). Index column order should reflect the query patterns, selectivity and ordering requirements. Do not collect indexes as decorations. sql Explain Transactions Indexes and Concurrency in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Application SQL / ORM PostgreSQL NestJS business logic… FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Normalization and Schema Evolution VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Normalization and Schema Evolution Design durable facts and change schemas without losing the mental model Persistence becomes understandable when the database stops being magic. Application SQL / ORM PostgreSQL NestJS business logic database commands durable relational state Phase 07 focus understand the database before Prisma Figure - Phase 07 isolates PostgreSQL fundamentals so later ORM code has a clear relational meaning. Book 6 of Phase 07 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Normalization and Schema Evolution Normalization is about one durable fact in one sensible place Bad repeated data Separated facts task row repeats project name projects, users, tasks and owner email linked by keys Goal store each durable fact in a sensible place; join related facts when reading Figure - Normalization reduces contradictory copies of the same fact; it is a design tool, not a rule to maximize table count. Suppose every task row stores project_name and project_owner_email. Renaming the project would require updating many task rows; missing one creates contradictory copies of the same fact. A normalized model stores the project facts once and lets tasks reference the project. The useful idea behind 1NF, 2NF and 3NF Form Practical intuition 1NF Store values in a queryable table shape; avoid repeating groups packed into one column. 2NF When a key has multiple columns, non-key facts should depend on the whole key. 3NF Non-key facts should describe the row identified by the key, not another non-key fact. You do not need to chant normal forms while coding. The professional habit is to ask: What fact does this row represent? Where is that fact authoritative? What contradictions become possible if I duplicate it? Denormalization is a trade-off, not a failure Sometimes duplicated or precomputed data is deliberately introduced for performance, reporting or historical snapshots. That is a design decision with synchronization costs. First understand the normalized source of truth; then denormalize when a measured requirement justifies it. Schema evolution is inevitable Production schemas change as requirements change. PostgreSQL supports ALTER TABLE operations, but application teams normally record schema changes as versioned migrations so environments can advance in a repeatable order. Phase 09 shows how Prisma migrations become that change history for TaskFlow. Schema evolution examples ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN due_at timestamptz; ALTER TABLE tasks ADD CONSTRAINT tasks_title_not_blank CHECK (length(btrim(title)) > 0); FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 Normalization and Schema Evolution A migration is not just the final schema The final schema answers what the database looks like now. Migration history answers how an existing database gets from an older valid state to the new valid state. Those are different concerns. Renames, destructive changes and data backfills ● Adding a nullable column is usually easier than immediately adding a required column to a table that already contains rows. ● Changing a column type can require conversion and may lock or rewrite data depending on the operation. ● Dropping a column destroys stored information; production migrations need backups, rollout planning and application compatibility. ● Large data backfills are operational work, not merely schema syntax. ● Application deployment and database migration order can matter when old and new application versions overlap. Preview of Prisma migrations Prisma will later generate migration SQL for many schema changes, but generated SQL is still database change code. Relationships are data rules, not drawing decorations. projects tasks comments id PK id PK id PK name project_id FK task_id FK one project many tasks many comments Relational database tables + constraints + relationships + transactions Figure - A relational schema stores facts in tables and uses keys/constraints to preserve valid relationships. Practice schema CREATE TABLE practice_projects ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL UNIQUE, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); CREATE TABLE practice_tasks ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, project_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES practice_projects(id), title text NOT NULL, completed boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false, priority smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 2 CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 3), due_at timestamptz, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); Turn product questions into relational questions Product question Database question Show open tasks for one project Filter practice_tasks by project_id and completed. Show project name beside each task Join tasks to projects through project_id. Count open tasks per project Filter, group by project and count. Delete a project What should happen to its tasks? Choose FK action from product meaning. Sort upcoming work Order by due_at while deciding how NULL due dates should appear. Find high-priority incomplete tasks quickly Which query pattern might justify a composite index? Seed practice rows Practice seed data FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 07 TaskFlow Data Modeling Lab INSERT INTO practice_projects (name) VALUES ('Course'), ('Portfolio') RETURNING id, name; INSERT INTO practice_tasks (project_id, title, priority) VALUES (1, 'Learn relational modeling', 1), (1, 'Practice joins', 2), (2, 'Build portfolio project', 1); Query 1 - open tasks for a project Project task list SELECT id, title, priority FROM practice_tasks WHERE project_id = 1 AND completed = false ORDER BY priority, created_at; Query 2 - project dashboard counts Simple project dashboard SELECT p.id, p.name, count(t.id) FILTER (WHERE t.completed = false) AS open_tasks, count(t.id) FILTER (WHERE t.completed = true) AS done_tasks FROM practice_projects AS p LEFT JOIN practice_tasks AS t ON t.project_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.name; Add an index because of a query, not because of a column Index tied to a repeated query pattern CREATE INDEX practice_tasks_project_completed_idx ON practice_tasks (project_id, completed); This index is justifiable if TaskFlow repeatedly requests tasks by project and completion state. It is not automatically justified merely because those columns exist. Think before final schema design ● Should project names be globally unique, or only unique inside a workspace? The answer changes the UNIQUE constraint. ● Should deleting a project delete tasks, prevent deletion, archive the project, or move tasks elsewhere? This changes referential and application behavior. ● Should priority be numeric, an enum-like text value, or its own table? Choose based on domain requirements, not aesthetic preference. ● Should tasks have one assignee or many? That changes relationship cardinality. ● Should completed_at be derived from completed, or stored as historical information? The business meaning matters. Professional database work therefore combines precise SQL with observability, transactions, backups, permissions and review discipline. Preview before update or delete Observe the target set first SELECT id, title, completed FROM tasks WHERE project_id = 10 AND completed = false; -- After verifying the target set: UPDATE tasks SET completed = true WHERE project_id = 10 AND completed = false RETURNING id, title; Production safety For high-impact operations, use an explicit transaction, inspect the affected rows, and commit only when the result matches your intention. On production systems, permissions and operational procedures should further limit dangerous direct writes. Parameterized queries prevent data from becoming SQL code Application code should not build SQL by concatenating untrusted strings. Database drivers and ORMs support parameterized queries so user input is transmitted as data rather than executable SQL structure. Prisma later handles normal parameterization for us, but understanding the security boundary still matters. Parameter placeholder concept -- Conceptual parameterized SQL SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE title ILIKE $1; -- $1 is a bound parameter, not concatenated SQL text. Debug SQL layer by layer 1 Schema: Does the table/column actually exist, and is the expected migration applied? 2 Type: Are values compatible with the target column type? 3 Constraint: Which NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE or FOREIGN KEY rule rejected the write? 4 Data: Does the row you expect actually exist? 5 Query: Does WHERE match the rows you think it matches? 6 Transaction: Is the transaction committed, rolled back, blocked or already failed? 7 Plan/performance: Is the query logically correct but doing far more work than expected? Is the duplicate expected or a race? violates foreign key constraint Does the referenced parent exist? Is the relationship ID correct? null value violates not-null constraint Which required field was omitted? Should it truly be required? violates check constraint Which domain rule rejected the candidate value? relation does not exist Wrong schema/database, missing migration or misspelled object? column does not exist Schema mismatch, typo or application ahead of database migration? Do not optimize the wrong query ● First prove the query returns the correct rows. ● Then measure the workload and inspect EXPLAIN output. ● Add or adjust an index because of repeated query patterns, not because a blog post says every foreign key must have the same index shape. ● Remember that indexes speed some reads while increasing storage and write maintenance. ● Do not use application-side loops to replace joins/aggregates when the database can answer the set-based question directly. Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan, not to guess Inspect a query plan EXPLAIN SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE project_id = 10 AND completed = false; Performance rule Measure before optimizing. A sequential scan on a tiny table can be completely reasonable. The goal is not to force index usage; the goal is to give PostgreSQL good data structures and let the planner choose an efficient plan. Level 1 - Follow 1 Write CREATE TABLE statements for a project and task table with primary key, NOT NULL title, completed default and project foreign key. 2 Write INSERT statements for two projects and three tasks. 3 Write a SELECT for incomplete tasks in one project ordered by priority. 4 Write an UPDATE that completes exactly one task and returns the modified row. 5 Write a DELETE that removes exactly one task and returns its id. Level 2 - Modify 1 Add an optional due_at timestamptz column and query only tasks with a due date. 2 Add a CHECK constraint that allows priority values 1 through 3. 3 Add a UNIQUE rule appropriate for a practice label table. 4 Change a query so projects with zero tasks still appear in the result. 5 Add a useful index for a repeated query that filters by project_id and completed. Level 3 - Implement Design a small labels feature without copying a solution. A task can have many labels and a label can belong to many tasks. Produce the tables, keys, constraints, join table, one INSERT flow and one JOIN query that returns task titles with label names. Level 4 - Engineer TaskFlow needs project archiving. Archived projects should remain queryable for audit/history, ordinary task lists should exclude them, and users must not accidentally create new tasks in archived projects. Decide which rules belong in the database and which belong in NestJS business logic. Document your reasoning; there may be more than one defensible design. Debugging Workshop — Phase 07: PostgreSQL Fundamentals Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk Business invariant -> table design -> key/constraint -> SQL query -> query plan/index -> transaction -> durable rows Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Treating IDs as the only integrity mechanism Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 2 — Missing composite uniqueness on membership-like tables Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. text: connections-pooling-and-ssl Connections Pooling and SSL FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Connections, Pooling and SSL VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Connections, Pooling and SSL Choose a connection mode instead of copying whichever URL appears first A connection string is infrastructure configuration. Its host, username and port encode how your client reaches PostgreSQL.… FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Connections, Pooling and SSL VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Connections, Pooling and SSL Choose a connection mode instead of copying whichever URL appears first A connection string is infrastructure configuration. Its host, username and port encode how your client reaches PostgreSQL. Figure 1 - Connection modes Persistent backend → Direct :5432 IPv4 dev / persistent → Session pooler :5432 Serverless / edge → Transaction pooler :6543 Supabase documents different connection modes for different runtime behavior. Volume 03 - Database Engineering FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Connections, Pooling and SSL Book 3 of Phase 08 Why there are multiple URLs PostgreSQL has a finite connection budget. Connection poolers sit between clients and the database so many application clients can share database connections more efficiently. Three important modes Mode Typical host/port Use when Important property Direct db.<ref>.supabase.co:5432 Persistent backend and IPv6- Direct PostgreSQL capable environments (or IPv4 session add-on) Shared session pooler host :5432 Persistent client when direct IPv6 is Session semantics pooler unavailable; common local- retained development choice Shared pooler host :6543 Serverless/edge functions with Transaction pooling; transaction short-lived connections session features are pooler limited For this course right now RECOMMENDED LEARNING CONNECTION For local Windows development, copy the Session pooler URL from Supabase's Connect dialog when direct IPv6 connectivity is uncertain. If your environment can reach the direct endpoint reliably, direct connection is also valid for a persistent backend. Never manufacture the pooler hostname Supabase explicitly warns that the shared pooler host can include a cluster index that cannot be inferred safely from region alone. Copy it from Connect. Connection-string anatomy postgresql://USERNAME:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT/DATABASE?sslmode=require Volume 03 - Database Engineering Book 3 of Phase 08 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Connections, Pooling and SSL Part Meaning USERNAME Database role. Shared pooler usernames include the project reference. PASSWORD Database password; percent-encode reserved URL characters. HOST Direct database endpoint or pooler endpoint. PORT 5432 or 6543 depending on mode. DATABASE Usually postgres for initial course work. sslmode Controls transport encryption behavior. Password encoding If a password contains reserved URI characters such as & , # , ? or a space, encode them before embedding the password inside a URL. Otherwise the parser can mistake password characters for URL syntax. SSL For application connections, set SSL to at least require . Supabase also documents stronger server verification with verify-full plus the project CA certificate. SECURITY NUANCE sslmode=require encrypts the connection, but it does not perform full CA/hostname verification. verify-full is stronger when configured with the appropriate certificate. Transaction-pooler limitations Transaction mode does not preserve session state across transactions and does not support prepared statements in the same way persistent sessions do. That is why the course will not casually use port 6543 for a long-running NestJS API. Figure 1 - Secret boundary Password manager → .env on developer machine → NestJS / CLI process → Supabase Postgres The secret should reach the process that needs it without becoming source code. Volume 03 - Database Engineering FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Secrets and Environment Boundaries Book 4 of Phase 08 The rule NEVER COMMIT Do not commit a real DATABASE_URL , database password, service-role key, access token or downloaded private credential into Git. Where Phase 08 stores connection information We will prepare the API directory for a future database URL without using Prisma yet. # apps/api/.env DATABASE_URL="postgresql://...real value..." Then document the variable without the secret: # apps/api/.env.example DATABASE_URL= Git ignore policy # root or API .gitignore .env .env.* !.env.example VERIFY, DO NOT ASSUME From the repository root, run git check-ignore -v apps/api/.env . You want evidence that Git ignores the file. PowerShell temporary environment variable For a one-session test, you can set a process environment variable: $env:DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://..." # verify only that a value exists; do not echo it in screenshots if ($env:DATABASE_URL) { "DATABASE_URL is set" } This value disappears when that PowerShell process exits. That makes it useful for temporary testing. Volume 03 - Database Engineering Book 4 of Phase 08 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Secrets and Environment Boundaries Why not put the URL in Next.js? subtitle: Supabase PostgreSQL
text: windows-psql-workflow Windows psql Workflow FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Windows psql Workflow VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Connect from Windows with psql Use the native PostgreSQL client to prove connectivity before adding an ORM When a raw PostgreSQL client works, we have isolated the database connection from framework complexity. Figure… FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Windows psql Workflow VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Connect from Windows with psql Use the native PostgreSQL client to prove connectivity before adding an ORM When a raw PostgreSQL client works, we have isolated the database connection from framework complexity. Figure 1 - Connection test isolates the database layer PowerShell → psql → Supabase endpoint → PostgreSQL This is a direct database-client test; Next.js, NestJS and Prisma are not involved. Volume 03 - Database Engineering FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Windows psql Workflow Book 5 of Phase 08 Why psql matters psql is PostgreSQL's command-line client. It lets us prove that host, port, role, password and SSL settings work before introducing Prisma. Verify the client In ordinary PowerShell: psql --version If Windows cannot find it, Phase 07's PostgreSQL tooling setup or PATH must be corrected before proceeding. Recommended connection style Copy the exact Session pooler values from Supabase. For a secure interactive connection, a parameter- style command avoids some URI encoding confusion: psql "sslmode=require host=<POOLER-HOST> port=5432 dbname=postgres user=postgres.<PROJECT- REF>" psql will prompt for the password if it is not supplied through another secure mechanism. Figure 1 - Verification layers Schema expectation → Database catalog → Actual rows Verify structure and data at the database layer before blaming higher layers. Volume 03 - Database Engineering FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Inspect the Real Database Book 7 of Phase 08 Inspection is part of development When persistence bugs appear later, you need to know whether the problem is in the API, ORM, migration, connection, schema or data. Database inspection narrows the search. Useful psql inspection commands \conninfo \dn \dt \d practice_projects \d practice_tasks \x auto Useful SQL inspection queries select current_database(), current_user, current_schema(); select table_schema, table_name from information_schema.tables where table_schema = 'public' order by table_name; select constraint_name, constraint_type from information_schema.table_constraints where table_name = 'practice_tasks' order by constraint_type, constraint_name; Catalog thinking information_schema exposes standardized metadata views. PostgreSQL also has its own pg_catalog system catalogs. You do not need to memorize the catalogs now; you need to understand that the database can describe itself. Table Editor versus SQL inspection Tool Strength Risk if overused Table Editor Fast visual confirmation Can hide the SQL/constraint mental model SQL Editor Explicit repeatable query logic Manual dashboard history is not a migration system psql Scriptable, close to raw PostgreSQL CLI requires deliberate connection handling Query plans preview Phase 07 introduced indexes. You can ask PostgreSQL how it plans a query: Volume 03 - Database Engineering Book 7 of Phase 08 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Inspect the Real Database explain select * from practice_tasks where project_id = 1; Do not optimize because a plan contains a sequential scan on a tiny practice table. Optimization starts from real workload and measurements. Know your server show server_version; show timezone; show search_path; This prevents assumptions about hosted server configuration from becoming invisible bugs. text: troubleshooting-and-database-safety Troubleshooting and Database Safety FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Troubleshooting and Database Safety VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Connection Troubleshooting and Database Safety Debug from the connection outward Do not rewrite application code when the error is really a host, port, password, SSL or network problem. Figure 1 - Connection… FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Troubleshooting and Database Safety VOLUME 03 - DATABASE ENGINEERING Connection Troubleshooting and Database Safety Debug from the connection outward Do not rewrite application code when the error is really a host, port, password, SSL or network problem. Figure 1 - Connection debugging order Mode → Host/port → DNS/IP → TLS → Credentials → SQL Debug from infrastructure facts toward application behavior. Volume 03 - Database Engineering FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Troubleshooting and Database Safety Book 8 of Phase 08 Error-driven troubleshooting Symptom Likely layer First checks Password authentication failed Credentials Correct password? Correct pooled username? Password URL encoded? Host cannot be resolved DNS / copied endpoint Did you copy the exact host from Connect? Connection timed out Network / IP mode / Direct endpoint may require IPv6; try session pooler firewall for IPv4. Connection refused Host/port/mode 5432 vs 6543? Wrong endpoint? SSL/certificate error TLS configuration sslmode setting, certificate path, hostname verification. Prepared statement/session Pooling mode Are you accidentally on transaction pooler 6543? behavior breaks relation does not exist Schema/search path/ Correct database? schema? Was SQL actually migration applied? Direct connection and IPv6 Supabase's direct connection is IPv6 by default unless the project has the IPv4 add-on. If your local ISP or runtime is IPv4-only, a direct host can fail even when the credentials are correct. The shared session pooler is the usual IPv4-friendly alternative. Do not confuse CORS with database connectivity CORS is a browser HTTP security mechanism. psql connects using the PostgreSQL protocol. If psql cannot reach Supabase, changing NestJS CORS settings cannot fix it. Do not use a browser-exposed database password If a connection works only after putting the database URL into NEXT_PUBLIC_... , the solution is worse than the problem. That would expose a privileged credential to browser JavaScript. Safety when using SQL Editor • Read destructive statements before running them. • Use transactions for risky multi-step changes when appropriate. • Do not casually run production SQL copied from an AI or forum. • Prefer repeatable migration files once Prisma enters the course. • Keep development and production projects visually distinct. Volume 03 - Database Engineering Book 8 of Phase 08 FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 08 Troubleshooting and Database Safety RLS and the public schema - preview only Supabase can expose tables through its Data APIs. Browser/client-library access has a different security model involving grants and Row Level Security. Our TaskFlow architecture uses NestJS as the business/ API boundary, so we will not design RLS policies in this phase. We will revisit database exposure and authorization in the security/authentication volumes. IMPORTANT Do not interpret "we are not using RLS yet" as "RLS does not matter." It means the course is separating concerns so authentication and authorization are taught with enough context. Smallest-correction rule If the username is wrong, fix the username. If the host is wrong, copy the correct host. Do not reinstall Node, recreate NestJS or reset the database when the evidence points to a connection parameter. Debugging Workshop — Phase 08: Supabase PostgreSQL Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk Application -> connection string/pooler -> Supabase Postgres -> database objects -> dashboard/observability Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Committing database credentials Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. text: prisma-mental-model-and-architecture Prisma Mental Model and Architecture PHASE 09 / BOOK 01 Prisma Mental Model & Architecture Understand every Prisma layer before installing it NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are locked… PHASE 09 / BOOK 01 Prisma Mental Model & Architecture Understand every Prisma layer before installing it NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are locked to 7.9.1. Newer Prisma releases are not substituted halfway through the course. 1. Why Add an ORM Now? We deliberately waited. If Prisma had appeared before SQL, keys, constraints, joins and transactions, database behavior would look like framework magic. Phase 07 and 08 removed that mystery. Prisma can now be understood as a typed programming interface over relational database work. NestJS service asks for data Prisma Client builds a typed query PrismaPg sends PostgreSQL protocol traffic PostgreSQL executes the query Plain JavaScript data returns Figure 1 - Runtime query lifecycle 2. Prisma Is Several Things, Not One Thing Piece Responsibility Not responsible for prisma CLI init, validate, generate, migrate, studio Serving HTTP requests schema.prisma Data models + generator + DB provider Storing credentials in Prisma 7 prisma.config.ts CLI configuration and datasource URL Runtime NestJS DI Prisma Client Generated type-safe query API Hosting PostgreSQL PrismaPg Driver adapter using pg Business rules PrismaService NestJS provider wrapping one client instance HTTP route design PostgreSQL Actual persistent relational database TypeScript types 3. Runtime vs Tooling Paths Runtime path Tooling path NestJS pnpm exec prisma PrismaService prisma.config.ts Prisma Client DIRECT_URL PrismaPg Migrate / Studio / introspection DATABASE_URL PostgreSQL PostgreSQL Figure 2 - Two connection purposes in the same project This distinction matters with Supabase. The long-running application can use a pooled runtime connection while migration tooling uses a session-capable or direct connection. The same database may be targeted, but the connection behavior and privilege requirements differ. 4. The NestJS Boundary Controllers should still handle HTTP. Services still own business rules. PrismaService is infrastructure: it gives application services a reusable database client. A controller should not become a place where authentication, ownership, query construction and response formatting are all mixed together. TodosController TodosService PrismaService Prisma Client PostgreSQL Figure 3 - Database access stays below application logic 5. What Prisma Does Not Replace • Database constraints: PostgreSQL remains the final integrity boundary. • Authorization: Prisma will execute a query you ask for; it does not decide whether a user should be allowed to make it. • Business logic: status transitions, approvals, payroll rules and domain policies still belong in application services. • SQL understanding: indexes, transactions, joins and query shape still matter. • Migrations review: generated SQL must still be inspected, especially for destructive changes. PowerShell - verify location Get-Location # Expected path ends with: taskflow\apps\api 2. Install Exact Versions PowerShell - install the locked Prisma stack # From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm add -D prisma@7.9.1 @types/pg pnpm add @prisma/client@7.9.1 @prisma/adapter-pg@7.9.1 pg dotenv @nestjs/config The CLI is a development dependency. The generated client runtime, adapter and pg driver are runtime dependencies because the NestJS API uses them while running. Package responsibilities Package Type Why it exists prisma@7.9.1 dev CLI: init, validate, generate, migrate, studio @prisma/client@7.9.1 runtime Runtime package used by generated Prisma Client @prisma/adapter-pg@7.9.1 runtime Prisma 7 PostgreSQL driver adapter pg runtime Underlying PostgreSQL driver dotenv runtime/tooling Loads .env for Prisma config/scripts @nestjs/config runtime Loads trusted backend configuration into Nest DI @types/pg dev TypeScript declarations for pg when needed 3. Verify the Local CLI PowerShell - use the project-local CLI # From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm exec prisma version Do not rely on a globally installed prisma executable. pnpm exec resolves the version declared by this project, which is exactly the reproducibility we want in a long course. Stop if one package reports a different version. 4. pnpm Build Approval If pnpm reports ignored dependency build scripts, treat that as a supply-chain security decision rather than a broken install. Newer Prisma releases are not substituted halfway through the course. 1. Initialize Prisma Initialization creates the Prisma workspace inside apps/api. It does not create your production architecture, and it does not replace the database you already created in Supabase. PowerShell - initialize Prisma inside apps/api # From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm exec prisma init 2. What prisma init Creates apps/api/.env apps/api/prisma.config.ts apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma Figure 1 - The three pieces to inspect after initialization .env Stores local environment values. It must never be committed with real secrets. prisma.config.ts Configures Prisma CLI behavior in Prisma 7, including the schema path, migration directory and the connection URL used by CLI commands. prisma/schema.prisma Defines the database provider, generated client and data models. In Prisma 7, the datasource URL no longer belongs here for this course. 3. Project Structure After Initialization Relevant paths only apps/api/ |-- .env |-- prisma.config.ts |-- prisma/ | `-- schema.prisma |-- src/ |-- package.json `-- ... 4. Do Not Re-run init as a Fix Once these files exist, errors should be diagnosed in place. Re-running initialization can overwrite assumptions or encourage deleting the evidence you need to debug. 5. Update the Example Environment File apps/api/.env.example # Runtime application connection (Phase 08 recommends a session-capable pooled URL for local NestJS). DATABASE_URL= # Prisma CLI / migration connection. Prefer a direct URL when reachable. DIRECT_URL= # Optional only if migrate dev cannot create an automatic shadow database. # NEVER point this at the same database as DIRECT_URL. SHADOW_DATABASE_URL= SECRET RULE Real DATABASE_URL, DIRECT_URL and SHADOW_DATABASE_URL values belong only in .env or a secure deployment secret store. They never belong in screenshots, documentation, Git commits or NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables. text: prisma-config-supabase-urls-and-shadow-database Prisma Config Supabase URLs and Shadow Database PHASE 09 / BOOK 05 Prisma Config, Supabase URLs & Shadow Database Separate runtime traffic from migration tooling NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are… PHASE 09 / BOOK 05 Prisma Config, Supabase URLs & Shadow Database Separate runtime traffic from migration tooling NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are locked to 7.9.1. Newer Prisma releases are not substituted halfway through the course. 1. Prisma CLI and NestJS Runtime Have Different Connection Jobs NestJS runtime Prisma CLI Uses DATABASE_URL Uses DIRECT_URL Long-running application traffic Migrations / introspection / Studio PrismaPg / pg pool Needs session semantics Session-capable pooled URL works migrate dev also needs shadow DB well locally Figure 1 - Separate the runtime and tooling connection roles 2. Configure prisma.config.ts apps/api/prisma.config.ts import "dotenv/config"; import { defineConfig, env } from "prisma/config"; export default defineConfig({ schema: "prisma/schema.prisma", migrations: { path: "prisma/migrations", }, datasource: { // CLI / migrations: direct or session-capable connection. url: env("DIRECT_URL"), }, }); The CLI now reads DIRECT_URL. For Supabase, prefer the direct database URL when your network can reach it. A session pooler connection on port 5432 is an alternative when direct IPv6 connectivity is unavailable. Do not use transaction pooling for migration tooling. 3. Environment Variables apps/api/.env.example # Runtime application connection (Phase 08 recommends a session-capable pooled URL for local NestJS). DATABASE_URL= # Prisma CLI / migration connection. Prefer a direct URL when reachable. DIRECT_URL= # Optional only if migrate dev cannot create an automatic shadow database. # NEVER point this at the same database as DIRECT_URL. SHADOW_DATABASE_URL= 4. Why migrate dev Needs a Shadow Database Prisma Migrate replays migration history in a temporary shadow database to detect drift and evaluate the next migration. That means migrate dev needs either permission to create/drop a shadow database automatically or a separately configured shadow database. Migration history Shadow database replay Detect drift / evaluate changes Generate SQL migration Apply to development database Figure 2 - migrate dev uses a shadow database before changing your dev schema DANGER SHADOW_DATABASE_URL must never point to the same database as DIRECT_URL. A shadow database is reset during migrate dev and can destroy data if misconfigured. 5. Supabase Privileges Supabase's current Prisma guidance recommends a dedicated Prisma database user with the privileges required for migrations, including CREATEDB when automatic shadow-database creation is used. Keep this as a development/migration concern; application runtime access should still follow least privilege as the course matures. 6. If Automatic Shadow Creation Fails Do not immediately switch to db push and ignore migration history. First diagnose whether the database user has CREATEDB. If cloud restrictions prevent automatic shadow creation, create a dedicated shadow database and set SHADOW_DATABASE_URL in prisma.config.ts. Optional prisma.config.ts change datasource: { url: env("DIRECT_URL"), shadowDatabaseUrl: env("SHADOW_DATABASE_URL"), }, Checkpoint • DATABASE_URL is reserved for runtime PrismaPg. • DIRECT_URL is used by Prisma CLI/migrations. • Transaction pooler 6543 is not used for migration tooling. • Shadow DB configuration is understood before migrate dev is run. prisma Explain Prisma Config Supabase URLs and Shadow Database in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Prisma Client Adapter and NestJS PrismaService
subtitle: Prisma 7.9.1 Architecture, Configuration & Migrations
text: prisma-client-adapter-and-nestjs-prismaservice Prisma Client Adapter and NestJS PrismaService PHASE 09 / BOOK 06 Prisma Client, PrismaPg & NestJS PrismaService Turn generated types into reusable backend infrastructure NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are… PHASE 09 / BOOK 06 Prisma Client, PrismaPg & NestJS PrismaService Turn generated types into reusable backend infrastructure NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are locked to 7.9.1. Newer Prisma releases are not substituted halfway through the course. 1. Generate Prisma Client From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm exec prisma generate Generation reads schema.prisma and emits a client tailored to the current models. Whenever the schema or generator configuration changes, regenerate explicitly. This course does not depend on migrate dev implicitly generating it. schema.prisma pnpm exec prisma generate src/generated/prisma PrismaClient type-safe API Figure 1 - Client generation is a build step, not a database migration 2. Prisma 7 Requires a Driver Adapter For direct PostgreSQL connections, Prisma 7 uses a database driver adapter. PrismaPg is the bridge between the generated Prisma Client and the pg driver connection pool. Prisma Client PrismaPg adapter pg driver/pool PostgreSQL Figure 2 - Runtime connectivity in Prisma 7 3. Wrap the Client in a NestJS Provider apps/api/src/prisma/prisma.service.ts import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from "@nestjs/common"; import { ConfigService } from "@nestjs/config"; import { PrismaPg } from "@prisma/adapter-pg"; import { PrismaClient } from "../generated/prisma/client"; @Injectable() export class PrismaService extends PrismaClient implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy { constructor(config: ConfigService) { const connectionString = config.getOrThrow<string>("DATABASE_URL"); const adapter = new PrismaPg({ connectionString }); super({ adapter }); } async onModuleInit() { await this.$connect(); } async onModuleDestroy() { await this.$disconnect(); } } The constructor reads DATABASE_URL through ConfigService, creates the adapter, and passes it to PrismaClient. The service then participates in Nest lifecycle hooks. 4. Export the Provider apps/api/src/prisma/prisma.module.ts import { Global, Module } from "@nestjs/common"; import { PrismaService } from "./prisma.service"; @Global() @Module({ providers: [PrismaService], exports: [PrismaService], }) export class PrismaModule {} Marking PrismaModule global avoids repetitive imports as features grow, but the important design point is still one shared PrismaService instance rather than creating a new PrismaClient in each request or service. 5. Load Trusted Backend Configuration apps/api/src/app.module.ts import { Module } from "@nestjs/common"; import { ConfigModule } from "@nestjs/config"; import { HealthModule } from "./health/health.module"; import { TodosModule } from "./todos/todos.module"; import { PrismaModule } from "./prisma/prisma.module"; @Module({ imports: [ ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true }), PrismaModule, HealthModule, TodosModule, ], }) export class AppModule {} 6. Why One Client Instance Matters Each Prisma Client with a PostgreSQL adapter can own a connection pool. Creating clients repeatedly can exhaust database connections. NestJS dependency injection gives us a natural process-wide provider. ANTI-PATTERN Do not put new PrismaClient({ adapter }) inside every controller method. That mixes infrastructure with HTTP logic and can create many connection pools. 7. Connectivity Probe Without Building CRUD Yet Use only as a connectivity check // Temporary diagnostic inside a service or one-off script const result = await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT 1 AS ok`; console.log(result); A raw SELECT 1 verifies runtime connectivity without skipping ahead into Phase 11 CRUD architecture. Checkpoint • Generated client exists. • NestJS imports the generated client from the configured path. • PrismaPg receives DATABASE_URL. • PrismaService is injectable and uses one client instance. • The API can connect and disconnect cleanly. prisma Explain Prisma Client Adapter and NestJS PrismaService in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Migration Lifecycle and First Migration
subtitle: Prisma 7.9.1 Architecture, Configuration & Migrations
text: migration-lifecycle-and-first-migration Migration Lifecycle and First Migration PHASE 09 / BOOK 07 Migration Lifecycle & First Migration Create schema history you can inspect, commit and deploy NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg… PHASE 09 / BOOK 07 Migration Lifecycle & First Migration Create schema history you can inspect, commit and deploy NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are locked to 7.9.1. Newer Prisma releases are not substituted halfway through the course. 1. Migration Is Schema History, Not a Magic Sync Button The Prisma schema is the desired model. A migration is an ordered SQL change that moves a database from one known state to another. Keeping that history in Git is what makes team and deployment workflows reproducible. Edit schema.prisma Validate migrate dev creates SQL Review migration.sql Apply to development DB Run prisma generate Commit schema + migration Figure 1 - Safe development migration workflow 2. Create the First Migration From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm exec prisma migrate dev --name init_todo If Prisma asks to reset a database containing data you care about, stop. Do not confirm reflexively. A reset is destructive and should be understood before proceeding. 3. Inspect the Generated SQL Generated migration directory prisma/ `-- migrations/ `-- <timestamp>_init_todo/ `-- migration.sql Open migration.sql. Compare it with the SQL concepts learned in Phase 07: CREATE TABLE, primary key, required columns and defaults. Prisma migrations are not opaque binary files; they are reviewable SQL. 4. The _prisma_migrations Table Prisma records applied migration metadata in the database so tooling can compare migration history with the actual development database. 5. Explicit Client Generation Run after migration/schema changes pnpm exec prisma generate PRISMA 7 COURSE RULE Run prisma generate explicitly. This avoids relying on version-specific assumptions about migrate dev side effects and makes the build step obvious to the learner. 6. Migration Status From: taskflow\apps\api pnpm exec prisma migrate status 7. Development vs Production Environment Command Purpose Development prisma migrate dev Create + apply migrations, detect drift, uses shadow DB Production / staging prisma migrate deploy Apply already-committed pending migrations; do not generate new schema de Any stage prisma migrate status Inspect migration state 8. Never Edit an Applied Shared Migration Casually Once a migration has been applied and shared with teammates or environments, rewriting it changes history. Fix forward with a new migration unless you are deliberately resetting an isolated development database. text: prisma-cli-workflow-development-and-production Prisma CLI Workflow Development and Production PHASE 09 / BOOK 08 Prisma CLI Workflow: Development & Production Use the smallest correct command for each stage NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg… PHASE 09 / BOOK 08 Prisma CLI Workflow: Development & Production Use the smallest correct command for each stage NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are locked to 7.9.1. Newer Prisma releases are not substituted halfway through the course. 1. The CLI Commands You Should Actually Remember Command When to use it pnpm exec prisma version Confirm exact local toolchain pnpm exec prisma validate Check config/schema syntax pnpm exec prisma generate Regenerate typed client pnpm exec prisma migrate dev --name ... Create/apply development migration pnpm exec prisma migrate status Inspect migration state pnpm exec prisma migrate deploy Apply committed migrations in production/staging pnpm exec prisma studio Inspect/edit data interactively in development 2. text: debugging-prisma-and-common-failures Debugging Prisma and Common Failures PHASE 09 / BOOK 09 Debugging Prisma & Common Failures Diagnose the failing layer instead of replacing the project NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg… PHASE 09 / BOOK 09 Debugging Prisma & Common Failures Diagnose the failing layer instead of replacing the project NestJS PrismaService Prisma Client PrismaPg driver adapter Supabase PostgreSQL Figure - The database access stack introduced in Phase 09 Course rule: Prisma CLI, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg are locked to 7.9.1. Newer Prisma releases are not substituted halfway through the course. 1. Debug Prisma by Layer Working directory / local package Prisma config Schema + generator Generated client Driver adapter Connection URL / network PostgreSQL privileges / schema Figure 1 - Start at the failing layer instead of rewriting the project 2. Wrong Version or Global CLI Use the project-local CLI pnpm exec prisma version If versions differ from 7.9.1, inspect package.json and the lockfile. Do not "fix" the docs to match a newer package accidentally installed. 3. Generated Client Module Error Symptoms may mention exports, require, ESM or module scope. In this NestJS CommonJS course, confirm the generator contains moduleFormat = "cjs" and regenerate the client. Regenerate after generator changes pnpm exec prisma generate 4. PrismaClient Requires an Adapter Prisma 7 direct database connections require a driver adapter. If the code constructs PrismaClient without PrismaPg, fix the construction path instead of downgrading packages. 5. DATABASE_URL vs DIRECT_URL Confusion Symptom Likely layer Nest API cannot query but CLI works DATABASE_URL / runtime adapter migrate/status fails but API query works DIRECT_URL / Prisma CLI path Browser fetch fails before API query HTTP/CORS, not Prisma P1001 / connection timeout Network/host/port/SSL Shadow database permission error CREATEDB or SHADOW_DATABASE_URL 6. Shadow Database Failure If migrate dev reports permission denied to create database, verify the migration user privileges. If automatic creation is not allowed, configure a dedicated shadow database. Never reuse the development database as the shadow target. 7. Pooled Connection Mistakes Transaction pooling is optimized for different workloads and does not preserve all session behavior migration tools expect. Use a direct or session-capable connection for Prisma CLI migration workflows. 8. Schema Changed but TypeScript Did Not The generated client is stale. Run prisma generate and rebuild. Schema changes do not magically rewrite TypeScript imports already produced on disk. 9. "Relation Does Not Exist" Check migration status and target database/schema. A perfectly typed generated client can still point at a database where the migration was never applied. 10. Common Anti-Patterns • Creating new PrismaClient instances in controller methods. • Putting DATABASE_URL into NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables. • Using migrate dev in production. • Ignoring migration SQL without review. • Using db push to avoid learning migrations in a production-style project. • Deleting the migrations directory whenever drift appears. • Mixing Prisma 8 docs into this locked 7.9.1 course. • Treating Prisma validation as authorization or business validation. text: entities-relationships-cardinality-and-ownership Entities Relationships Cardinality and Ownership Entities, Relationships, Cardinality & Ownership Turn product language into relational structure Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean… Entities, Relationships, Cardinality & Ownership Turn product language into relational structure Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. Start with business language, not tables A common modeling mistake is to begin by inventing table names. Start instead with statements the business expects to remain true. Example: a workspace has many projects; a project belongs to exactly one workspace; a task belongs to one project; a workspace has many members; a user can belong to many workspaces. Figure 1 - Business rules become relationships Business statement ↓ Cardinality ↓ Foreign key / join model ↓ Database invariant The schema is a durable encoding of business relationships, not a mirror of one screen. Entity candidates Candidate Why it exists Not just a field because... User Identity referenced across workspaces It has its own lifecycle and relationships Workspace Collaboration/security boundary Many projects and memberships depend on it Membership User-to-workspace participation It has role/status metadata Project Groups tasks inside a workspace It has ownership, dates and task relationships Task Work item tracked by the system It has state, priority and relationships Cardinality Relationship Meaning Relational shape Workspace 1 -> many Projects Each project belongs to one workspace projects.workspace_id FK Project 1 -> many Tasks Each task belongs to one project tasks.project_id FK User many <-> many Workspace Users join many workspaces and vice versa memberships join table Optionality is part of cardinality "A task may have an assignee" is different from "every task must have an assignee." The first permits a NULL assignee reference. The second should be NOT NULL. Optionality should follow domain rules, not convenience. Ownership vs association A task can be associated with an assignee without the assignee owning the containing project. Ownership affects security and lifecycle decisions. Model this distinction explicitly rather than assuming every foreign key means ownership. A useful review question: If the parent disappears, should the child disappear too? If the answer is unclear, you have not finished modeling lifecycle ownership. subtitle: Relational Data Modeling
text: optionality-keys-and-constraints Optionality Keys and Constraints Optionality, Keys & Constraints Put invariants in the database instead of only in application code Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the… Optionality, Keys & Constraints Put invariants in the database instead of only in application code Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. A valid row is more than a TypeScript object Database constraints remain active regardless of which application code writes the row. They are therefore the final line of defense for structural integrity. Figure 1 - Integrity layers UI validation ↓ API validation ↓ Business rules ↓ Database constraints The closer a rule is to a permanent data invariant, the stronger the case for enforcing it in the database too. Primary keys Every durable entity needs a stable identity. For TaskFlow, UUID-style IDs are appropriate for entities that may cross service/API boundaries. The course will use UUID-compatible Prisma String IDs generated with uuid() for production entities. Natural vs surrogate keys Key type Example Trade-off Natural email address Readable but business values can change Surrogate generated UUID Stable identity independent of business attributes Uniqueness Uniqueness should reflect business invariants. Example: a workspace slug may be globally unique; a membership should be unique for the pair (workspaceId, userId); project names may or may not be unique depending on product rules. @@unique([workspaceId, userId]) NULL is a domain decision Field Possible rule Schema implication Project.name Always required NOT NULL Task.description Optional narrative nullable Task.assigneeId Unassigned is allowed nullable FK Field Possible rule Schema implication Task.completedAt Only present when completed nullable timestamp Check-like invariants Prisma schema syntax does not express every possible PostgreSQL CHECK constraint directly. When the database must guarantee an invariant that exceeds ORM-level expressiveness, use reviewed SQL migrations rather than pretending the invariant does not exist. Do not encode every business rule as a database constraint. Workflow rules that require external state, permissions, or multiple aggregates usually belong in application services. Use the database for structural invariants it can enforce reliably. subtitle: Relational Data Modeling
text: many-to-many-membership-and-composite-uniqueness Many to Many Membership and Composite Uniqueness Many-to-Many Membership & Composite Uniqueness Model collaboration as a first-class relationship Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean… Many-to-Many Membership & Composite Uniqueness Model collaboration as a first-class relationship Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. Why a bare many-to-many is not enough Users and workspaces are many-to-many, but their relationship has meaningful data: role, status, joinedAt, and possibly invitation metadata. That means the relationship deserves its own entity: Membership. Figure 1 - Explicit join entity User ↓ Membership role / status / joinedAt ↓ Workspace Membership is not plumbing. It is a domain record with its own behavior and constraints. Core invariant A user should normally have at most one active membership record per workspace. Encode the structural uniqueness with a composite unique constraint. model Membership { id String @id @default(uuid()) userId String workspaceId String role MembershipRole @default(MEMBER) joinedAt DateTime @default(now()) user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id]) workspace Workspace @relation(fields: [workspaceId], references: [id]) @@unique([workspaceId, userId]) @@index([userId]) } Why both an id and composite uniqueness? The surrogate id gives the membership a stable independent identity for APIs/audit events. The composite uniqueness protects the relationship invariant. They solve different problems. Role belongs on membership A user can be ADMIN in Workspace A and MEMBER in Workspace B. Therefore role cannot be modeled as one global User.role if role is workspace-scoped. This is a foundational enterprise pattern: identity is global, permissions are often contextual. HRIS department membership, tenant membership, project membership and organization membership all use similar relational reasoning. Assignment should target membership or user? For TaskFlow, a task assignee ultimately represents a user participating in the workspace. Modeling assignee as userId is simpler, but then service logic must verify workspace membership. Modeling assigneeMembershipId makes membership validity structural but couples task assignment to membership row lifecycle. The course will use assigneeId -> User for clarity and enforce membership in the service layer later. modeling Explain Many to Many Membership and Composite Uniqueness in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. subtitle: Relational Data Modeling
text: enums-lookup-tables-and-state-modeling Enums Lookup Tables and State Modeling Enums, Lookup Tables & State Modeling Choose the right representation for finite business states Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable… Enums, Lookup Tables & State Modeling Choose the right representation for finite business states Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. Not every string should be free text Values such as task status and priority usually come from a constrained set. Free-text values create invalid states such as "INPROGRESS", "in_progress", and "Doing" describing the same concept. Three common options Approach Good for Cost Application string Prototype-only values Weak integrity Database/Prisma enum Small stable finite set Schema migration to change values Lookup table Admin-configurable or metadata-rich set More joins and lifecycle complexity TaskFlow choice enum TaskStatus { TODO IN_PROGRESS DONE CANCELED } enum TaskPriority { LOW MEDIUM HIGH URGENT } enum MembershipRole { OWNER ADMIN MEMBER } Why enums here? These values are small, have clear semantics, and are expected to change infrequently. They are part of the application contract and are good candidates for enums. When a lookup table would be better If each status needs configurable color, ordering, SLA behavior, translations, or customer-defined values, it has become data rather than a fixed code-level state. A lookup table may then be more appropriate. Do not use enums for values likely to be customized per tenant. Schema migrations are a poor substitute for normal application data management. State transitions are not automatically database constraints An enum can guarantee that status is one of the allowed values, but it does not guarantee valid transitions such as TODO -> DONE. Transition permissions and workflow rules belong in the service layer unless a database trigger is intentionally part of the architecture. state Explain Enums Lookup Tables and State Modeling in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Deletion Referential Actions and Lifecycle
subtitle: Relational Data Modeling
text: deletion-referential-actions-and-lifecycle Deletion Referential Actions and Lifecycle Deletion, Referential Actions & Lifecycle Design what happens when related data disappears Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should… Deletion, Referential Actions & Lifecycle Design what happens when related data disappears Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. Delete is a business operation A foreign key answers whether related rows may exist. A referential action answers what the database should do when the referenced row is updated or deleted. This should follow ownership and retention requirements. Action Meaning Typical use Cascade Delete children automatically Strong ownership, e.g. project-local tasks Restrict / NoAction Block parent deletion Records must be handled deliberately SetNull Keep child, clear optional reference Optional assignee/reference Application-managed Service performs explicit archival/deletion workflow Audited enterprise processes TaskFlow lifecycle choices Relationship Suggested behavior Reason Workspace -> Project Cascade in learning model Projects have no meaning outside workspace Project -> Task Cascade Tasks belong to project User -> Membership Cascade/explicit cleanup dependingMembership audit needs depends on user identity User -> Task assignee SetNull Task should survive account removal Workspace -> Membership Cascade Membership is scoped to workspace workspace Workspace @relation(fields: [workspaceId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade) assignee User? @relation(fields: [assigneeId], references: [id], onDelete: SetNull) Soft deletion is not free Adding deletedAt looks simple but changes almost every query, uniqueness rule, reporting workflow, restore behavior and index strategy. Do not add soft deletion merely because enterprise systems often use it. Production retention requirements may require archival instead of cascading hard deletes. The course model teaches relational ownership, but a regulated HRIS or accounting system should derive lifecycle from explicit retention policy. Exercise Choose and justify an on-delete behavior for comments, file attachments, activity log rows, and workspace invitations. There is no universally correct answer; the point is to connect lifecycle semantics to referential actions. modeling Explain Deletion Referential Actions and Lifecycle in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. subtitle: Relational Data Modeling
text: indexes-and-query-driven-design Indexes and Query Driven Design Indexes & Query-Driven Design Design access paths from real application queries Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean… Indexes & Query-Driven Design Design access paths from real application queries Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. Do not index every column Indexes trade storage and write cost for faster access paths. Index design should start from important query patterns, not from a desire to "optimize" every field. Figure 1 - Query-driven indexing Product requirement ↓ Frequent query ↓ Filter / join / sort columns ↓ Candidate index ↓ Measure with real workload Indexes are consequences of access patterns. Expected TaskFlow queries Query Likely columns List projects in workspace workspaceId + createdAt/name List tasks in project projectId + status + createdAt My assigned tasks assigneeId + status Find memberships for user userId Resolve workspace by slug slug unique Candidate Prisma indexes model Task { // ... @@index([projectId, status]) @@index([assigneeId, status]) @@index([createdAt]) } model Project { // ... @@index([workspaceId]) } Composite index order matters An index on (projectId, status) is naturally useful for queries beginning with projectId. It is not equivalent to (status, projectId) for every workload. The order should reflect leading filter/selectivity and sort patterns. Foreign keys are not automatically all the indexes you need A foreign-key constraint protects referential integrity. Query performance is a separate concern. PostgreSQL does not automatically create an index on the referencing foreign-key column simply because the foreign key exists. Performance design rule: model correctness first, then choose indexes from observed high-value queries, and validate with EXPLAIN/production-like data later. authentication Explain Indexes and Query Driven Design in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. subtitle: Relational Data Modeling
text: normalization-and-denormalization Normalization and Denormalization Normalization & Denormalization Avoid duplicated truth without turning the schema into theory theater Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data… Normalization & Denormalization Avoid duplicated truth without turning the schema into theory theater Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. What normalization is trying to prevent Normalization reduces contradictory copies of the same fact. If workspace name is repeated on every task, renaming the workspace requires changing many rows and creates opportunities for inconsistency. Figure 1 - One source of truth Task rows repeat workspaceName ↓ Update anomaly ↓ Normalize Workspace ↓ Tasks reference workspace indirectly through Project Relationships replace duplicated facts with references to authoritative records. Practical normal form mindset Question Healthy direction Does each row represent one thing? Yes - avoid repeating groups Does an attribute depend on the whole identity? Yes - avoid partial dependencies Is a fact stored in the entity that owns it? Yes - avoid transitive duplication Do not over-normalize labels into pointless tables A three-value stable priority does not automatically need a task_priorities table. Normalization is about dependency and truth, not maximizing table count. When denormalization can be intentional Read-heavy reporting, immutable historical snapshots, analytics, search documents, or expensive aggregate views can justify duplicated derived data. But denormalization should name the consistency strategy explicitly. Never duplicate a field because JOINs "feel slow" without measurement. Relational databases are designed to join normalized data efficiently when keys and indexes are appropriate. TaskFlow examples • Workspace name belongs on Workspace, not Task. • Membership role belongs on Membership, not globally on User. • Task status belongs on Task because it is a fact about that task. • A future immutable audit event may snapshot labels because history should not change when the live record changes. modeling Explain Normalization and Denormalization in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. subtitle: Relational Data Modeling
text: migration-planning-and-safe-schema-evolution Migration Planning and Safe Schema Evolution Migration Planning & Safe Schema Evolution Change durable data without treating migrations as generated noise Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the… Migration Planning & Safe Schema Evolution Change durable data without treating migrations as generated noise Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure ↓ Production-ready relational model ↓ Persistent TaskFlow CRUD Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it. A schema change is a data change Once production data exists, changing schema can affect stored rows, constraints, application compatibility, indexes, lock duration, and rollback strategy. Migrations deserve code review. Figure 1 - Safe change workflow Change business requirement ↓ Edit schema ↓ Generate migration ↓ Review SQL ↓ Backfill / stage if needed ↓ Apply + verify The migration file is part of the application codebase and deployment story. Additive changes are easiest Adding a nullable column is usually easier than immediately adding a required column to a populated table. For required new data, use a staged migration: add nullable/default, backfill, validate, then enforce NOT NULL. Example staged change Step Action 1 Add optional workspace timezone 2 Deploy code that can write it 3 Backfill existing workspaces 4 Add required constraint if product truly requires it 5 Remove temporary compatibility code Renames can be destructive if generated naively An ORM may interpret a field rename as drop-old + add-new, which can lose data. Review generated SQL and use deliberate SQL rename operations or migration edits when preserving existing data matters. Environment workflow Environment Command intent Development migrate dev creates/tests migration CI / staging / production migrate deploy applies committed migrations Never production ad-hoc migrate dev against live data A rollback is not automatically "run the migration backward." Many database changes are irreversible after data is transformed or deleted. Production change planning should prefer forward fixes, backups, compatibility windows, and explicit restore strategy. Phase 10 migration plan • Replace the minimal Todo-only learning model with the TaskFlow production model in a controlled development migration. • Review generated SQL before applying. • Use a development database/shadow workflow only. • Verify tables, foreign keys, uniqueness and indexes after migration. • Do not seed production-like identities until authentication design is introduced. prisma Explain Migration Planning and Safe Schema Evolution in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Debugging Workshop — Phase 10: Relational Data Modeling Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk Business nouns -> entities -> relationships/cardinality -> constraints -> Prisma models -> migration -> seeded graph Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.
