subtitle: Persistent Task CRUD API
text: from-memory-to-durable-state From Memory to Durable State From Memory to Durable State Why the storage lifetime must move beyond the Node.js process Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone In-memory Todo API ↓ Durable database boundary ↓ TaskFlow Task resource Phase 11 replaces process memory… From Memory to Durable State Why the storage lifetime must move beyond the Node.js process Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone In-memory Todo API ↓ Durable database boundary ↓ TaskFlow Task resource Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior. Memory solved the wrong problem The array from Phase 05 was useful because it isolated HTTP behavior. It was never meant to be durable storage. A process-local array belongs to one running Node.js process; when that process stops, the array stops existing with it. Figure 1 - The persistence gap POST /todos ↓ NestJS process memory ↓ Restart process ↓ data disappears The failure is not a bug in HTTP. It is a storage-lifetime problem. Durable state changes the ownership model Once Task rows live in PostgreSQL, NestJS no longer owns their lifetime. NestJS owns the rules for creating and changing them; PostgreSQL owns durable storage and relational constraints. Concern In-memory array PostgreSQL + Prisma Lifetime Until process exits Survives application restarts Relations Manual objects only Foreign keys + relations Concurrency One process perspective Database concurrency model Integrity Application discipline Application + database constraints Inspection Debugger/log output SQL, Prisma Studio, dashboard Why we move from Todo to Task Phase 10 established Task as a real domain entity: it belongs to a Project, has a status and priority, and can later be assigned to a User. We therefore evolve the API to /tasks instead of keeping a fake Todo resource disconnected from the production model. Real-world transfer The same transition happens when a prototype PayrollRun, PurchaseRequest, LeaveRequest, or InventoryMovement stops being a JavaScript object and becomes durable business data. Persistence does not remove the service layer A common beginner mistake is to treat Prisma as the service. Prisma knows how to access data; it does not know TaskFlow business semantics. The service remains the place where application rules and meaningful not-found behavior live. Figure 2 - Responsibility boundary TasksController: HTTP input/output ↓ TasksService: application behavior ↓ PrismaService: reusable database dependency ↓ PostgreSQL: durable relational state Each layer becomes easier to change because its responsibility is explicit. What changes and what stays stable • HTTP verbs and REST resource semantics from Phase 05 remain valid. • CORS and fetch behavior from Phase 06 remain valid. • The storage implementation changes from memory to PostgreSQL. • The data model from Phase 10 becomes executable schema. • The frontend still talks to an HTTP API; it never receives database credentials. state Explain From Memory to Durable State in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: schema-migration-and-development-seed Schema Migration and Development Seed Schema Migration and Development Seed Evolve additively, generate safely, seed the minimum relational graph Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone Phase 09 learning schema ↓ Add TaskFlow domain + preserve legacy table ↓ Seed Workspace + Project… Schema Migration and Development Seed Evolve additively, generate safely, seed the minimum relational graph Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone Phase 09 learning schema ↓ Add TaskFlow domain + preserve legacy table ↓ Seed Workspace + Project Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior. STEP 1 - Evolve the Prisma schema safely Phase 09 created a small Todo table for learning. Phase 10 designed the real TaskFlow domain. A production-minded migration should prefer additive change over casually dropping a table that might contain useful data. Migration strategy Keep the old PostgreSQL table for now by mapping it to a clearly named LegacyTodo model. Add the new User, Workspace, Membership, Project, and Task models in the same schema. Retire legacy data only after an explicit cleanup/migration decision. model LegacyTodo { id String @id @default(cuid()) title String completed Boolean @default(false) createdAt DateTime @default(now()) updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt @@map("Todo") } The Prisma model name changes for application clarity, while @@map("Todo") preserves the existing database table name. The new TaskFlow models are then added beside it. Run schema checks before migration From taskflow\apps\api run: pnpm exec prisma format pnpm exec prisma validate Validation should succeed before Prisma touches the database. If it does not, stop here. Migration output is not the place to discover a malformed schema. Create the domain migration pnpm exec prisma migrate dev --name add_taskflow_domain Review the SQL Open the generated migration.sql before treating the migration as complete. Confirm that the migration creates the TaskFlow tables and does not unexpectedly DROP the learning Todo table. Regenerate the client The generated Prisma Client is derived from schema.prisma. New models are not available to TypeScript until the client is regenerated. pnpm exec prisma generate pnpm run build Figure 1 - Schema-to-runtime lifecycle schema.prisma ↓ migrate dev ↓ PostgreSQL schema ↓ prisma generate ↓ generated Prisma Client ↓ NestJS build Database structure and TypeScript client code are related, but they are not the same artifact. STEP 2 - Seed the minimum relational graph A Task requires projectId, and a Project requires a Workspace. Rather than weakening those relations for convenience, Phase 11 creates a tiny development graph that satisfies the real model. Workspace -> Membership <- User -> Project -> Task The included prisma/seed.ts is idempotent for the learning Workspace/User/Membership. The module we actually need The old TodosModule stored data in memory. Phase 11 introduces TasksModule because Task is now the durable domain resource. We do not create repository abstractions yet; PrismaService already gives the service a clean database dependency. src/tasks/ tasks.module.ts tasks.controller.ts tasks.service.ts tasks.types.ts Module wiring import { Module } from "@nestjs/common"; import { TasksController } from "./tasks.controller"; import { TasksService } from "./tasks.service"; @Module({ controllers: [TasksController], providers: [TasksService], }) export class TasksModule {} PrismaModule is global from Phase 09, so TasksModule does not need to import it explicitly. TasksService can request PrismaService through Nest dependency injection. Application module import { Module } from "@nestjs/common"; import { ConfigModule } from "@nestjs/config"; import { HealthModule } from "./health/health.module"; import { PrismaModule } from "./prisma/prisma.module"; import { TasksModule } from "./tasks/tasks.module"; @Module({ imports: [ ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true }), PrismaModule, HealthModule, TasksModule, ], }) export class AppModule {} Why remove TodosModule from AppModule? The old /todos endpoint represented temporary storage. Leaving it registered beside /tasks would create two competing resource models and confuse the learning architecture. Compile-time request shapes - temporary import { TaskPriority, TaskStatus, } from "../generated/prisma/client"; // These are compile-time shapes only. Phase 12 replaces this temporary // boundary with DTOs + runtime validation. export type CreateTaskInput = { projectId: string; title: string; description?: string | null; }; export type UpdateTaskInput = { title?: string; description?: string | null; status?: TaskStatus; priority?: TaskPriority; }; These TypeScript types help the editor and compiler, but they do not validate JSON received from the network. A caller can still send an invalid string at runtime. Phase 12 replaces this temporary boundary with DTOs and runtime validation. The update body in this phase is intentionally small: title, description, status, and priority. @Patch(":id") update( @Param("id") id: string, @Body() body: UpdateTaskInput, ) { return this.tasksService.update(id, body); } Prisma update async update(id: string, input: UpdateTaskInput) { try { return await this.prisma.task.update({ where: { id }, data: input, }); } catch (error) { this.rethrowMissingTask(error, id); } } Prisma performs a targeted UPDATE for the row selected by the unique id. updatedAt changes automatically because the schema marks it with @updatedAt. Why catch P2025? For the locked Prisma 7 client used by this course, an update or delete that depends on a missing record can raise PrismaClientKnownRequestError with code P2025. We translate that database-client error into 404 for the HTTP contract. private rethrowMissingTask( error: unknown, id: string, ): never { if ( error instanceof Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError && error.code === "P2025" ) { throw new NotFoundException( `Task ${id} was not found.`, ); } throw error; } PowerShell update $patch = @{ status = "DONE" priority = "HIGH" } | ConvertTo-Json Invoke-RestMethod ` -Method Patch ` -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:4000/tasks/$taskId" ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $patch Important limitation TypeScript says status is TaskStatus, but raw JSON is still untrusted at runtime. text: delete-and-error-semantics Delete and Error Semantics Delete and Error Semantics 204 deletion, missing rows, and honest HTTP meaning Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone DELETE /tasks/:id ↓ Prisma delete ↓ 204 or 404 Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior.… Delete and Error Semantics 204 deletion, missing rows, and honest HTTP meaning Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone DELETE /tasks/:id ↓ Prisma delete ↓ 204 or 404 Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior. DELETE /tasks/:id - remove a durable row Deletion is a useful place to separate database return values from HTTP response semantics. Prisma can return the deleted row internally, while the HTTP endpoint can intentionally return 204 No Content. @Delete(":id") @HttpCode(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) async remove(@Param("id") id: string) { await this.tasksService.remove(id); } async remove(id: string) { try { return await this.prisma.task.delete({ where: { id }, }); } catch (error) { this.rethrowMissingTask(error, id); } } Test deletion PowerShell can expose the HTTP status directly with Invoke-WebRequest: $response = Invoke-WebRequest ` -Method Delete ` -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:4000/tasks/$taskId" $response.StatusCode Expected result 204 means the request succeeded and there is intentionally no response body. A later GET for the same id should return 404. Error mapping is not a global architecture yet Phase 11 handles the one Prisma error needed for CRUD semantics close to TasksService. Phase 13 will introduce a more systematic error strategy and exception mapping. We do not build a giant global abstraction before there is enough repeated behavior to justify one. Situation HTTP meaning Current handling Task does not exist 404 Not Found NotFoundException Create succeeds 201 Created Nest POST default Read/update succeeds 200 OK Nest default Delete succeeds 204 No Content Explicit @HttpCode Malformed body Not robust yet Phase 12 Unexpected database failure 500-class failure Propagates to Nest Do not turn every database error into 400 A timeout, connection failure, constraint violation, and missing row are not the same condition. Error handling should preserve meaning. text: persistence-verification-and-database-inspection Persistence Verification and Database Inspection Persistence Verification and Database Inspection Prove durability with restart tests, Prisma Studio, and SQL Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone Create database row ↓ Restart NestJS ↓ Read the same row Phase 11 replaces process memory with… Persistence Verification and Database Inspection Prove durability with restart tests, Prisma Studio, and SQL Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone Create database row ↓ Restart NestJS ↓ Read the same row Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior. The restart test - proof of persistence The strongest Phase 11 demonstration is intentionally simple: create a Task, stop NestJS, start NestJS again, and read the same Task. If it survives, storage lifetime has moved out of the Node.js process and into PostgreSQL. Figure 1 - Persistence proof POST /tasks ↓ row committed to PostgreSQL ↓ stop NestJS ↓ start NestJS ↓ GET /tasks ↓ same row still exists Persistence is observable behavior, not a diagram label. Verification sequence • Create at least two Tasks with POST /tasks. • Record one Task id and its updatedAt value. • Stop the API process with Ctrl+C. • Start the API again from apps/api using pnpm run start:dev. • Call GET /tasks and GET /tasks/:id. • Confirm the same ids and values remain. Inspect through Prisma Studio From apps/api you can open a development inspection UI: pnpm exec prisma studio Use Studio as an inspection/development tool, not as a substitute for application rules. The important question is whether the Task table contains the same rows the API returns. Inspect through Supabase The Supabase Table Editor or SQL Editor gives a second perspective. Querying the table directly helps separate database truth from API rendering problems. select id, "projectId", title, status, priority, "createdAt", "updatedAt" from "Task" order by "createdAt" desc; Debugging principle If the row exists in PostgreSQL but GET /tasks does not return it, debug the NestJS/Prisma query path. If the row never reached PostgreSQL, debug the create request or database write path. Database constraints still matter Try to reason about what happens if a Task references a Project that does not exist. The foreign key protects relational integrity even if application code contains a bug. text: runtime-validation-mental-model Runtime Validation Mental Model Runtime Validation Mental Model Why TypeScript types are not runtime validation and where trust boundaries belong Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone JSON crosses the network ↓ Schema validates at runtime ↓ Service applies business rules… Runtime Validation Mental Model Why TypeScript types are not runtime validation and where trust boundaries belong Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone JSON crosses the network ↓ Schema validates at runtime ↓ Service applies business rules ↓ Database enforces persistence constraints Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic. Static types are not a firewall A TypeScript annotation exists for the compiler and editor. By the time JSON arrives over HTTP, the sender is not constrained by your TypeScript source code. Postman, PowerShell, a browser, a mobile app, or a malicious caller can send any syntactically valid JSON value. type CreateTaskInput = { projectId: string; title: string; }; // This type cannot stop a network caller from sending: { "projectId": 123, "title": false, "admin": true } Figure 1 - Trust boundary External caller ↓ HTTP / JSON ↓ Runtime validation boundary ↓ Controller receives validated value ↓ Service applies business rules ↓ Prisma persists valid domain data Validation belongs at the system boundary because that is where untrusted external data enters trusted application code. Validation vs business rules vs database constraints Question Best first owner Example Is this input shaped correctly? Validation schema title is a non-empty string Is this request allowed by the Service/business logic assignee belongs to workspace domain? Must this invariant hold for Database constraint foreign key references a real Project persisted rows? Strong systems usually use all three layers. Validation is not a replacement for database constraints, and database constraints are not a replacement for meaningful application rules. DTO does not have to mean class In older NestJS examples, DTO usually means a class decorated with class-validator annotations. NestJS 12 adds a first-class schema-first workflow. In this course, a DTO means the validated data shape crossing the HTTP boundary. We infer the TypeScript DTO type from the Zod schema instead of manually duplicating it in a class. export const createTaskSchema = z.strictObject({ projectId: z.uuid(), title: z.string().trim().min(1).max(200), }); export type CreateTaskDto = z.infer<typeof createTaskSchema>; One source of truth The schema is executable at runtime and also produces the TypeScript type. This removes a common source of drift where validation says one thing while a separately maintained interface says another. Parsing may also transform Validation libraries can do more than return yes/no. Trimming, coercion, defaults, and transformations can change the value that crosses the boundary. For that reason, think in terms of input -> parse -> validated output rather than input -> boolean. text: zod-4-and-nestjs-12-standard-schema Zod 4 and NestJS 12 Standard Schema Zod 4 + NestJS 12 Standard Schema Install Zod, lock the version, and use NestJS 12 built-in schema-first validation Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Zod schema metadata ↓ StandardSchemaValidationPipe ↓ validated controller parameter Phase 12… Zod 4 + NestJS 12 Standard Schema Install Zod, lock the version, and use NestJS 12 built-in schema-first validation Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Zod schema metadata ↓ StandardSchemaValidationPipe ↓ validated controller parameter Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic. STEP 1 - Install Zod in the API package Zod belongs to apps/api because Phase 12 uses it to validate NestJS request inputs. Do not add it to the monorepo root merely because multiple applications might use it someday. From taskflow\apps\api run: pnpm add zod@4.6.5 Then verify the package version from the same directory: pnpm list zod Course lock Zod 4.6.5 is locked for this phase. If a newer patch appears later, keep the book series internally consistent unless the course is intentionally upgraded. Why Zod in this course? • Schema definitions execute at runtime. • The same schema can infer TypeScript types. • Zod implements the Standard Schema interface used by NestJS 12. • It works in Node.js and browsers, which gives us future reuse options without forcing shared packages today. • The API can express strict object boundaries, enums, UUIDs, string rules, nullable fields, and custom refinements. NestJS 12 changed the recommended teaching path Historically, many NestJS courses used class-validator + class-transformer or a custom ZodValidationPipe. Those approaches still exist. NestJS 12, however, added first-class Standard Schema support to route parameter decorators and a built-in StandardSchemaValidationPipe. Approach Good fit TaskFlow Phase 12 ValidationPipe + class-validator Existing class-decorator DTO projects Not selected Custom Zod pipe Older Nest versions / special behavior Not necessary StandardSchemaValidationPipe + Zod Schema-first NestJS 12 projects Selected STEP 2 - Register validation globally The route decorators will attach schema metadata. The global pipe is what actually validates that metadata before the controller handler runs. import { StandardSchemaValidationPipe } from "@nestjs/common"; // inside bootstrap() app.useGlobalPipes(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe()); Figure 1 - NestJS validation position Fastify receives request ↓ Nest resolves route parameters ↓ StandardSchemaValidationPipe validates schema metadata ↓ Controller method is invoked ↓ Service runs When schema validation fails, the controller method is not called. Do not validate twice Once the schema is attached to @Body() or @Param() and the global StandardSchemaValidationPipe is registered, do not immediately call createTaskSchema.parse(body) again inside the service. text: task-schemas-and-inferred-dtos Task Schemas and Inferred DTOs Task Schemas & Inferred DTOs Create/update schemas, UUIDs, enums, nullable fields, strict objects, and DTO inference Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone field schemas ↓ request object schemas ↓ z.infer DTO types Phase 12 introduces an… Task Schemas & Inferred DTOs Create/update schemas, UUIDs, enums, nullable fields, strict objects, and DTO inference Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone field schemas ↓ request object schemas ↓ z.infer DTO types Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic. Create the Task schemas Replace the temporary tasks.types.ts idea from Phase 11 with a schema-first file. The schema is now the boundary contract; DTO types are inferred from it. import { z } from "zod"; import { TaskPriority, TaskStatus, } from "../generated/prisma/client"; const taskTitleSchema = z .string() .trim() .min(1) .max(200); const taskDescriptionSchema = z .string() .trim() .max(2000) .nullable(); export const taskIdSchema = z.uuid(); export const createTaskSchema = z.strictObject({ projectId: z.uuid(), title: taskTitleSchema, description: taskDescriptionSchema.optional(), }); export const updateTaskSchema = z .strictObject({ title: taskTitleSchema.optional(), description: taskDescriptionSchema.optional(), status: z.enum(TaskStatus).optional(), priority: z.enum(TaskPriority).optional(), }) .refine( (value) => Object.keys(value).length > 0, "At least one updatable field must be provided.", ); export type CreateTaskDto = z.infer<typeof createTaskSchema>; export type UpdateTaskDto = z.infer<typeof updateTaskSchema>; Why z.strictObject? A normal object schema can choose how to handle unknown keys. For API request bodies in this phase, we deliberately reject unknown properties. This catches misspellings and prevents clients from assuming unsupported fields are accepted. { "projectId": "...", "title": "Ship feature", "admin": true } // strict object => reject "admin" Reject vs strip Silently stripping unknown fields can be useful in some systems. TaskFlow chooses rejection at the API boundary because a 400 response exposes client mistakes early and makes the request contract explicit. Title rules • string: callers cannot submit numbers, booleans, arrays, or objects as a title. • trim: whitespace at both ends is normalized before the service receives it. • min(1): a string containing only spaces becomes empty after trim and fails. • max(200): request payload size and domain expectations are bounded. Nullable and optional are different Shape Meaning description omitted Client did not provide this field description: null Client explicitly clears / sets no description description: "text" Client supplies a description This distinction becomes especially useful for PATCH semantics, where omitted means “do not change” while null can mean “clear the current value.” Enums come from the generated domain model TaskStatus and TaskPriority are imported from the generated Prisma client so the validation vocabulary remains aligned with the domain enum vocabulary already used by persistence. Update schema: all fields optional, empty object forbidden PATCH should permit any supported subset of fields, but an empty update does not express a meaningful change. The refine rule makes that contract explicit. .refine( (value) => Object.keys(value).length > 0, "At least one updatable field must be provided.", ); validation Explain Task Schemas and Inferred DTOs in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: controller-integration-and-validation-pipeline Controller Integration and Validation Pipeline Controller Integration & Validation Pipeline Attach schemas to @Body and @Param and keep controllers/services focused Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Fastify request ↓ Nest parameter extraction ↓ schema validation ↓ controller ↓ service Phase 12… Controller Integration & Validation Pipeline Attach schemas to @Body and @Param and keep controllers/services focused Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Fastify request ↓ Nest parameter extraction ↓ schema validation ↓ controller ↓ service Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic. Attach schemas to controller parameters NestJS 12 route parameter decorators can carry Standard Schema metadata. The controller remains concise because validation is declared where the data enters the handler. import { Body, Controller, Delete, Get, HttpCode, HttpStatus, Param, Patch, Post, } from "@nestjs/common"; import { TasksService } from "./tasks.service"; import { createTaskSchema, CreateTaskDto, taskIdSchema, updateTaskSchema, UpdateTaskDto, } from "./tasks.schemas"; @Controller("tasks") export class TasksController { constructor(private readonly tasksService: TasksService) {} @Post() create( @Body({ schema: createTaskSchema }) body: CreateTaskDto, ) { return this.tasksService.create(body); } @Get() findAll() { return this.tasksService.findAll(); } @Get(":id") findOne( @Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string, ) { return this.tasksService.findOne(id); } @Patch(":id") update( @Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string, @Body({ schema: updateTaskSchema }) body: UpdateTaskDto, ) { return this.tasksService.update(id, body); } @Delete(":id") @HttpCode(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) async remove( @Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string, ) { await this.tasksService.remove(id); } } Read the create route in English @Post() create( @Body({ schema: createTaskSchema }) body: CreateTaskDto, ) { return this.tasksService.create(body); } • @Post() maps POST /tasks. • @Body(...) extracts the JSON body. • schema: createTaskSchema attaches the runtime contract. • the global StandardSchemaValidationPipe parses the value before the method runs. • CreateTaskDto documents the validated output type at compile time. • TasksService receives already validated request shape data. Path parameters need validation too HTTP path parameters arrive as strings. A malformed task identifier should be rejected before Prisma receives a query for it. @Get(":id") findOne( @Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string, ) { return this.tasksService.findOne(id); } Figure 1 - Invalid UUID short-circuit GET /tasks/not-a-uuid ↓ taskIdSchema fails ↓ 400 Bad Request ↓ TasksService is not called ↓ Prisma is not queried Validation reduces unnecessary database work and creates a clearer client error. The service becomes simpler The service no longer needs to defend against “title is a boolean” or “projectId is an object.” Its remaining responsibilities are business/application behavior and persistence orchestration. Valid request { "projectId": "3d9c5d68-4d2f-4db0-a48a-48b5adf0988b", "title": " Validate TaskFlow input ", "description": "Schema-first validation" } The title received by the service is trimmed because the Zod schema produces the parsed output. Invalid: blank title { "projectId": "3d9c5d68-4d2f-4db0-a48a-48b5adf0988b", "title": " " } Figure 2 - Blank-title failure raw body ↓ trim title ↓ empty string ↓ min(1) fails ↓ 400 response The Project lookup never runs because shape validation fails earlier. Invalid: malformed projectId { "projectId": "project-123", "title": "Should not reach the service" } This fails UUID syntax validation. That is different from a syntactically valid UUID that simply does not identify an existing Project; the latter reaches TasksService and becomes a Project-not-found business result. subtitle: DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
text: update-task-validation Update Task Validation Update Task Validation PATCH semantics, optional fields, nullable values, enums, and empty-update rejection Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone PATCH body ↓ updateTaskSchema ↓ service ↓ Prisma update Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary… Update Task Validation PATCH semantics, optional fields, nullable values, enums, and empty-update rejection Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone PATCH body ↓ updateTaskSchema ↓ service ↓ Prisma update Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic. PATCH /tasks/:id - partial updates have different semantics Create and update inputs are related but not identical. POST requires the fields needed to create a new Task. PATCH represents a partial change to an existing Task. Field POST create PATCH update projectId required not editable in this phase title required optional description optional optional / nullable status defaulted by DB/domain optional enum update priority defaulted by DB/domain optional enum update Valid partial update { "status": "IN_PROGRESS", "priority": "HIGH" } Invalid enum { "status": "ALMOST_DONE" } The API vocabulary is the domain enum. A typo or invented state should be rejected before Prisma receives it. Empty PATCH body {} Every property is optional, but the object itself must contain at least one supported field. The refinement rule rejects a no-op PATCH. Clearing a nullable field { "description": null } Because null is explicitly allowed, this request means “clear the description.” Omitting description means “leave the current description unchanged.” Why not derive update with .partial() blindly? Zod can derive a partial object, and that is useful. But update contracts often diverge from create contracts: immutable fields may disappear, different fields may become editable, and empty updates may need rejection. Explicit update schemas can be easier to reason about in business APIs. Design principle Prefer a schema that expresses the real HTTP contract over maximum schema cleverness. Reuse small field schemas such as taskTitleSchema when it improves consistency without hiding meaning. validation Explain Update Task Validation in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Path Query and Unknown Field Validation
subtitle: DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
text: path-query-and-unknown-field-validation Path Query and Unknown Field Validation Path, Query & Unknown-Field Validation UUID parameters, query coercion mental model, strict objects, and layered boundary defense Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone path/query/body input ↓ schema policy ↓ validated values Phase 12 introduces an explicit… Path, Query & Unknown-Field Validation UUID parameters, query coercion mental model, strict objects, and layered boundary defense Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone path/query/body input ↓ schema policy ↓ validated values Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic. Validate every external entry point deliberately Request bodies are only one input source. Path parameters, query strings, headers, and eventually uploaded files all cross trust boundaries. The validation technique depends on the input and phase. UUID path parameters export const taskIdSchema = z.uuid(); @Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string The same schema is reused by GET, PATCH, and DELETE, making the route contract consistent. Query parameters arrive as strings We intentionally postpone the full Task filtering API until Phase 15, but the mental model starts here. A URL such as ?page=2 still enters as text. If the handler wants a number, the schema must coerce or parse it intentionally. const pageSchema = z.coerce.number().int().positive(); // "2" -> 2 // "banana" -> validation failure Transformation needs intention Coercion is convenient, but do not coerce every malformed input into something valid. Decide which representations your API deliberately accepts. Unknown fields: reject, strip, or preserve? Policy Behavior When it can make sense Reject 400 on unexpected property Strict APIs, catch client mistakes early Strip Remove unknown properties Compatibility-oriented form payloads Preserve Keep extras Extensible metadata contracts TaskFlow Phase 12 chooses reject for write DTOs using z.strictObject. This is a contract choice, not a universal law. Prototype pollution and framework boundaries NestJS itself includes protections around request transformation and dangerous prototype keys. subtitle: DTOs, Zod & Input Validation
text: shared-schemas-and-boundary-design Shared Schemas and Boundary Design Shared Schemas & Boundary Design When to share validation, why transport schemas are not Prisma models, and avoiding premature packages Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone API transport contract ↓ application/domain rules ↓ persistence model Phase… Shared Schemas & Boundary Design When to share validation, why transport schemas are not Prisma models, and avoiding premature packages Phase 12 - DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone API transport contract ↓ application/domain rules ↓ persistence model Phase 12 introduces an explicit runtime validation boundary before controller and service logic. Should Zod schemas be shared with Next.js now? Zod can run in both Node.js and browsers, so it is tempting to immediately move every schema into packages/validators. That may eventually be useful, but Phase 12 does not create a shared package merely because sharing is possible. Question If yes... Does the frontend need exactly the same request contract? A shared schema may reduce drift. Does moving the schema create package/build complexity now? Keep it API-local until the benefit is concrete. Does the backend schema import server-only generated Prisma Avoid shipping server coupling into a browser package. code? Would a shared transport schema be stable across clients? Shared validation may become valuable. Our current task schemas import generated Prisma enums. That is convenient inside the API but is also a signal that blindly exporting the file to a browser package could couple frontend code to backend persistence generation. A future shared-contract direction Figure 1 - Possible later evolution packages/validators: transport-only schemas ↓ apps/web imports browser-safe request schema ↓ apps/api imports same transport schema ↓ NestJS service maps validated transport data to domain/persistence Share a contract because multiple consumers genuinely need it, not because the monorepo has a packages folder. Validation schema is not your database model A transport schema describes what an API caller may send. Prisma schema describes durable relational structure. They overlap, but they should not be treated as identical artifacts. Transport/API concern Database concern title max length policy column type / persisted value unknown request keys not applicable to row schema PATCH omits unchanged field UPDATE operation semantics projectId must be UUID text foreign key relation must reference existing Project Architecture rule Do not make the frontend speak Prisma. Do not make Prisma schema the HTTP API. Let each boundary have the representation that matches its responsibility. Avoid validation duplication inside service methods Once a service is only callable through validated controllers, it can often assume transport shape correctness. But service methods may later be reused by jobs, CLI tools, tests, or internal workflows. At that point, decide whether those callers need their own validated boundary or a stronger domain-level invariant. Do not simply sprinkle schema.parse() everywhere. authentication Explain Shared Schemas and Boundary Design in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Lab A - Install and wire validation • From apps/api install zod@4.6.5. • Register StandardSchemaValidationPipe globally in main.ts. • Create tasks.schemas.ts. • Remove the temporary tasks.types.ts once controller/service imports have been migrated. • Build the API before running it. Lab B - Create schema tests Payload Expected valid projectId + title 201 missing title 400 title with only spaces 400 title > 200 chars 400 projectId not UUID 400 unknown admin field 400 valid UUID for missing Project 404 Lab C - Update schema tests Payload Expected {"status":"DONE"} success for existing Task {"status":"ALMOST_DONE"} 400 {"description":null} success; clear description {} 400 {"projectId":"..."} 400 unknown field Lab D - Path parameter tests • GET /tasks/not-a-uuid should return 400 without querying the service for a Task. • GET /tasks/ should pass validation and then return 404 from application logic. • PATCH and DELETE should apply the same UUID contract. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 12: DTOs, Zod & Input Validation Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk untrusted JSON/query -> schema parse -> typed validated value -> business rules -> persistence Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Assuming TypeScript validates runtime JSON Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 2 — Duplicating client and server validation rules without a sharing strategy Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. text: error-taxonomy-and-api-contract Error Taxonomy and API Contract Error Taxonomy & API Contract Expected failures, unexpected faults, HTTP semantics, machine codes, and public error design Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Failure occurs ↓ Classify meaning ↓ Choose safe status/code ↓ Return stable contract Phase 13… Error Taxonomy & API Contract Expected failures, unexpected faults, HTTP semantics, machine codes, and public error design Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Failure occurs ↓ Classify meaning ↓ Choose safe status/code ↓ Return stable contract Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Not every failure is the same Professional error handling begins by classifying failures before choosing a status code or message. Treating every exception as a generic 500 makes the API hard to use. Treating every failure as a client mistake hides real server faults. Category Example Expected handling Invalid request blank title, malformed UUID 400 with validation details Missing resource valid Task ID does not exist 404 with domain code State conflict duplicate unique value / relation conflict 409 Authentication later missing/invalid token 401 Authorization later identity lacks permission 403 Unexpected fault bug, unavailable dependency, unknown exception 500 sanitized to client Figure 1 - Expected failure vs unexpected fault Request enters system ↓ Can the application explain the failure safely? ↓ Yes -> stable 4xx response ↓ No -> log diagnostics internally ↓ Return sanitized 500 A client-facing API should expose actionable contract information without exposing server internals. Status code is not the whole contract Two 404 responses can mean different application situations. A stable application error code lets clients distinguish them without parsing English text. { "statusCode": 404, "code": "TASK_NOT_FOUND", "message": "Task ... was not found.", "requestId": "7", "timestamp": "2026-09-18T...Z", "path": "/tasks/..." } Human message vs machine code Field Purpose statusCode HTTP semantics; proxies, clients and tooling understand it code Stable machine-readable application meaning message Human-readable explanation details Optional structured validation information requestId Correlation between client failure and server log timestamp When the server produced the error path Which endpoint failed Do not parse English messages Frontend code should branch on statusCode or code, not on exact English wording such as message.includes("not found"). Messages can change for clarity; stable codes are the contract. Error handling is a boundary concern Business services should explain domain failures. The global exception boundary should format those failures for HTTP. Database adapters should not dictate the public API. This separation prevents infrastructure-specific error text from becoming a client contract. errors Explain Error Taxonomy and API Contract in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: nestjs-exception-layer-and-request-lifecycle NestJS Exception Layer and Request Lifecycle NestJS Exception Layer & Request Lifecycle How filters fit into NestJS 12 request processing and why global error boundaries beat repetitive try/catch Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone request ↓ guards/interceptors/pipes ↓ controller/service ↓ uncaught exception ↓ filter… NestJS Exception Layer & Request Lifecycle How filters fit into NestJS 12 request processing and why global error boundaries beat repetitive try/catch Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone request ↓ guards/interceptors/pipes ↓ controller/service ↓ uncaught exception ↓ filter ↓ response Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. NestJS already has an exception layer Nest catches unhandled exceptions after request processing and converts HttpException subclasses into HTTP responses. Unknown errors become a generic 500. Exception filters exist when an application needs more control over response shape, logging, or error translation. Figure 1 - Relevant request lifecycle Incoming request ↓ middleware ↓ guards ↓ interceptors (before) ↓ pipes / validation ↓ controller ↓ service ↓ interceptors (after) ↓ exception filters when an uncaught exception occurs ↓ HTTP response The filter is the final HTTP error boundary for exceptions that were not already handled. Why not try/catch every controller? • Controllers become repetitive and harder to read. • Validation errors happen before many controller handlers run. • Infrastructure errors can escape from deeper providers. • Response formatting drifts between endpoints. • A global filter centralizes HTTP error serialization without forcing all business logic into the filter. HttpException is already useful NestJS exceptions such as BadRequestException, NotFoundException, ConflictException, UnauthorizedException, and ForbiddenException communicate HTTP intent. TaskFlow keeps using those concepts, but enriches selected exceptions with stable application codes. throw new NotFoundException({ code: "TASK_NOT_FOUND", message: `Task ${taskId} was not found.`, }); Catch everything - carefully A @Catch() filter can normalize both known and unknown errors. The filter must not accidentally expose stack traces, SQL, credentials, or raw Prisma messages to clients. Unknown faults should be logged internally and returned as a generic 500 response. Fastify-friendly implementation NestJS documents a platform-agnostic catch-all filter using HttpAdapterHost. TaskFlow follows that pattern instead of calling Express response.json(), so the code remains correct with the Fastify adapter selected earlier in the course. Global registration through dependency injection Because our filter needs HttpAdapterHost and our interceptor needs Logger behavior, register them as APP_FILTER / APP_INTERCEPTOR providers rather than manually creating ad-hoc instances throughout controllers. providers: [ { provide: APP_INTERCEPTOR, useClass: RequestLoggingInterceptor, }, { provide: APP_FILTER, useClass: ApiExceptionFilter, }, ] nest Explain NestJS Exception Layer and Request Lifecycle in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Design the TaskFlow error envelope The API now needs a format that is useful to browser code, PowerShell tests, future mobile clients, and production logs. Keep it small. Every field should answer a real debugging or client-handling question. export type ApiErrorDetails = string[] | Record<string, unknown>; export type ApiErrorResponse = { statusCode: number; code: string; message: string; requestId: string; timestamp: string; path: string; details?: ApiErrorDetails; }; Examples by failure type // 400 validation { "statusCode": 400, "code": "BAD_REQUEST", "message": "Request validation failed.", "details": ["title: String must contain at least 1 character(s)"], "requestId": "12", "timestamp": "...", "path": "/tasks" } // 404 domain failure { "statusCode": 404, "code": "TASK_NOT_FOUND", "message": "Task 123... was not found.", "requestId": "13", "timestamp": "...", "path": "/tasks/123..." } // 500 unexpected fault { "statusCode": 500, "code": "INTERNAL_ERROR", "message": "An unexpected server error occurred.", "requestId": "14", "timestamp": "...", "path": "/tasks" } Why requestId belongs in the client response When a user reports a failure, “it broke at 2:13 AM” is weak evidence. A request identifier gives support and engineering teams an exact correlation key that can be searched in server logs. Figure 1 - Correlation workflow Client receives requestId = 14 ↓ Support includes 14 in bug report ↓ Engineer searches structured logs for requestId 14 ↓ Server log shows method, path, status, exception context A correlation identifier connects a sanitized public response to private server diagnostics without exposing those diagnostics. text: request-ids-and-structured-logging Request IDs and Structured Logging Request IDs & Structured Logging Use Fastify request IDs, response headers, timing, and NestJS 12 structured logger metadata Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Fastify request.id ↓ interceptor ↓ x-request-id + success log ↓ exception filter for failures… Request IDs & Structured Logging Use Fastify request IDs, response headers, timing, and NestJS 12 structured logger metadata Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Fastify request.id ↓ interceptor ↓ x-request-id + success log ↓ exception filter for failures Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Fastify already gives every request an ID Fastify Request includes an id field. We can reuse it as the TaskFlow correlation identifier instead of inventing a separate request-context system during this phase. import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, Logger, NestInterceptor, } from "@nestjs/common"; import { FastifyReply, FastifyRequest } from "fastify"; import { Observable } from "rxjs"; import { tap } from "rxjs/operators"; @Injectable() export class RequestLoggingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor { private readonly logger = new Logger(RequestLoggingInterceptor.name); intercept( context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler, ): Observable<unknown> { const http = context.switchToHttp(); const request = http.getRequest<FastifyRequest>(); const reply = http.getResponse<FastifyReply>(); const requestId = String(request.id); const startedAt = performance.now(); reply.header("x-request-id", requestId); return next.handle().pipe( tap(() => { this.logger.log("Request completed", { requestId, method: request.method, path: request.url, statusCode: reply.statusCode, durationMs: Math.round(performance.now() - startedAt), }); }), ); } } What the interceptor owns • Read Fastify request.id. • Return the same identifier in the x-request-id response header for successful responses. • Measure request duration. • Write one structured completion log after successful controller execution. • Avoid swallowing exceptions; failures continue to the global exception filter. Do not blindly trust caller-provided request IDs Fastify can be configured to use an incoming request-id header, but its documentation warns that callers can then choose arbitrary values unless you validate them. TaskFlow keeps Fastify-generated IDs for now. NestJS 12 structured logger metadata NestJS 12 treats plain objects passed after the message as structured parameters. That makes metadata such as requestId, method, path, durationMs, and statusCode easy to keep together in one log record. this.logger.log("Request completed", { requestId, method: request.method, path: request.url, statusCode: reply.statusCode, durationMs, }); Success and failure logs have different owners The interceptor logs successful completion. The exception filter logs rejected requests and unexpected faults because it knows the final error classification and public status code. This avoids duplicate error logs for the same exception. text: global-apiexceptionfilter Global ApiExceptionFilter Global ApiExceptionFilter Build a Fastify-compatible catch-all filter with HttpAdapterHost and safe normalization Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone exception ↓ normalize ↓ log ↓ httpAdapter.reply Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans… Global ApiExceptionFilter Build a Fastify-compatible catch-all filter with HttpAdapterHost and safe normalization Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone exception ↓ normalize ↓ log ↓ httpAdapter.reply Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Build the global ApiExceptionFilter The filter is intentionally a translation boundary. It receives unknown exceptions, decides which failures are safe and known, creates one public envelope, logs diagnostics, then writes the response through NestJS HttpAdapterHost. import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpException, HttpStatus, Logger, } from "@nestjs/common"; import { HttpAdapterHost } from "@nestjs/core"; import { FastifyRequest } from "fastify"; import { Prisma } from "../../generated/prisma/client"; import { ApiErrorResponse } from "./api-error-response"; @Catch() export class ApiExceptionFilter implements ExceptionFilter { private readonly logger = new Logger(ApiExceptionFilter.name); constructor(private readonly httpAdapterHost: HttpAdapterHost) {} catch(exception: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost): void { const { httpAdapter } = this.httpAdapterHost; const context = host.switchToHttp(); const request = context.getRequest<FastifyRequest>(); const response = context.getResponse(); const result = this.normalize(exception); const requestId = String(request.id); const path = httpAdapter.getRequestUrl(request); const body: ApiErrorResponse = { statusCode: result.statusCode, code: result.code, message: result.message, requestId, timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), path, ...(result.details ? { details: result.details } : {}), }; if (result.statusCode >= 500) { this.logger.error("Unhandled request failure", { requestId, method: request.method, path, statusCode: result.statusCode, exceptionName: exception instanceof Error ? exception.name : typeof exception, stack: exception instanceof Error ? exception.stack : undefined, }); } else { this.logger.warn("Request rejected", { requestId, method: request.method, path, statusCode: result.statusCode, code: result.code, }); } httpAdapter.reply(response, body, result.statusCode); } private normalize(exception: unknown): { statusCode: number; code: string; message: string; details?: string[] | Record<string, unknown>; } { if (exception instanceof HttpException) { return this.fromHttpException(exception); } if (exception instanceof Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError) { return this.fromPrismaError(exception); } return { statusCode: HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, code: "INTERNAL_ERROR", message: "An unexpected server error occurred.", }; } private fromHttpException(exception: HttpException) { const statusCode = exception.getStatus(); const response = exception.getResponse(); if (typeof response === "string") { return { statusCode, code: this.defaultCode(statusCode), message: response, }; } if (response && typeof response === "object") { const body = response as { code?: unknown; message?: unknown; }; if (Array.isArray(body.message)) { return { statusCode, code: typeof body.code === "string" ? body.code : this.defaultCode(statusCode), message: "Request validation failed.", details: body.message.map(String), }; } if (typeof body.message === "string") { return { statusCode, code: typeof body.code === "string" ? body.code : this.defaultCode(statusCode), message: body.message, }; } } return { statusCode, code: this.defaultCode(statusCode), message: "Request failed.", }; } private fromPrismaError( exception: Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError, ) { switch (exception.code) { case "P2002": return { statusCode: HttpStatus.CONFLICT, code: "UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT", message: "A resource with the same unique value already exists.", }; case "P2003": return { statusCode: HttpStatus.CONFLICT, code: "RELATION_CONFLICT", message: "The operation conflicts with an existing relationship.", }; case "P2025": return { statusCode: HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, code: "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND", message: "The requested resource was not found.", }; default: return { statusCode: HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, code: "DATABASE_ERROR", message: "A database operation failed.", }; } } private defaultCode(statusCode: number): string { switch (statusCode) { case HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST: return "BAD_REQUEST"; case HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED: return "UNAUTHORIZED"; case HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN: return "FORBIDDEN"; case HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND: return "NOT_FOUND"; case HttpStatus.CONFLICT: return "CONFLICT"; default: return `HTTP_${statusCode}`; } } } Three normalization paths Input exception Normalization path Public result HttpException Preserve status, code/message where 4xx/5xx contract supplied Prisma known request error Translate known P-codes 409/404 or sanitized DB failure Anything else Treat as unexpected fault 500 INTERNAL_ERROR Validation details without framework coupling The filter does not need to know that Zod created the validation error. It inspects the HttpException response. If the message is an array, TaskFlow uses a stable top-level message and moves those strings into details. if (Array.isArray(body.message)) { return { statusCode, code: "BAD_REQUEST", message: "Request validation failed.", details: body.message.map(String), }; } Adapter-agnostic response writing httpAdapter.reply( response, body, result.statusCode, ); Why this matters Earlier NestJS examples often use Express Response.json(). text: prisma-error-translation Prisma Error Translation Prisma Error Translation Translate Prisma 7 P2002, P2003, and P2025 without leaking ORM internals Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Prisma error ↓ domain context if available ↓ safe HTTP mapping Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary… Prisma Error Translation Translate Prisma 7 P2002, P2003, and P2025 without leaking ORM internals Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Prisma error ↓ domain context if available ↓ safe HTTP mapping Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Translate Prisma errors deliberately Prisma errors are implementation details. Clients should receive HTTP/domain semantics, not raw ORM error text. TaskFlow catches a small set of understood Prisma 7 codes and gives them stable meanings. Prisma code Meaning TaskFlow HTTP mapping P2002 Unique constraint failed 409 UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT P2003 Foreign key constraint failed 409 RELATION_CONFLICT P2025 Required record for operation not found 404 RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND Other known Known Prisma failure not explicitly modeled 500 DATABASE_ERROR request error Do not return Prisma message directly // BAD public response { "message": "Invalid this.prisma.task.create() invocation ... Unique constraint failed ..." } Sensitive implementation detail Raw ORM messages may contain model names, operation context, field names, local paths, or other details that clients do not need. Log what engineers need privately; expose a safe contract publicly. Where P2025 should be handled For a Task update/delete, the service knows the domain context and can produce TASK_NOT_FOUND. That is more useful than allowing the global filter to produce generic RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND. The global P2025 mapping remains a safety net for errors that escape from less contextual code. Figure 1 - Context first, global fallback second TasksService catches expected P2025 ↓ Throws TaskNotFoundException with TASK_NOT_FOUND ↓ Global filter only formats the exception ↓ Unexpected uncaught P2025 elsewhere ↓ Global filter returns generic RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND Translate errors as close as possible to the layer that understands their business meaning, while keeping a global safety boundary. Conflict does not always mean 409 Use 409 when the request is structurally valid but conflicts with current server state. Do not mechanically map every database exception to 409. Connection failures, malformed schema, timeouts, and unknown database faults are server-side operational failures, not client conflicts. prisma Explain Prisma Error Translation in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: service-vs-filter-boundaries Service vs Filter Boundaries Service vs Filter Boundaries Domain-specific exceptions, contextual translation, and keeping business meaning out of global infrastructure code Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone service understands use case ↓ exception carries meaning ↓ filter formats HTTP Phase 13 creates… Service vs Filter Boundaries Domain-specific exceptions, contextual translation, and keeping business meaning out of global infrastructure code Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone service understands use case ↓ exception carries meaning ↓ filter formats HTTP Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Create application-specific exceptions only when they add meaning NestJS already has NotFoundException and ConflictException. TaskFlow subclasses them only when a stable application code or reusable domain message earns its place. import { ConflictException, NotFoundException, } from "@nestjs/common"; export class TaskNotFoundException extends NotFoundException { constructor(taskId: string) { super({ code: "TASK_NOT_FOUND", message: `Task ${taskId} was not found.`, }); } } export class ProjectNotFoundException extends NotFoundException { constructor(projectId: string) { super({ code: "PROJECT_NOT_FOUND", message: `Project ${projectId} was not found.`, }); } } export class ResourceConflictException extends ConflictException { constructor(message: string, code = "RESOURCE_CONFLICT") { super({ code, message }); } } TasksService now communicates domain meaning The service decides that a missing Task is a Task-domain event, not merely a Prisma event. That keeps the public API independent from which ORM we use. import { Injectable } from "@nestjs/common"; import { Prisma } from "../generated/prisma/client"; import { PrismaService } from "../prisma/prisma.service"; import { ProjectNotFoundException, TaskNotFoundException, } from "../common/errors/application.exceptions"; import { CreateTaskDto, UpdateTaskDto, } from "./tasks.schemas"; @Injectable() export class TasksService { constructor(private readonly prisma: PrismaService) {} findAll() { return this.prisma.task.findMany({ orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" }, }); } async findOne(id: string) { const task = await this.prisma.task.findUnique({ where: { id }, }); if (!task) { throw new TaskNotFoundException(id); } return task; } async create(input: CreateTaskDto) { const project = await this.prisma.project.findUnique({ where: { id: input.projectId }, select: { id: true }, }); if (!project) { throw new ProjectNotFoundException(input.projectId); } return this.prisma.task.create({ data: input, }); } async update(id: string, input: UpdateTaskDto) { try { return await this.prisma.task.update({ where: { id }, data: input, }); } catch (error) { this.rethrowMissingTask(error, id); } } async remove(id: string) { try { await this.prisma.task.delete({ where: { id }, }); } catch (error) { this.rethrowMissingTask(error, id); } } private rethrowMissingTask(error: unknown, id: string): never { if ( error instanceof Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError && error.code === "P2025" ) { throw new TaskNotFoundException(id); } throw error; } } Responsibility boundaries Layer Owns Zod / pipe Request shape validity TasksService Task/Project existence and business meaning Prisma Persistence operations and database protocol ApiExceptionFilter HTTP serialization, safe fallback, final logging Anti-pattern: filter contains business rules // Avoid turning the global filter into this: if (exception.code === "P2025" && request.url.startsWith("/tasks")) { // infer Task business meaning from URL here... } Architecture rule The global filter should not reverse-engineer domain context from routes or database metadata. Services know the use case. Filters know HTTP error serialization. Anti-pattern: swallowing unknown errors If a service catches unknown Error and turns it into BadRequestException, a programming bug can masquerade as a client mistake. text: safe-production-error-exposure Safe Production Error Exposure Safe Production Error Exposure Sanitized client responses, protected diagnostics, logging hygiene, and privacy-aware failure handling Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone client-safe response ↓ requestId ↓ private structured diagnostic log Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and… Safe Production Error Exposure Sanitized client responses, protected diagnostics, logging hygiene, and privacy-aware failure handling Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone client-safe response ↓ requestId ↓ private structured diagnostic log Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Production errors should be boring to clients and rich to engineers The client needs a safe message, stable code, and requestId. Engineers need internal context such as exception name, stack, method, path, status, and timing. These are different audiences. Information Public response Protected server log status / code Yes Yes human-safe message Yes Yes requestId Yes Yes stack trace No Yes for unexpected faults raw SQL No Usually no; only under controlled diagnostics DATABASE_URL / credentials Never Never request password/token Never Never Prisma raw error text Usually no May be logged carefully if sanitized Structured logging example this.logger.error("Unhandled request failure", { requestId, method: request.method, path, statusCode: 500, exceptionName: exception.name, stack: exception.stack, }); Do not log request bodies by default Bodies can contain passwords, tokens, personal data, payroll values, applicant information, employee records, or uploaded document metadata in future TaskFlow-derived systems. Logging everything because it is convenient is not professional observability. Security and privacy rule Error handling is also data-handling design. Decide what logs are allowed to contain before production, who can read them, and how long they are retained. text: client-error-consumption-and-debugging Client Error Consumption and Debugging Client Error Consumption & Debugging Parse the stable envelope in Next.js and distinguish API failures from transport failures Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone fetch ↓ network vs HTTP response ↓ ApiClientError ↓ UI recovery Phase 13 creates… Client Error Consumption & Debugging Parse the stable envelope in Next.js and distinguish API failures from transport failures Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone fetch ↓ network vs HTTP response ↓ ApiClientError ↓ UI recovery Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Frontend should consume the contract, not framework accidents Next.js should not need to know whether NestJS, Zod, Prisma, PostgreSQL, or Fastify produced the failure. It should parse TaskFlow's stable API error response. export type ApiErrorResponse = { statusCode: number; code: string; message: string; requestId: string; timestamp: string; path: string; details?: string[] | Record<string, unknown>; }; export class ApiClientError extends Error { constructor( public readonly statusCode: number, public readonly code: string, message: string, public readonly requestId?: string, public readonly details?: ApiErrorResponse["details"], ) { super(message); } } export async function throwIfNotOk(response: Response) { if (response.ok) return; let payload: ApiErrorResponse | undefined; try { payload = (await response.json()) as ApiErrorResponse; } catch { // The server may have returned a non-JSON infrastructure error. } throw new ApiClientError( response.status, payload?.code ?? "HTTP_ERROR", payload?.message ?? "The request failed.", payload?.requestId, payload?.details, ); } Typical UI decisions Error condition Possible UI behavior BAD_REQUEST + details Show field/form feedback or a request summary TASK_NOT_FOUND Show “Task no longer exists” and navigate back UNAUTHORIZED later Prompt login / refresh session FORBIDDEN later Explain missing permission CONFLICT Explain stale/duplicate state and offer recovery INTERNAL_ERROR Show generic failure + requestId for support Network error is not the same as API error If fetch cannot reach the server, there may be no HTTP status, no JSON envelope, and no requestId. That is a transport failure. If the API returns 404/409/500, fetch receives an HTTP response and the TaskFlow error parser can process the body. Figure 1 - Client failure split fetch() call ↓ No HTTP response -> transport/network error ↓ HTTP response received ↓ response.ok false -> parse ApiErrorResponse ↓ throw ApiClientError The UI can now distinguish connectivity from server-declared application failures. Debug with requestId first When an INTERNAL_ERROR reaches the browser, show a short message and the requestId. Do not dump stack traces into the UI. text: hands-on-lab-and-phase-exit Hands On Lab and Phase Exit Hands-On Lab & Phase Exit Error matrix, correlation exercise, engineering challenges, oral exam, and completion checklist Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone implement ↓ trigger errors ↓ correlate logs ↓ verify contract ↓ explain architecture Phase 13 creates… Hands-On Lab & Phase Exit Error matrix, correlation exercise, engineering challenges, oral exam, and completion checklist Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone implement ↓ trigger errors ↓ correlate logs ↓ verify contract ↓ explain architecture Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs. Hands-on lab The exit lab proves that TaskFlow has one coherent error boundary instead of a collection of framework-default responses. Lab A - Add the error contract • Create ApiErrorResponse. • Add TaskNotFoundException and ProjectNotFoundException. • Update TasksService to throw domain-specific exceptions where context is known. • Keep unknown exceptions re-thrown. Lab B - Add global filter and request logging • Create ApiExceptionFilter using HttpAdapterHost. • Create RequestLoggingInterceptor using Fastify request.id. • Register both globally with APP_FILTER and APP_INTERCEPTOR. • Verify successful responses expose x-request-id. • Verify 4xx/5xx error bodies contain requestId. Lab C - Error matrix Scenario Expected GET /tasks/not-a-uuid 400 BAD_REQUEST, requestId GET valid missing Task UUID 404 TASK_NOT_FOUND, requestId POST missing/invalid body 400 BAD_REQUEST + details POST valid body, missing Project 404 PROJECT_NOT_FOUND Known unique conflict (where available) 409 UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT P2025 escaping contextual service handling 404 RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND fallback Deliberate unexpected Error in dev test route 500 INTERNAL_ERROR, no stack in response Lab D - Correlation exercise • Trigger one failing request. • Copy requestId from the JSON response. • Find the matching NestJS log entry. • Confirm the client response is sanitized while the log has diagnostic context. • Remove any temporary route used to create an artificial 500. Debugging Workshop — Phase 13: Professional Error Handling Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. text: controller-vs-service-responsibilities Controller vs Service Responsibilities Controller vs Service Responsibilities Keep HTTP translation thin while providers execute application use cases Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone HTTP request v Controller v TasksService v PrismaService Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit… Controller vs Service Responsibilities Keep HTTP translation thin while providers execute application use cases Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone HTTP request v Controller v TasksService v PrismaService Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple. A controller translates HTTP; a service executes a use case NestJS documentation recommends that controllers handle HTTP requests and delegate more complex work to providers. TaskFlow now makes that separation concrete: controllers translate transport concerns; TasksService owns Task use cases and rules. Controller owns TasksService owns route + HTTP method business workflow path/body extraction domain invariants validation pipe invocation cross-model checks status semantics orchestration of reads/writes delegate to provider meaningful application exceptions Thin does not mean useless A controller still has an important responsibility: it defines the transport contract. Thin means it does not decide whether DONE can return to TODO, whether an assignee belongs to a workspace, or how completedAt should change. @Patch(":id") update( @Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string, @Body(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe(updateTaskSchema)) input: UpdateTaskDto, ) { return this.tasksService.update(id, input); } Figure 1 - Use-case ownership HTTP PATCH /tasks/:id v Controller validates/extracts transport data v TasksService evaluates Task rules v PrismaService persists valid state The service is where transport-independent application meaning lives. Service layer is not a pass-through layer If TasksService only forwards every input directly to prisma.task.update(), it is not protecting business behavior. As rules appear, the service should coordinate the use case before the write. Avoid controller business logic Putting transition tables or membership queries into TasksController makes the same rules difficult to reuse from jobs, tests, CLI tools, or future non-HTTP entry points. The opposite anti-pattern: god service A service can also grow too large. Do not respond by extracting arbitrary classes early. First group methods by use case and keep private rule helpers local. title: Business Invariants and Rule Ownership
subtitle: Service & Business Logic Architecture
text: business-invariants-and-rule-ownership Business Invariants and Rule Ownership Business Invariants & Rule Ownership Separate transport validation, business rules, authorization, and database constraints Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Request shape v Application invariant v Database integrity Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit… Business Invariants & Rule Ownership Separate transport validation, business rules, authorization, and database constraints Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Request shape v Application invariant v Database integrity Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple. Invariant: a rule that must remain true A business invariant is a statement the application should protect across valid operations. It is different from a TypeScript type, a request shape, and often different from a database constraint. Rule Best first owner title is a string <= 200 chars Zod boundary projectId references an existing row PostgreSQL FK + service-friendly 404 assignee belongs to Project workspace TasksService DONE sets completedAt TasksService workspaceId + userId unique PostgreSQL unique constraint caller may edit this Task authorization layer later Why some rules cannot be expressed as simple database constraints The assignee rule crosses Task -> Project -> Workspace and Membership. PostgreSQL can ensure assigneeId references a real User, but the current model does not encode the stronger rule that the User must also belong to the Task workspace. The application service therefore checks that invariant. Figure 1 - Assignee invariant Task belongs to Project v Project belongs to Workspace v Candidate User v Membership(workspaceId,userId) must exist v Only then assign Task A valid foreign key is necessary but not sufficient for this business rule. subtitle: Service & Business Logic Architecture
text: task-status-workflow-and-derived-state Task Status Workflow and Derived State Task Status Workflow & Derived State Explicit transitions, completedAt consistency, and operations with business meaning Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Current Task status v Transition policy v Derived state v Persist Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented… Task Status Workflow & Derived State Explicit transitions, completedAt consistency, and operations with business meaning Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Current Task status v Transition policy v Derived state v Persist Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple. Model Task status as a workflow, not a free-form field Zod can prove that a status value is one of TODO, IN_PROGRESS, DONE, or CANCELED. It cannot decide whether a specific transition is allowed from the current persisted state. That requires reading the Task and applying workflow policy. const ALLOWED_STATUS_TRANSITIONS = { TODO: [IN_PROGRESS, CANCELED], IN_PROGRESS: [TODO, DONE, CANCELED], DONE: [IN_PROGRESS], CANCELED: [TODO], }; From Allowed next states TODO IN_PROGRESS, CANCELED IN_PROGRESS TODO, DONE, CANCELED DONE IN_PROGRESS CANCELED TODO Figure 1 - Status transition reasoning Read current status v Requested status differs? v Check transition policy v Reject invalid transition with 409 v Apply derived side effects v Persist valid update The update becomes an application operation, not an arbitrary column assignment. Derived state: completedAt When Task status changes to DONE, TaskFlow records completedAt. When a DONE Task is reopened, completedAt is cleared. That makes status and completion timestamp internally consistent. if (to === TaskStatus.DONE) return new Date(); if (from === TaskStatus.DONE) return null; Why not let the frontend set completedAt? The client may request a business action such as completing a Task, but the server owns the authoritative timestamp and invariant. Otherwise clients can create contradictory states such as status=TODO with completedAt populated. CRUD field update vs business operation PATCH remains a valid transport for this phase, but TasksService interprets status as a workflow change rather than blindly forwarding it. In larger domains, an explicit operation such as POST /purchase-orders/:id/approve can be clearer than a generic field patch because approval has business meaning and side effects. ci Explain Task Status Workflow and Derived State in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence.
