text: business-validation-and-time-based-policies Business Validation and Time Based Policies Business Validation & Time-Based Policies Why semantically valid state needs more than Zod request validation Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Valid timestamp v Business clock/policy v Accept or reject Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods… Business Validation & Time-Based Policies Why semantically valid state needs more than Zod request validation Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Valid timestamp v Business clock/policy v Accept or reject Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple. Business validation is not the same as transport validation Phase 12 protects the request boundary. Phase 14 protects the application state. These validations run at different moments and answer different questions. Question Layer Example response Is dueAt a valid ISO datetime? Zod 400 BAD_REQUEST Does this course allow a new past due date? TasksService 400 DUE_DATE_IN_PAST Does projectId exist? TasksService + DB 404 PROJECT_NOT_FOUND Is assigneeId a UUID? Zod 400 BAD_REQUEST Is assignee a Workspace member? TasksService 409 ASSIGNEE_NOT_WORKSPACE_M EMBER A policy may use current time A due-date-in-the-past rule depends on application meaning and the current clock. It is not just a string-format rule. The service therefore parses the already validated timestamp and compares it with the current time. private assertDueDate(dueAt?: string | null): void { if (!dueAt) return; if (new Date(dueAt).getTime() < Date.now()) { throw new DueDateInPastException(); } } Be careful with clocks Time-based business rules eventually deserve a controllable Clock dependency in heavily tested domains. We do not introduce that abstraction yet because formal unit testing and time simulation arrive later. The book calls out the trade-off so the learner understands why Date.now() may later become a seam. Do not duplicate the same rule everywhere If the frontend also warns about past dates, that improves UX, but the backend remains authoritative. Client validation is convenience; server business logic protects the system. validation Explain Business Validation and Time Based Policies in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. subtitle: Service & Business Logic Architecture
text: prisma-transactions-and-atomic-workflows Prisma Transactions and Atomic Workflows Prisma Transactions & Atomic Workflows Choose nested writes, transaction arrays, or interactive transactions only when a use case needs them Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Business operation v Dependent DB steps v Transaction boundary v… Prisma Transactions & Atomic Workflows Choose nested writes, transaction arrays, or interactive transactions only when a use case needs them Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Business operation v Dependent DB steps v Transaction boundary v Commit or rollback Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple. Transactions protect one business operation across multiple database steps A transaction is appropriate when a use case must treat multiple dependent reads/writes as one unit. Prisma 7 supports nested writes, sequential $transaction([...]), and interactive $transaction(async tx => ...). Scenario Transaction? Reason Update one Task title No extra transaction One Prisma update is already atomic Create Task row only No extra transaction Single write Create parent + related rows Nested write can provide Dependent writes transactional behavior Check membership then assign as one workflow Interactive transaction can group Read/check then write the workflow Two unrelated read queries for a dashboard Usually no Atomicity may not be required return this.prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => { const task = await tx.task.findUnique(...); const membership = await tx.membership.findUnique(...); if (!membership) { throw new AssigneeNotWorkspaceMemberException(assigneeId); } return tx.task.update({ where: { id }, data: { assigneeId }, }); }); Keep interactive transactions short Do not call slow external APIs, wait for user input, or perform long CPU work inside an interactive transaction. The database resources remain tied to that transaction while the callback is running. Transaction does not automatically solve every concurrency problem Isolation level and retry strategy still matter for strict concurrent invariants. Phase 14 introduces transaction scope; deeper concurrency control belongs later. Do not claim that wrapping arbitrary code in $transaction makes all race conditions impossible. Use the transaction client inside the callback Queries that belong to the transaction must use tx, not the outer PrismaService. This is why the membership helper accepts either PrismaService or Prisma.TransactionClient in the reference snapshot. ci Explain Prisma Transactions and Atomic Workflows in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. subtitle: Service & Business Logic Architecture
text: anti-patterns-and-architecture-theater Anti Patterns and Architecture Theater Anti-Patterns & Architecture Theater Avoid controller business logic, blind Prisma patches, transaction-everywhere, and premature layers Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Simple architecture v Pressure appears v Add only needed structure Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service… Anti-Patterns & Architecture Theater Avoid controller business logic, blind Prisma patches, transaction-everywhere, and premature layers Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Simple architecture v Pressure appears v Add only needed structure Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple. Common business-layer anti-patterns The fastest way to understand the service layer is to see what happens when responsibilities leak. Anti-pattern 1 - Controller performs database queries @Patch(":id") async update(...) { const task = await this.prisma.task.findUnique(...); // business checks here return this.prisma.task.update(...); } This couples HTTP handling directly to persistence and makes the use case harder to reuse. Anti-pattern 2 - Prisma update object becomes the business model return prisma.task.update({ where: { id }, data: input, // every valid field is treated as a legal business transition }); Request-shape validity does not mean every state transition is allowed. Anti-pattern 3 - Error filter decides business meaning Phase 13 already established that the global filter formats errors. It should not infer Task workflow rules from URLs or Prisma codes. Anti-pattern 4 - transaction everywhere Wrapping every single Prisma operation in $transaction adds complexity without improving atomicity. One database write already succeeds or fails atomically. Anti-pattern 5 - Clean Architecture cosplay TaskController -> TaskUseCaseFacade -> TaskApplicationService -> TaskDomainService -> TaskRepositoryInterface -> PrismaTaskRepository -> TaskMapper -> Prisma More layers are not automatically more professional Use layers because they isolate a real kind of change or complexity. At TaskFlow's current scale, Controller -> TasksService -> PrismaService is still an excellent architecture. Anti-pattern 6 - service knows HTTP framework details TasksService should throw meaningful application exceptions, not manipulate Fastify Reply or manually construct transport responses. That keeps business behavior reusable outside HTTP. architecture Explain Anti Patterns and Architecture Theater in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Debugging Workshop — Phase 14: Service & Business Logic Architecture Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. text: collection-api-mental-model Collection API Mental Model Collection API Mental Model Treat filters, search, sorting and pagination as one public query contract Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Collection resource v Query parameters v Normalized collection state v Result representation Phase 15 turns… Collection API Mental Model Treat filters, search, sorting and pagination as one public query contract Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Collection resource v Query parameters v Normalized collection state v Result representation Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. A collection endpoint is a query interface GET /tasks is not just an array-returning function. It is a public query interface between clients and a dataset. A professional contract needs explicit choices about scope, filters, search, order, pagination, defaults, limits, and response metadata. Concern Question Scope Which Tasks may this endpoint expose? Filter Which exact attributes narrow the collection? Search Which text fields participate and with what semantics? Sort Which fields may control ordering? Stability How are ties broken? Pagination How many rows may one request return? Metadata How will a UI know whether more pages exist? Query parameters express collection state Collection choices normally belong in the URL because they describe which representation of the collection the client wants. This makes URLs bookmarkable, shareable, inspectable in DevTools, and repeatable during debugging. /tasks?status=IN_PROGRESS&priority=HIGH&page=2&pageSize=20 Avoid endpoint explosion Do not create one route for every filter combination such as /high-priority-tasks, /completed-tasks, /my-high-priority-tasks. Keep the resource stable and express queryable collection state with validated parameters. Weak design Stronger collection design /tasks/high-priority /tasks?priority=HIGH /tasks/completed /tasks?status=DONE /searchTasks?q=x /tasks?search=x /tasks/page/2 /tasks?page=2 Later authorization will narrow scope further A query parameter can ask for projectId or assigneeId, but it must never be trusted as proof that the caller is allowed to see that scope. Authorization arrives later and will intersect with these filters. pagination Explain Collection API Mental Model in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Query DTOs and Zod Validation
subtitle: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
text: query-dtos-and-zod-validation Query DTOs and Zod Validation Query DTOs & Zod Validation Normalize strings, coerce numbers, apply defaults, cap page size, and reject unsupported parameters Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Raw query strings v Zod validation v TaskListQueryDto v TasksService Phase 15… Query DTOs & Zod Validation Normalize strings, coerce numbers, apply defaults, cap page size, and reject unsupported parameters Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Raw query strings v Zod validation v TaskListQueryDto v TasksService Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. Validate query strings at the HTTP boundary Query strings arrive as strings. page=2 is initially the string "2", not the number 2. Phase 15 uses Zod coercion for numeric pagination fields and strict allow-lists for enums and sort options. import { z } from "zod"; import { TaskPriority, TaskStatus, } from "../generated/prisma/client"; export const taskSortFieldSchema = z.enum([ "createdAt", "updatedAt", "dueAt", "title", ]); export const sortOrderSchema = z.enum(["asc", "desc"]); export const taskListQuerySchema = z.strictObject({ projectId: z.uuid().optional(), assigneeId: z.uuid().optional(), status: z.enum(TaskStatus).optional(), priority: z.enum(TaskPriority).optional(), search: z.string().trim().min(1).max(100).optional(), sort: taskSortFieldSchema.default("createdAt"), order: sortOrderSchema.default("desc"), page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1), pageSize: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20), }); export type TaskListQueryDto = z.infer<typeof taskListQuerySchema>; export type TaskSortField = z.infer<typeof taskSortFieldSchema>; export type SortOrder = z.infer<typeof sortOrderSchema>; Why defaults belong in the boundary schema Defaults such as page=1, pageSize=20, sort=createdAt, and order=desc are part of the API contract. Applying them once at validation means TasksService receives a normalized query instead of repeatedly handling undefined values. Request Validated meaning /tasks page=1, pageSize=20, createdAt desc ?page=0 400 - page must be >= 1 ?pageSize=1000 400 - server cap is 100 ?sort=dropTable 400 - field is not allow-listed ?status=almost_done 400 - invalid enum value ?search= 400 after trim/min length Integrate with NestJS 12 @Get() findAll( @Query(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe(taskListQuerySchema)) query: TaskListQueryDto, ) { return this.tasksService.findAll(query); } Boundary rule Do not pass raw query strings into Prisma. Normalize and constrain them first. This is both safer and easier to reason about. Why pageSize has a hard maximum Without a server-controlled cap, a client can request pageSize=1000000 and effectively bypass pagination. The product may later choose 50 or 200, but the backend must own the upper bound. validation Explain Query DTOs and Zod Validation in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Prisma Filtering and Where Design
subtitle: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
text: prisma-filtering-and-where-design Prisma Filtering and Where Design Prisma Filtering & where Design Translate only approved public filters into Prisma query objects Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Validated filters v Prisma where v SQL predicates Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into… Prisma Filtering & where Design Translate only approved public filters into Prisma query objects Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Validated filters v Prisma where v SQL predicates Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. Build Prisma where from validated filters After validation, each optional filter can be translated into a Prisma TaskWhereInput. The service should build this intentionally instead of forwarding the entire query object to Prisma. private buildWhere(query: TaskListQueryDto): Prisma.TaskWhereInput { return { ...(query.projectId ? { projectId: query.projectId } : {}), ...(query.assigneeId ? { assigneeId: query.assigneeId } : {}), ...(query.status ? { status: query.status } : {}), ...(query.priority ? { priority: query.priority } : {}), }; } Figure 1 - Filter translation URL query string v Zod normalizes values v TaskListQueryDto v buildWhere() v Prisma TaskWhereInput v PostgreSQL WHERE predicates The transport contract is translated into persistence-specific query input inside the service layer. AND is the natural default The example means projectId + status + priority filters all apply together. That is usually what users expect when they add several table filters: narrow the result set by all selected criteria. Relation filters remain possible Prisma supports relation filters, but do not expose every relational capability as a public query parameter. Add only filters the product genuinely needs, document them, validate them, then index the resulting workload if measurements justify it. Query DTO is not Prisma input TaskListQueryDto is our public HTTP contract. Prisma.TaskWhereInput is an internal persistence shape. Keeping the translation explicit prevents clients from gaining accidental access to arbitrary database query capability. authentication Explain Prisma Filtering and Where Design in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Search Semantics and Case Insensitive Text
subtitle: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
text: search-semantics-and-case-insensitive-text Search Semantics and Case Insensitive Text Search Semantics & Case-Insensitive Text Design simple search behavior while understanding its database trade-offs Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone search=payroll v OR title/description v PostgreSQL text matching Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into… Search Semantics & Case-Insensitive Text Design simple search behavior while understanding its database trade-offs Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone search=payroll v OR title/description v PostgreSQL text matching Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. Search is not the same as exact filtering Filtering asks for exact structured attributes such as status=IN_PROGRESS. Search usually asks whether text resembles a user-entered phrase. TaskFlow begins with a deliberately simple case-insensitive substring search across title and description. ...(query.search ? { OR: [ { title: { contains: query.search, mode: "insensitive" } }, { description: { contains: query.search, mode: "insensitive" } }, ], } : {}) Request Meaning ?status=DONE Exact structured filter ?priority=HIGH Exact structured filter ?search=payroll Text contains search across chosen fields ?status=DONE&search;=payroll DONE tasks AND text search Search semantics must be documented Does search mean starts-with, contains, token matching, fuzzy matching, or full-text relevance? A production API must choose. Phase 15 chooses contains so behavior stays obvious while the architecture is learned. B-tree index warning PostgreSQL substring search such as ILIKE/contains is not automatically accelerated by an ordinary B-tree index. If TaskFlow search becomes large or latency-sensitive, measure it and consider a search-specific strategy such as trigram or full-text indexing. Do not pretend a normal title index solves arbitrary substring search. Search is product behavior, not a database checkbox A payroll system might search employee code, legal name, and payroll batch number. Procurement might search PO number, supplier, and description. The fields and semantics should reflect user tasks, then database design follows. pagination Explain Search Semantics and Case Insensitive Text in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Safe Sorting and Stable Order
subtitle: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
text: safe-sorting-and-stable-order Safe Sorting and Stable Order Safe Sorting & Stable Order Allow-list sort fields and add deterministic tie-breaking for pagination Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone sort + order v Allow-list mapping v Primary order v Unique tiebreaker Phase 15 turns an… Safe Sorting & Stable Order Allow-list sort fields and add deterministic tie-breaking for pagination Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone sort + order v Allow-list mapping v Primary order v Unique tiebreaker Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. Sorting must be allow-listed Never accept an arbitrary field name and inject it into dynamic ordering. Phase 15 validates sort against a small public set and maps each option to a known Prisma orderBy shape. private buildOrderBy(sort: TaskSortField, order: SortOrder) { switch (sort) { case "updatedAt": return [{ updatedAt: order }, { id: "asc" }]; case "dueAt": return [{ dueAt: order }, { id: "asc" }]; case "title": return [{ title: order }, { id: "asc" }]; case "createdAt": default: return [{ createdAt: order }, { id: "asc" }]; } } Why add id as a tiebreaker? createdAt, dueAt, updatedAt, and title are not guaranteed unique. Without a deterministic secondary key, rows tied on the primary sort can move between requests, making paginated results appear unstable. Figure 1 - Stable ordering Sort by createdAt desc v Several rows share timestamp v Tie remains ambiguous v Add id asc tiebreaker v One deterministic total order Stable pagination starts with stable ordering. Null sorting deserves a product decision dueAt is optional. Decide whether tasks without due dates should appear first or last when sorting by dueAt. Prisma/PostgreSQL support explicit null ordering in appropriate query shapes, but the course keeps the initial mapping simple and asks you to make the product decision before optimizing the query. Sorting is part of the API contract Changing default sort later can visibly reorder every page. Treat it like behavior, not an implementation detail. pagination Explain Safe Sorting and Stable Order in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Offset Pagination and Count Metadata
subtitle: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
text: offset-pagination-and-count-metadata Offset Pagination and Count Metadata Offset Pagination & Count Metadata Implement numbered pages with skip/take and truthful totals Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone page/pageSize v skip/take v findMany + count v data + meta Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection… Offset Pagination & Count Metadata Implement numbered pages with skip/take and truthful totals Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone page/pageSize v skip/take v findMany + count v data + meta Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. Offset pagination is the first TaskFlow implementation Offset pagination maps naturally to numbered pages. Prisma expresses it with skip and take. The SQL concept is OFFSET/LIMIT. This is easy to understand and fits administrative tables where users expect page numbers and direct page navigation. const skip = (query.page - 1) * query.pageSize; const items = await prisma.task.findMany({ where, orderBy, skip, take: query.pageSize, }); page pageSize skip rows requested 1 20 0 1-20 2 20 20 21-40 3 50 100 101-150 The deep-page trade-off Offset pagination becomes more expensive as the offset grows because the database still has to advance past earlier rows. That does not make offset pagination wrong; it means you should use it where numbered navigation matters and dataset depth is reasonable, then measure real performance. Count the same filtered set For numbered pages, the UI often wants totalItems and totalPages. The count query must use the same where filter as the page query. If the filters differ, the metadata lies. const [items, totalItems] = await prisma.$transaction([ prisma.task.findMany({ where, orderBy, skip, take: pageSize }), prisma.task.count({ where }), ]); Why group page + count? This groups the two related reads into one database transaction call and keeps their query intent together. It does not mean every read-only list endpoint always requires a transaction; it is one practical way to execute related operations together in this course. pagination Explain Offset Pagination and Count Metadata in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Cursor Pagination and Strategy Selection
subtitle: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
text: cursor-pagination-and-strategy-selection Cursor Pagination and Strategy Selection Cursor Pagination & Strategy Selection Understand feed-style pagination and choose it for the right product interaction Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Product navigation need v Offset or cursor v Stable traversal Phase 15 turns an… Cursor Pagination & Strategy Selection Understand feed-style pagination and choose it for the right product interaction Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Product navigation need v Offset or cursor v Stable traversal Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. Cursor pagination solves a different product problem Cursor pagination resumes after a known record instead of asking the database to skip N previous rows. It is often a better fit for feeds, infinite scroll, exports, and very deep traversal. A cursor must align with ordering Do not copy a cursor example mechanically. If the product sorts by createdAt but the cursor is unrelated to that order, boundary behavior can become surprising. A robust feed normally uses an order and cursor strategy that together define one stable traversal, often including a unique tiebreaker. Figure 1 - Pagination decision Does UI need numbered pages / direct jumps? v Yes -> offset is reasonable v No -> is traversal/feed very deep? v Yes -> design cursor pagination v Measure real behavior and workload Choose from product interaction and dataset behavior, not from fashion. text: paginated-response-contract Paginated Response Contract Paginated Response Contract Return collection data with explicit navigation metadata instead of a bare array Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Filtered rows v Count v Pagination math v Response envelope Phase 15 turns an unbounded… Paginated Response Contract Return collection data with explicit navigation metadata instead of a bare array Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Filtered rows v Count v Pagination math v Response envelope Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. A paginated response needs a deliberate envelope Returning only Task[] forces the frontend to guess whether more data exists. TaskFlow adds metadata that directly supports numbered navigation and summary text. { "data": [ ... ], "meta": { "page": 2, "pageSize": 20, "totalItems": 143, "totalPages": 8, "hasPreviousPage": true, "hasNextPage": true } } Calculate metadata centrally const totalPages = Math.ceil(totalItems / query.pageSize); return { data: items, meta: { page: query.page, pageSize: query.pageSize, totalItems, totalPages, hasPreviousPage: query.page > 1, hasNextPage: query.page < totalPages, }, }; What if page is beyond the last page? There are several defensible contracts: return an empty data array with accurate metadata, clamp to the last page, or reject the page. TaskFlow uses the simplest explicit behavior: page remains what the client requested and data may be empty. The metadata tells the truth. Do not silently move the client to another page unless the API documents that policy. Counts are not free COUNT(*) over a heavily filtered or joined dataset can become expensive. Numbered-page UX may justify it; infinite-scroll APIs often avoid exact totals. text: index-aware-query-design Index Aware Query Design Index-Aware Query Design Connect real query shapes to PostgreSQL indexes without over-indexing Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Observe query v EXPLAIN / measure v Candidate index v Measure again Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection… Index-Aware Query Design Connect real query shapes to PostgreSQL indexes without over-indexing Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Observe query v EXPLAIN / measure v Candidate index v Measure again Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract. Indexes should follow real collection queries Phase 10 already added indexes for project/status and assignee/status. Phase 15 teaches how to evaluate whether listing and sorting patterns need additional support. Do not generate an index for every filter combination. Common query shape Index idea to evaluate projectId + status Existing [projectId,status] assigneeId + status Existing [assigneeId,status] projectId + createdAt ordering Possible [projectId,createdAt] projectId + status + createdAt Possible [projectId,status,createdAt] if measured substring title/description search Different search-specific strategy may be needed Multicolumn index order matters For PostgreSQL B-tree indexes, leading columns matter most. An index on (projectId,status,createdAt) is especially useful for queries that constrain the leading projectId and then status before ordering/scanning createdAt. It is not a magical index for every combination of those columns. Figure 1 - Index design loop Observe real endpoint query v Inspect generated SQL / EXPLAIN v Measure latency and rows scanned v Identify repeated predicate/order pattern v Add minimal useful index v Measure again Index design is empirical engineering, not schema decoration. Sorting can sometimes use an index PostgreSQL B-tree indexes can provide ordered scans. A matching index may avoid a separate sort step, but planner choices depend on selectivity, table size, and the full query. Keep using EXPLAIN instead of guessing. Write cost remains real Every extra index consumes storage and must be maintained on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Hands-on lab The Phase 15 lab proves that your collection endpoint is bounded, validated, predictable, and useful to a real UI. Lab A - Query contract • Create tasks-query.schemas.ts. • Add projectId, assigneeId, status, priority, search, sort, order, page, and pageSize. • Use coercion for numeric query strings. • Cap pageSize at 100. • Reject unknown query parameters with a strict object. Lab B - Prisma translation • Build a Prisma.TaskWhereInput from only the validated public filters. • Add case-insensitive title/description search. • Map allow-listed sort fields explicitly. • Add id as a stable secondary order. • Implement skip/take offset pagination. Lab C - Response contract • Return data + meta instead of a raw array. • Count using the same where filter. • Calculate totalPages and previous/next flags. • Verify an out-of-range page returns an empty data array with truthful metadata. Lab D - PowerShell smoke matrix Scenario Expected GET /tasks Defaults applied, <=20 rows ?status=IN_PROGRESS&priority;=HIGH Both filters applied ?search=payroll Case-insensitive substring match ?sort=title■=asc Deterministic sorted page ?page=0 400 validation error ?pageSize=1000 400 validation error ?sort=dropTable 400 validation error ?page=999999 200 with empty data + truthful meta Exercise levels Level Challenge 1 - Follow Implement the reference query contract and pass the smoke tests. 2 - Modify Add dueBefore and dueAfter ISO datetime filters with clear inclusive/exclusive semantics. 3 - Implement Add an unassigned=true filter without allowing contradictory assigneeId + unassigned=true combinations. Level Challenge 4 - Engineer Design the list endpoint for a payroll employee table with department, employment status, search, sortable columns, and either offset or cursor pagination. Justify every query parameter and index candidate before coding. Architecture oral exam • Why should arbitrary query parameters never be forwarded directly into Prisma? • Why does stable pagination require deterministic ordering? • Why is pageSize capped by the backend? • Why can offset pagination degrade on deep pages? • When is cursor pagination a better product fit? • Why can exact total counts be expensive? • Why is an ordinary B-tree index not enough for arbitrary substring search? • Why should filters and page often live in the URL? • What evidence should exist before adding a new database index? Phase exit checklist • GET /tasks no longer returns an unbounded collection. • query params are validated and normalized before TasksService. • public filters translate explicitly to Prisma where input. • search semantics are documented and intentionally simple. • sorting is allow-listed and deterministic. • offset pagination returns useful metadata. • you can explain when cursor pagination is preferable. • you understand the cost of count queries. • index design is tied to observed workload rather than guesswork. • Next.js can represent collection state with URL search parameters. Debugging Workshop — Phase 15: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk URL query state -> validated query object -> Prisma where/order/cursor -> PostgreSQL plan -> page response -> frontend navigation Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. text: identity-authentication-and-authorization Identity Authentication and Authorization Identity, Authentication & Authorization Separate who the caller is from what the caller may do Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Claimed identity v Authenticator verification v Authenticated subject v Authorization decision Phase 16 builds the security mental… Identity, Authentication & Authorization Separate who the caller is from what the caller may do Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Claimed identity v Authenticator verification v Authenticated subject v Authorization decision Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. Identity is not the same thing as authentication A useful security model starts by naming different concepts precisely. "User", "login", "JWT", and "permission" are not interchangeable terms. Concept Meaning Example Digital identity A subject represented inside a system User record / auth subject Identifier A value used to refer to that identity email, username, user ID Credential / Evidence used to authenticate password, passkey, OTP, security key authenticator Authentication (AuthN) Verify the claimed identity sign in successfully Session Continuity across requests after authentication session cookie or token set Authorization (AuthZ) Decide what the identity may do may edit this Task? Figure 1 - From claimed identity to allowed action Caller claims an identity v Authenticator is verified v System establishes authenticated session v API derives trusted subject v Authorization checks resource/action v Business operation executes Authentication establishes who; authorization decides what that authenticated subject may do. Identification alone is not proof Typing an email address tells the system which account you claim to be. It does not prove you own that account. Likewise, sending userId=123 from a browser does not prove you are User 123. # Wrong trust model GET /tasks?userId=123 # Browser says who it wants to be. # The API has no authentication proof. The trust-boundary rule Anything the browser can freely choose is untrusted input. Identity becomes trusted only after the backend verifies an authenticator or a token issued by an identity system it trusts. Core invariant Never derive authorization from a user ID, email, role, or permission value merely because the browser sent it. Authentication vs authorization failure Situation Typical meaning No valid authentication 401 Unauthorized (historical HTTP name; semantically unauthenticated) Authenticated but forbidden 403 Forbidden Authenticated and allowed Proceed to service/business rules authorization Explain Identity Authentication and Authorization in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: passwords-mfa-and-modern-authenticators Passwords MFA and Modern Authenticators Passwords, MFA & Modern Authenticators Understand credential security without building a password system from scratch Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Password / passkey / factor v Identity provider verifies v Authentication result Phase 16 builds the security… Passwords, MFA & Modern Authenticators Understand credential security without building a password system from scratch Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Password / passkey / factor v Identity provider verifies v Authentication result Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. Passwords are authenticators, not database values to store directly A password is evidence the user knows a secret. A secure identity system never needs the original password after enrollment. It stores a slow password hash designed to resist offline guessing if the credential database is stolen. Figure 1 - Password verification concept User enters password v Password hashing function + salt v Compare against stored verifier v Match? v Authentication succeeds or fails The original password should not be recoverable from the stored verifier. Why SHA-256 alone is not password storage General-purpose hashes are intentionally fast. Password storage needs a deliberately expensive password hashing function so each attacker guess costs meaningful CPU/memory. OWASP currently recommends Argon2id first, with alternatives such as scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 in appropriate environments. Term Purpose Salt Unique per-password value that defeats precomputed tables Password hash Slow verifier derived from password + salt Pepper Optional server-side secret kept separately from the password database Work factor Cost configuration that makes guessing more expensive TaskFlow decision We will use Supabase Auth instead of writing password hashing, reset flows, email verification, breach defenses, and credential lifecycle ourselves. Understanding these concepts tells you why delegating identity is a security architecture choice, not laziness. MFA and stronger authenticators Multi-factor authentication combines independent categories of evidence. Passkeys/WebAuthn use public-key cryptography and are phishing-resistant compared with reusable shared secrets. TaskFlow does not implement passkeys in Phase 16, but a 2026 full-stack developer should recognize that passwords are only one authenticator option. Authenticator Strength / trade-off Password Widely supported; phishable; requires safe storage and recovery TOTP app Adds possession factor; codes can still be phished Authenticator Strength / trade-off SMS OTP Better than password-only in some contexts, but vulnerable to SIM/telephony attacks WebAuthn / passkey Public-key, origin-bound, phishing-resistant; modern preferred direction Never log credentials • Do not log plaintext passwords. • Do not log password reset tokens. • Do not log MFA secrets or recovery codes. • Do not send credentials in URL query strings. • Use TLS/HTTPS for authentication traffic. authentication Explain Passwords MFA and Modern Authenticators in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: sessions-cookies-and-browser-storage Sessions Cookies and Browser Storage Sessions, Cookies & Browser Storage Understand authenticated continuity and the security consequences of storage choices Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Successful authentication v Session continuity v Cookie / browser boundary v Later authenticated requests Phase 16 builds… Sessions, Cookies & Browser Storage Understand authenticated continuity and the security consequences of storage choices Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Successful authentication v Session continuity v Cookie / browser boundary v Later authenticated requests Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. HTTP is stateless; authenticated applications need continuity After login, the server needs a way to associate later HTTP requests with the authenticated subject. A session provides that continuity. The session can be represented by an opaque identifier stored server-side, by tokens, or by a provider-specific combination. Figure 1 - Stateful session concept Credentials verified v Server creates session record v Browser receives opaque session ID cookie v Next request sends cookie automatically v Server looks up session v Trusted user context reconstructed The browser holds an identifier; the authoritative session state remains server-side. Cookie security attributes Attribute What it protects / controls Secure Browser sends cookie only over secure HTTPS connections HttpOnly JavaScript cannot read the cookie through document.cookie SameSite Controls whether cookie is sent in cross-site contexts Path / Domain Restricts where the cookie is sent; use the narrowest practical scope Max-Age / Expires Controls cookie lifetime Set-Cookie: __Host-taskflow_session=<opaque-id>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax Illustrative, not yet implementation Phase 17 will use Supabase Auth and its current SSR/browser integration guidance. Do not copy this cookie as a custom authentication system. Browser storage is a security decision localStorage and sessionStorage are readable by JavaScript executing in the origin. OWASP currently advises not storing authentication tokens, session identifiers, JWTs, or refresh tokens there when a safer HttpOnly cookie or backend-for-frontend/session pattern is available. XSS can read JavaScript-accessible storage. Storage Automatically sent? JavaScript readable? Important risk HttpOnly cookie Yes, by cookie rules No CSRF must be considered Non-HttpOnly cookie Yes Yes XSS can read it; CSRF also relevant localStorage No Yes XSS can exfiltrate credential/token sessionStorage No Yes XSS can exfiltrate credential/token Server memory/session No browser access No Requires server-side session management store Cookie security is not one checkbox HttpOnly helps keep JavaScript from reading a cookie, but it does not stop the browser from sending that cookie automatically. That is why cookie authentication still requires intentional SameSite and CSRF design. subtitle: Authentication Fundamentals
text: jwt-structure-claims-and-verification JWT Structure Claims and Verification JWT Structure, Claims & Verification Decode for inspection, verify for trust, and validate the claims your API requires Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone JWT received v Signature + algorithm verification v Issuer/audience/time checks v Trusted subject claims… JWT Structure, Claims & Verification Decode for inspection, verify for trust, and validate the claims your API requires Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone JWT received v Signature + algorithm verification v Issuer/audience/time checks v Trusted subject claims Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. A JWT is a claims container, not magic authentication JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact representation of claims. In common signed form it contains three dot-separated base64url segments: header, payload, signature. The payload is typically readable. Signing protects integrity/authenticity when properly verified; it does not automatically encrypt the claims. xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz | | | header payload signature Registered claims you should recognize Claim Meaning Why API cares iss Issuer Was this token issued by the identity system we trust? sub Subject Which authenticated identity does the token represent? aud Audience Was this token intended for this API/resource server? exp Expiration Is the token still within its acceptance lifetime? nbf Not before Is the token valid yet? iat Issued at When was it minted? Useful context, not proof alone jti JWT ID Unique token identifier in some token lifecycle designs Figure 1 - Correct JWT verification Receive JWT v Parse header/claims v Accept only expected algorithms v Verify signature with trusted key v Validate issuer v Validate audience where required v Validate exp / nbf policy v Only then trust subject/claims Decoding is inspection. Verification plus claim validation is authentication evidence. The dangerous shortcut // WRONG mental model const payload = decodeJwt(token); const userId = payload.sub; // trusted? NO. // Decoding only proves the token contained text. // It does not prove who created it or whether it was modified. JWT payloads are not secret Do not put passwords, database credentials, API secrets, or data that must remain confidential into an ordinary signed JWT payload. Verification policy is application-specific RFC 7519 defines claims; JWT Best Current Practice requires applications to verify the claims and algorithms relevant to their use. TaskFlow will later validate tokens against the expected Supabase Auth issuer/key material and API policy instead of accepting arbitrary JWTs. authentication Explain JWT Structure Claims and Verification in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Access Refresh Tokens and Bearer Risk
subtitle: Authentication Fundamentals
text: access-refresh-tokens-and-bearer-risk Access Refresh Tokens and Bearer Risk Access Tokens, Refresh Tokens & Bearer Risk Understand short-lived API credentials, refresh lifecycles, and replay risk Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Authentication v Access token v Protected API v Expiry v Refresh flow Phase 16 builds the… Access Tokens, Refresh Tokens & Bearer Risk Understand short-lived API credentials, refresh lifecycles, and replay risk Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Authentication v Access token v Protected API v Expiry v Refresh flow Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. Access tokens and refresh tokens have different jobs An access token is presented to a protected resource such as the TaskFlow API. A refresh token is presented to the authorization/authentication system to obtain a new access token. Refresh tokens usually live longer and therefore deserve stronger protection. Figure 1 - Token lifecycle User authenticates v Authorization server issues access + maybe refresh token v Client calls API with access token v Access token expires v Client presents refresh token to auth server v New access token issued The refresh token should not be sent to every protected API request. Token Used with Typical lifetime idea Primary risk Access token Resource/API server Shorter Stolen token can call API until expiry/revocation constraints Refresh token Auth/token endpoint Longer Stolen token can mint new access tokens Bearer means possession is enough RFC 6750 defines bearer-token usage. A bearer token works for whoever possesses it unless additional sender-constraining mechanisms are used. Therefore an access token must be handled like a credential, not like a harmless identifier. GET /tasks HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer <access-token> Never put bearer tokens in URLs URLs leak into browser history, logs, analytics, referrer data, screenshots, and monitoring systems. Use the Authorization header for protected API requests. Short lifetime limits damage If an access token leaks, a shorter expiry reduces the attack window. OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice also recommends restricting token privileges and audience as much as practical. Refresh token rotation Modern OAuth security guidance requires public clients that receive refresh tokens to use sender-constrained refresh tokens or refresh-token rotation. With rotation, each refresh produces a new refresh token and invalidates the prior one, enabling replay detection. Figure 2 - Refresh rotation concept Refresh token R1 v Use R1 once v Auth server returns access token + R2 v R1 becomes invalid v Replay of R1 signals compromise The exact behavior belongs to the identity provider; application code should not invent its own rotation scheme casually. authentication Explain Access Refresh Tokens and Bearer Risk in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: login-logout-expiry-and-revocation Login Logout Expiry and Revocation Login, Logout, Expiry & Revocation Treat authentication as a complete lifecycle instead of a login screen Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Unauthenticated v Authenticated session v Expiry/refresh v Logout/revocation Phase 16 builds the security mental model before… Login, Logout, Expiry & Revocation Treat authentication as a complete lifecycle instead of a login screen Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Unauthenticated v Authenticated session v Expiry/refresh v Logout/revocation Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. Authentication is a lifecycle, not a login button A production system must reason about login, continuation, expiry, refresh, logout, password change, compromised sessions, and sensitive-operation re-authentication. "Logged in" is not a permanent boolean. Figure 1 - Authentication lifecycle Unauthenticated v Authenticate v Session established v Authenticated requests v Access token/session expiry v Refresh or re-authenticate v Logout / revoke / security event v Unauthenticated again Every transition has security and UX consequences. Logout has two dimensions Layer What logout may need to do Client Remove/expire local session material and authenticated UI state Identity provider Invalidate or revoke refresh/session state where supported API Reject expired/revoked/invalid tokens according to provider and local policy Why deleting UI state is not enough If a refresh token or server session is still valid, merely redirecting to /login does not terminate the security session. A complete logout flow follows the identity provider session model. Security events can invalidate sessions • Password change. • Explicit sign-out from all devices. • Account disabled or deleted. • Refresh-token replay detected. • Administrator or user revocation. • Risk-based security event. Re-authentication for sensitive operations Applications may require recent authentication before changing a password, adding a payout account, viewing recovery codes, or performing other high-risk actions. title: XSS CSRF CORS and HTTPS
subtitle: Authentication Fundamentals
text: xss-csrf-cors-and-https XSS CSRF CORS and HTTPS XSS, CSRF, CORS & HTTPS Separate browser threats and match mitigations to the correct security problem Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Browser storage/cookies v Cross-site/browser threat v Correct security control Phase 16 builds the security mental model… XSS, CSRF, CORS & HTTPS Separate browser threats and match mitigations to the correct security problem Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Browser storage/cookies v Cross-site/browser threat v Correct security control Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. XSS, CSRF, and CORS are different problems Authentication bugs often come from mixing browser security concepts. These mechanisms overlap in consequences but solve different threats. Concept Question XSS Can attacker-controlled JavaScript execute in our origin? CSRF Can another site cause the browser to send an authenticated request the user did not intend? CORS May browser JavaScript read/call a cross-origin resource under the server CORS policy? HTTPS/TLS Can network attackers read/modify traffic in transit? Authentication Who is the caller? Authorization May that caller perform this action? Cookie authentication and CSRF Browsers automatically attach eligible cookies. That convenience creates CSRF risk: another site may be able to trigger a request while the victim browser includes its authenticated cookie. SameSite is an important mitigation, but applications may also need CSRF tokens or origin checks depending on architecture and request patterns. Figure 1 - CSRF shape Victim is authenticated to TaskFlow v Victim visits attacker site v Attacker page triggers TaskFlow request v Browser may attach TaskFlow cookie v TaskFlow must distinguish intended vs cross-site request Cookie authentication requires cross-site request reasoning. JavaScript-readable tokens and XSS If an access or refresh token is stored where application JavaScript can read it, injected JavaScript can potentially exfiltrate it. HttpOnly cookies reduce direct token theft through JavaScript, but they do not magically solve all XSS impact because malicious scripts can still issue actions as the user while running in the origin. CORS is not authentication CORS is a browser-enforced cross-origin access policy. It does not prove who a request came from. Non-browser clients do not rely on browser CORS enforcement. An API with permissive CORS still needs authentication and authorization; an API with strict CORS is not automatically secure. HTTPS is mandatory for credentials Bearer tokens, cookies, passwords, and authentication codes must be protected in transit. Secure cookie semantics also depend on HTTPS in production. cors Explain XSS CSRF CORS and HTTPS in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: nestjs-guard-and-protected-api-mental-model NestJS Guard and Protected API Mental Model NestJS Guard & Protected API Mental Model Understand the future token-verification boundary before implementing it Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Protected request v Auth guard v Verified identity v Controller/service Phase 16 builds the security mental model… NestJS Guard & Protected API Mental Model Understand the future token-verification boundary before implementing it Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Protected request v Auth guard v Verified identity v Controller/service Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. The NestJS guard is a verification boundary Phase 18 will implement the guard, but the mental model belongs here. The guard runs before protected controller logic and either establishes a trusted authenticated subject or rejects the request. Figure 1 - Protected API request HTTP request v Extract Authorization bearer token v Verify signature / expected token policy v Validate required claims v Build authenticated-user context v Continue to controller v Service enforces authorization A decoded token does not reach business logic until verification succeeds. Typical API outcomes Condition Result No token on protected route 401 Malformed/invalid signature token 401 Expired token 401 Wrong issuer/audience for API policy 401 Valid user, lacks resource permission 403 Valid user, allowed Controller/service continue Do not confuse authentication with role checks The authentication guard should establish who the caller is. Authorization logic can then evaluate workspace membership, ownership, role, or permissions. Keeping these concerns separable makes policy easier to reason about and test. Request -> AuthGuard: who are you? -> Authorization/Service: may you do this? -> Business rule: is this operation valid? -> Prisma/PostgreSQL Route protection strategy In real applications you must choose whether routes are protected by default with explicit public exceptions, or public by default with explicit guards. Security-sensitive systems generally benefit from fail-closed thinking: it should be harder to accidentally expose a new route. title: Threat Modeling Observability and Debugging
subtitle: Authentication Fundamentals
text: threat-modeling-observability-and-debugging Threat Modeling Observability and Debugging Threat Modeling, Observability & Debugging Trace credentials and failures without leaking secrets or weakening security Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Credential lifecycle v Failure evidence v Safe logs v Root-cause fix Phase 16 builds the security mental… Threat Modeling, Observability & Debugging Trace credentials and failures without leaking secrets or weakening security Phase 16 - Authentication Fundamentals Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Credential lifecycle v Failure evidence v Safe logs v Root-cause fix Phase 16 builds the security mental model before any Supabase Auth integration code is introduced. Threat-model authentication by following the credential When debugging or designing auth, trace where credentials and identity assertions move. Ask where they can be read, replayed, logged, copied, expired, or incorrectly trusted. Figure 1 - Credential exposure review Authenticator / login v Session or tokens issued v Browser storage boundary v Network transmission v NestJS verification v Logs / telemetry v Logout / revocation Every arrow is a possible leak, replay, or trust bug. Common failure matrix Symptom Likely layer to inspect Login fails before API call Identity provider / credentials / redirect flow Browser has session but NestJS returns 401 Token forwarding or API token verification 401 only after some time Access token expiry / refresh lifecycle Valid user gets 403 Authorization / membership / permission logic Works in PowerShell but browser fails before request Browser/CORS/session forwarding issue Works locally, fails in HTTPS production Cookie domain/Secure/SameSite/origin configuration Users appear as wrong account Subject mapping/session contamination - severe security bug Authentication logs should be useful but non-secret • requestId / correlation ID • route / method • authentication success/failure category • verified subject identifier only where appropriate for audit policy • issuer/audience mismatch category • token expiration category • provider error code • never raw password, bearer token, refresh token, cookie, or reset token Rate limiting and abuse Authentication endpoints are attractive targets for password guessing, credential stuffing, OTP abuse, and account enumeration. Production identity architecture needs rate limiting, monitoring, lockout/risk controls, and neutral error messages where appropriate. A managed identity provider helps, but application-specific endpoints still need abuse reasoning. Debug from evidence Do not fix a 401 by disabling signature checks, accepting any issuer, lengthening tokens indefinitely, or turning protected routes public. Hands-on reasoning lab Phase 16 is intentionally concept-heavy. The lab tests whether you can reason about authentication architecture before a provider SDK hides the mechanics. Lab A - Classify the concept Scenario Concept User types email Identification / claimed identity Password verified Authentication Browser receives authenticated continuity state Session NestJS verifies access token Authentication evidence verification User may update only Tasks in their Workspace Authorization Task cannot transition directly DONE -> TODO Business rule, not auth Lab B - Find the security mistake • Frontend sends userId in POST /tasks and service trusts it as owner. • JWT payload is base64-decoded and sub is trusted without signature verification. • Refresh token is placed in a URL query parameter. • Authorization header is written to request logs. • JWT is stored in localStorage without discussing XSS risk. • Cookie auth is enabled with SameSite=None but CSRF is never considered. • CORS allowlist is treated as proof that the request is authenticated. • Logout only hides the dashboard but leaves a valid provider session alive. Lab C - Draw the future TaskFlow flow On paper, draw: User -> Supabase Auth -> session/access token -> Next.js -> Authorization header -> NestJS guard -> trusted subject -> TasksService -> membership/ownership check -> Prisma. Label every point where trust changes. Exercise levels Level Challenge 1 - Follow Explain AuthN vs AuthZ, access vs refresh token, and HttpOnly vs JavaScript-readable storage. 2 - Modify Design a logout lifecycle for a shared-office computer where the user expects sign-out to terminate future token refresh. 3 - Implement (design) Write pseudocode for a NestJS guard that returns 401 for missing, expired, wrong-issuer, or invalid-signature tokens without implementing cryptography yourself. 4 - Engineer Threat-model authentication for an HRIS payroll approval screen. Identify authenticator strength, session storage, re-authentication, authorization, audit logging, token exposure, logout/revocation, and recovery risks. subtitle: Supabase Authentication
text: supabase-auth-architecture-and-keys Supabase Auth Architecture and Keys Supabase Auth Architecture & Keys Place identity, sessions, keys, Next.js, and NestJS in the correct security boundaries Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Supabase Auth v Next.js session v NestJS later verifies bearer token v Business authorization remains… Supabase Auth Architecture & Keys Place identity, sessions, keys, Next.js, and NestJS in the correct security boundaries Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Supabase Auth v Next.js session v NestJS later verifies bearer token v Business authorization remains separate Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. Supabase Auth is the identity provider, not the application backend TaskFlow already has a NestJS backend that owns application rules and Prisma persistence. Supabase Auth is introduced to establish identity and manage the authentication session. It does not replace TasksService, authorization rules, or the NestJS API. Figure 1 - Responsibility split Supabase Auth: credentials + session + access token v Next.js: web session and authenticated pages v NestJS (Phase 18): verify bearer token v Service layer: ownership, membership, permissions v Prisma/PostgreSQL: durable business data Authentication and business authorization remain separate layers. Concern Owner in TaskFlow Password verification / email confirmation Supabase Auth Cookie-backed SSR session Next.js + @supabase/ssr JWT verification for protected API NestJS guard in Phase 18 Task ownership / Workspace permission NestJS service/authorization layer Business records Prisma + PostgreSQL Why two Supabase packages? @supabase/supabase-js is the base SDK. @supabase/ssr wraps it for frameworks where the same authenticated session must be readable on the browser and server through cookies. Current Supabase guidance recommends @supabase/ssr for Next.js cookie-backed sessions. Publishable key vs secret key The Project URL and Publishable key are intentionally used by the browser-facing client. A service-role or secret key has elevated privileges and must never be placed in NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables, browser bundles, or source examples. Do not confuse the key with the user A public/publishable project key identifies the Supabase project/client capability. The signed-in user identity still comes from the authenticated session and verified access token. supabase Explain Supabase Auth Architecture and Keys in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. Next.js 16 uses Proxy for the request boundary Next.js renamed Middleware to Proxy in version 16. Supabase relies on this request boundary because Server Components cannot reliably write refreshed auth cookies themselves. Figure 1 - Proxy refresh path Browser sends auth cookies v proxy.ts runs v createServerClient reads cookies v getClaims verifies/refreshes access token v request cookies updated v response Set-Cookie updated v Server Component renders with synchronized session Proxy keeps browser and server session state synchronized. Why getClaims belongs here Current Supabase guidance says to use getClaims when protecting pages and user data. It verifies the access token signature against the project JWKS when asymmetric signing keys are used, and it refreshes a session that is near expiry. Do not protect SSR pages with getSession().user getSession reads session storage but does not itself revalidate the stored user identity. Use getClaims for verified identity, or getUser when a fresh Auth-server user record is required. text: signin-signout-and-session-lifecycle SignIn SignOut and Session Lifecycle Sign-In, Sign-Out & Session Lifecycle Create and terminate real Supabase sessions without confusing UI state with security state Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Sign in v Cookie session v Authenticated use v Local sign out Phase 17… Sign-In, Sign-Out & Session Lifecycle Create and terminate real Supabase sessions without confusing UI state with security state Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Sign in v Cookie session v Authenticated use v Local sign out Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. Sign-in establishes the cookie-backed session TaskFlow uses a Server Action to submit email/password to Supabase Auth. When authentication succeeds, @supabase/ssr writes the session into cookies through the server client/response path. const { error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password, }) if (error) { redirect('/login?error=Unable+to+sign+in') } revalidatePath('/', 'layout') redirect('/account') Why the public error is generic Supabase sign-in errors can intentionally avoid distinguishing a missing account from a wrong password. TaskFlow preserves that privacy behavior instead of displaying account-enumeration hints. Sign-out scope is a product decision Supabase JavaScript signOut supports global, local, and others scopes. JavaScript defaults to global. TaskFlow explicitly chooses local for the ordinary Sign out button so one browser session does not unexpectedly terminate the user on every other device. await supabase.auth.signOut({ scope: 'local' }) Scope Meaning local Terminate the current session only global Terminate all refresh sessions for the user others Terminate other sessions while keeping current session Access-token nuance Revoking/signing out refresh-session state does not magically invalidate an already issued access token before its exp time. text: getclaims-getuser-getsession-and-access-token-handoff getClaims getUser getSession and Access Token Handoff getClaims, getUser, getSession & API Token Handoff Use each Supabase Auth method for its intended trust job and prepare the NestJS boundary Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Verified claims v Fresh user record v Raw session/token v… getClaims, getUser, getSession & API Token Handoff Use each Supabase Auth method for its intended trust job and prepare the NestJS boundary Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Verified claims v Fresh user record v Raw session/token v NestJS handoff Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. Three Auth methods, three jobs Current Supabase SSR guidance distinguishes getClaims, getUser, and getSession. Using each for the correct reason prevents subtle trust bugs. Method Use when Trust note getClaims() Protect pages/data; verify JWT identity Verifies token signature/claims; preferred for SSR protection getUser() Need fresh user record from Auth server Network request; catches account/session state changes getSession() Need raw access/refresh token or expiry Do not trust embedded user by itself in server cookie context Phase 18 handoff: forwarding the access token TaskFlow has a separate NestJS API. To call it, Next.js will eventually need the raw access token. getSession is appropriate for retrieving the token as transport material, but Next.js must not treat the session.user object as the final authorization proof. const { data: { session }, } = await supabase.auth.getSession() const accessToken = session?.access_token // Phase 18: // Authorization: Bearer <accessToken> // NestJS verifies it before trusting sub/claims. Transport is not trust Next.js retrieving an access token does not make NestJS trust it. Phase 18 creates the verification boundary in the API. Revocation gap A correctly signed, unexpired access token can remain valid until exp even after the underlying refresh session is revoked. The Supabase advanced guide recommends getUser where detecting server-side session termination immediately matters. This is a product/security policy choice, not a reason to call getUser on every render automatically. authentication Explain getClaims getUser getSession and Access Token Handoff in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: ssr-caching-refresh-and-auth-debugging SSR Caching Refresh and Auth Debugging SSR Caching, Refresh & Auth Debugging Diagnose session failures without weakening cookie or token security Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Cookie synchronization v Refresh v Cache boundaries v Debug evidence Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in… SSR Caching, Refresh & Auth Debugging Diagnose session failures without weakening cookie or token security Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Cookie synchronization v Refresh v Cache boundaries v Debug evidence Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. SSR authentication fails in ways ordinary client-only auth does not Cookie synchronization, token refresh, route prefetching, caching, and response headers all affect SSR authentication. Random logout symptoms often come from session cookies not being propagated consistently. Symptom First layer to inspect User signs in then appears logged out on Server Proxy/session-cookie refresh path Component Works client-side, fails server-side server.ts cookies + Proxy Confirmation returns to wrong host Supabase Site URL / redirect configuration Repeated random logout Proxy response/cookies being replaced incorrectly One user receives another session CDN/ISR caching authenticated response - critical getSession has user but protected page should reject Use getClaims/getUser for identity verification Do not cache authenticated Set-Cookie responses publicly Supabase warns that session refresh writes Set-Cookie. If a CDN caches that response and serves it to another visitor, session leakage can occur. Current @supabase/ssr versions provide cache-related headers during refresh; the Proxy must apply those headers. Authenticated routes should not use ISR casually. Next.js route prefetching Authentication flows that depend on a browser first processing new cookies can interact poorly with prefetching. Keep the SSR guide current, test real navigation behavior, and use dynamic rendering for authenticated pages when request-time session state is required. Debug with observable boundaries • Confirm NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and publishable key are loaded in apps/web. • Confirm the dashboard Site URL matches the browser origin. • Inspect the /auth/confirm request and redirect chain. • Inspect Set-Cookie responses without copying token values into logs/screenshots. • Confirm proxy.ts matcher actually runs for protected routes. • Confirm getClaims returns verified claims after sign-in/refresh. • Do not fix auth by disabling cookie security or exposing a secret key. authentication Explain SSR Caching Refresh and Auth Debugging in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: security-boundaries-and-nestjs-handoff Security Boundaries and NestJS Handoff Security Boundaries & NestJS Handoff Define exactly what Phase 17 protects and what remains untrusted until Phase 18 Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Next.js authenticated session v Access token transport v NestJS verification next v Authorization later… Security Boundaries & NestJS Handoff Define exactly what Phase 17 protects and what remains untrusted until Phase 18 Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Next.js authenticated session v Access token transport v NestJS verification next v Authorization later Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. Phase 17 stops at the web-session boundary The user can now authenticate to Supabase and maintain a Next.js SSR session. The NestJS API is not protected yet. Keeping this boundary explicit prevents a dangerous illusion that a protected page automatically means a protected backend. Figure 1 - Current vs next phase Phase 17: Supabase Auth session established v Next.js obtains access token when needed v Phase 18: send Authorization Bearer token to NestJS v NestJS verifies token v Trusted authenticated user attached to request v Phase 19: ownership/RBAC authorization Authentication is built layer by layer instead of trusting the browser. What may be browser-visible Value Browser-visible? Supabase Project URL Yes Supabase Publishable key Yes Access token Credential - browser/session system may possess it; never log it Refresh token Highly sensitive session credential; never log/expose intentionally Supabase Secret / service-role key Never DATABASE_URL Never Do not use the database Auth schema as application authorization logic Supabase Auth maintains identity information in its auth schema. TaskFlow still has its own domain User, Membership, Workspace, Project, and Task records. Phase 19 will establish the explicit link from verified auth subject to application authorization data. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. Hands-on lab: make authentication observable Complete the lab in order. Do not proceed because the login page looks correct; proceed because each session transition is verified. Lab A - Install and configure • From taskflow\apps\web install @supabase/supabase-js@2.116.0 and @supabase/ssr@0.12.7. • Create .env.local from .env.local.example using your project URL and Publishable key. • Configure Site URL and the signup confirmation template in the Supabase dashboard. • Create browser.ts/server.ts equivalents and proxy.ts exactly once - do not create duplicate auth clients per feature. Lab B - Verify flows Test Expected result Open /account signed out Redirect to /login Create account with confirmation enabled Message asks you to check email; no false authenticated UI Open confirmation email /auth/confirm verifies token hash and redirects to /account Refresh /account repeatedly Session remains valid; no random logout Sign out Current session ends; protected page redirects again Use invalid/expired confirmation link Safe auth error page Lab C - Explain the trust chain Draw this without looking at the book: Credentials -> Supabase Auth -> cookie-backed session -> Proxy/getClaims -> verified claims -> protected Next.js page -> raw access token when calling NestJS -> NestJS verification in Phase 18. Exercise levels Level Challenge 1 - Follow Reproduce the reference auth flow and verify every transition. 2 - Modify Add a public /about route while keeping /account and /tasks protected. Explain where the rule belongs. 3 - Implement Add a "Sign out all devices" action that intentionally uses global scope and clearly labels the effect. 4 - Engineer Design an HRIS login/session policy: email confirmation, MFA trigger, local vs global logout, fresh-user checks for payroll approval, and session-revocation expectations. Phase exit checklist • You can explain why @supabase/ssr exists in addition to supabase-js. • You know which Supabase values may be NEXT_PUBLIC and which must never be public. • You can implement the browser client, server client, and Next.js 16 Proxy session path. • You use getClaims for protected SSR identity checks rather than trusting getSession().user. • You can explain email confirmation token-hash exchange. • You can explain local vs global sign out. • You understand why authenticated responses must not be cached across users. • You can retrieve an access token for transport to NestJS without treating it as verified by NestJS. • You understand that Phase 17 authenticates the web session but does not yet secure the NestJS API.
