text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 17: Supabase Authentication Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk auth form -> Supabase Auth -> session/cookies -> Next.js server/client auth helpers -> protected UI -> access token handoff Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Using service-role key in browser code Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. text: from-session-to-trusted-api-identity From Session to Trusted API Identity PHASE 18 - BOOK 01 From Session to Trusted API Identity Why a Next.js login is not enough for NestJS Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user… From Session to Trusted API Identity Why a Next.js login is not enough for NestJS Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically verified by the backend. Two separate trust boundaries TaskFlow has two server processes. Next.js can read its cookie-backed Supabase session, while NestJS receives an ordinary HTTP request. NestJS must establish trust independently. Different servers, different responsibilities Next.js NestJS • cookie session • receives headers • refresh lifecycle • no cookie knowledge assumed • Supabase SSR client • must verify bearer JWT • can obtain access token • creates request identity Wrong architecture GET /tasks?userId=5c53... // Browser claims who the user is. // The API trusts an unverified identifier. A UUID is not proof of identity. Anyone can send someone else's UUID. Correct architecture Identity establishment Next.js gets current access token Authorization: Bearer <JWT> NestJS extracts bearer token Supabase verification validates JWT Verified sub becomes authenticated user id Authentication vs authorization Question Layer Typical result Who is calling? Auth guard 401 when not authenticated May this user access this resource? Authorization/business layer 403 when authenticated but forbidden Is the requested workflow valid?Service/business rules 400/409 depending on rule The trust statement After verification, claims.sub may be used as the authenticated Supabase user identifier. Before verification, decoded JWT contents are attacker-controlled input. text: next-js-to-nestjs-bearer-token-handoff Next.js to NestJS Bearer Token Handoff PHASE 18 - BOOK 02 Next.js -> NestJS Bearer Token Handoff Sending the session access token without leaking it into URLs or logs Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course… Next.js -> NestJS Bearer Token Handoff Sending the session access token without leaking it into URLs or logs Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically verified by the backend. The HTTP contract GET /auth/me HTTP/1.1 Host: 127.0.0.1:4000 Authorization: Bearer <SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN> The access token belongs in the standard Authorization header. It should not be placed in query strings, route parameters, analytics events, or logs. Server-side Next.js helper // apps/web/src/lib/api/authenticated-fetch.ts import { createClient } from '@/lib/supabase/server' export async function authenticatedApiFetch( path: string, init: RequestInit = {}, ) { const supabase = await createClient() const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getSession() if (error || !data.session?.access_token) { throw new Error('Authenticated session required') } const headers = new Headers(init.headers) headers.set( 'Authorization', `Bearer ${data.session.access_token}`, ) return fetch( `${process.env.API_BASE_URL}${path}`, { ...init, headers, cache: 'no-store' }, ) } Phase 17 taught the difference between trusting a session and merely reading cookie contents. This helper is used only after the server-side auth layer has established the current session. Browser-side calls A browser Client Component can also obtain the current session access token from Supabase and call NestJS. That path is subject to CORS because the browser is crossing origins. const { data } = await supabase.auth.getSession() await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:4000/auth/me', { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.session?.access_token}`, }, }) Do not do this /auth/me?token=eyJ... console.log(accessToken) localStorage.setItem('debug-token', accessToken) Bearer tokens are credentials. Treat them like secrets during their lifetime. Source note: verified against current Supabase Auth/getClaims/signing-key guidance and NestJS authentication/authorization docs. subtitle: NestJS Authentication Guards
text: server-side-supabase-token-verification Server Side Supabase Token Verification PHASE 18 - BOOK 03 Server-Side Supabase Token Verification Using getClaims() in a NestJS 12-compatible service Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only… Server-Side Supabase Token Verification Using getClaims() in a NestJS 12-compatible service Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically verified by the backend. Why getClaims() Supabase documents auth.getClaims(jwt) as the preferred way to verify Supabase-issued JWTs. With asymmetric signing keys it verifies against the project JWKS and benefits from caching; with legacy symmetric signing it can fall back to the Auth server. Install in apps/api cd "C:\path\to\taskflow\apps\api" pnpm add @supabase/supabase-js@2.116.0 Environment # apps/api/.env SUPABASE_URL=https://<project-ref>.supabase.co SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=sb_publishable_... The publishable key is not a privileged server secret. It identifies the project/client context; the user JWT proves the caller identity. Do not use a Supabase secret/service-role key merely to verify ordinary user access tokens. Verification service // auth/supabase-auth.service.ts import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common' import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config' import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js' @Injectable() export class SupabaseAuthService { private readonly url: string private readonly client constructor(config: ConfigService) { this.url = config.getOrThrow<string>('SUPABASE_URL') const key = config.getOrThrow<string>( 'SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY', ) this.client = createClient(this.url, key, { auth: { persistSession: false, autoRefreshToken: false, }, }) } async verifyAccessToken(token: string) { const { data, error } = await this.client.auth.getClaims(token) if (error || !data?.claims?.sub) { throw new UnauthorizedException( 'Invalid or expired access token', ) } const expectedIssuer = `${this.url}/auth/v1` if (data.claims.iss !== expectedIssuer) { throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid token issuer') } return data.claims } } Why extra issuer checking? getClaims() performs cryptographic verification. We still keep the expected project issuer explicit in TaskFlow so a token from another Supabase project cannot silently become an application identity. Audience / role policy For ordinary TaskFlow users, require a user access token whose audience/role corresponds to the authenticated user context. The exact claims are read from the verified payload, never from an unverified decode. text: build-the-nestjs-authguard Build the NestJS AuthGuard PHASE 18 - BOOK 04 Build the NestJS AuthGuard Turning verification into a reusable request gate Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only… Build the NestJS AuthGuard Turning verification into a reusable request gate Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically verified by the backend. Guard responsibility AuthGuard canActivate() Incoming request Extract Authorization header Require Bearer scheme Verify Supabase JWT Attach authenticated identity Allow controller execution Authenticated identity type // common/types/authenticated-user.ts export type AuthenticatedUser = { id: string email?: string role?: string sessionId?: string } Guard implementation // auth/supabase-auth.guard.ts import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable, UnauthorizedException, } from '@nestjs/common' import type { FastifyRequest } from 'fastify' import { SupabaseAuthService } from './supabase-auth.service' type AuthenticatedRequest = FastifyRequest & { user?: { id: string email?: string role?: string sessionId?: string } } @Injectable() export class SupabaseAuthGuard implements CanActivate { constructor( private readonly auth: SupabaseAuthService, ) {} async canActivate( context: ExecutionContext, ): Promise<boolean> { const request = context.switchToHttp() .getRequest<AuthenticatedRequest>() const token = this.extractBearerToken(request) const claims = await this.auth.verifyAccessToken(token) request.user = { id: claims.sub, email: typeof claims.email === 'string' ? claims.email : undefined, role: typeof claims.role === 'string' ? claims.role : undefined, sessionId: typeof claims.session_id === 'string' ? claims.session_id : undefined, } return true } private extractBearerToken( request: FastifyRequest, ): string { const value = request.headers.authorization const [scheme, token] = value?.split(' ') ?? [] if (scheme !== 'Bearer' || !token) { throw new UnauthorizedException( 'Bearer access token required', ) } return token } } What the guard does not do • It does not decide Workspace permissions. • It does not decide Task ownership. • It does not decide whether a workflow transition is allowed. • It does not query Prisma merely to prove the JWT signature. Authentication creates trusted identity. Authorization and business rules remain separate layers. Start explicit @Controller('tasks') @UseGuards(SupabaseAuthGuard) export class TasksController { // every endpoint in this controller is authenticated } Controller-wide protection is easy to see and fits TaskFlow while we are still learning the boundary. Public endpoints remain public @Controller('health') export class HealthController { @Get() check() { return { status: 'ok' } } } Global guard later NestJS supports registering an authentication guard globally and using metadata such as @Public() for anonymous routes. This can be safer when most of an API should be protected, because forgetting a decorator no longer accidentally creates a public endpoint. providers: [ { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: SupabaseAuthGuard, }, ] Why we do not switch globally yet • We want the trust boundary visible while learning. • Phase 19 will add authorization and may influence guard composition. • Public-vs-protected route inventory should be explicit before default-deny is enabled. Recommended production direction For an internal business system where almost every endpoint is private, authenticated by default with a small explicit public-route escape hatch is usually easier to audit than protecting hundreds of routes one by one. Authentication failure matrix Scenario HTTP Public meaning No Authorization header 401 Authentication required Wrong auth scheme 401 Bearer token required Expired token 401 Authentication expired Invalid signature 401 Credentials invalid Wrong issuer/project 401 Credentials invalid Verified user lacks permission 403 Authenticated but forbidden Do not leak verification internals A client does not need to know whether signature verification failed because of a key ID, algorithm, or JWK cache detail. Keep precise diagnostics in safe server logs and return a stable public 401 contract. Phase 13 integration The guard can throw UnauthorizedException. The existing global exception filter then adds TaskFlow fields such as requestId, timestamp, path, and stable error code. { "statusCode": 401, "code": "UNAUTHORIZED", "message": "Authentication required.", "requestId": "42", "path": "/tasks", "timestamp": "2026-09-18T..." } Frontend behavior • 401: refresh/re-establish session or redirect to login. • 403: show an authorization/permission message; logging in again may not help. • Network failure: do not mislabel it as authentication failure. 401 and 403 must remain distinct. Authentication and authorization are different security decisions. Source note: verified against current Supabase Auth/getClaims/signing-key guidance and NestJS authentication/authorization docs. text: cors-authorization-headers-and-preflight CORS Authorization Headers and Preflight PHASE 18 - BOOK 08 CORS and Authorization Headers Why browser bearer requests can trigger preflight Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only… CORS and Authorization Headers Why browser bearer requests can trigger preflight Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically verified by the backend. Browser path Cross-origin authenticated request Browser Client Component OPTIONS preflight when required NestJS CORS policy Actual request with Authorization AuthGuard verifies token NestJS CORS configuration app.enableCors({ origin: 'http://localhost:3000', methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PATCH', 'DELETE', 'OPTIONS'], allowedHeaders: [ 'Content-Type', 'Authorization', ], }) Important distinction CORS does not verify the access token. CORS controls whether browser JavaScript may make/read cross-origin requests. The AuthGuard verifies authentication. Server-to-server path A Next.js Server Component calling NestJS from the server is not subject to the browser's CORS enforcement. The bearer token still must be verified because CORS and authentication solve different problems. Common debugging sequence • Does Network show an OPTIONS request? • Does the preflight response allow Authorization? • Does the actual request contain Authorization: Bearer ...? • Does NestJS return 401 from the guard or was the browser blocked before the request? text: signing-keys-jwks-and-2026-supabase-choices Signing Keys JWKS and 2026 Supabase Choices PHASE 18 - BOOK 09 Signing Keys, JWKS, Rotation and 2026 Supabase Choices Understanding what getClaims() is doing for you Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user… Signing Keys, JWKS, Rotation and 2026 Supabase Choices Understanding what getClaims() is doing for you Phase 18 trust boundary Next.js authenticated session Authorization: Bearer <access token> NestJS authentication guard Verified Supabase identity Controller and business service Course principle: a user ID becomes trusted only after the access token has been cryptographically verified by the backend. Modern Supabase signing keys Supabase now supports asymmetric signing keys and publishes trusted public keys through the project JWKS endpoint. Public keys verify tokens but cannot mint new ones. GET https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/ auth/v1/.well-known/jwks.json Why getClaims() fits this course Concern getClaims() behavior Asymmetric keys Verifies against JWKS, with caching Key rotation Supabase client handles JWK lookup/cache behavior Legacy HS256 Falls back to Auth server verification NestJS version Framework-independent base client call Alternative: direct jose verification For projects committed to asymmetric signing keys, a backend can use a JWT library such as jose with a remote JWKS and explicitly validate issuer, audience and expiration. Supabase documents this pattern. We do not choose it as the primary course implementation because getClaims() also handles legacy signing-key projects. @supabase/server in 2026 Supabase now recommends @supabase/server for bearer-token backend APIs and ships a NestJS adapter. Version 1.x is public beta. At the time of this phase, the package adapter table lists NestJS 10 and 11, while TaskFlow is NestJS 12. We therefore use the framework-independent verification path and can revisit the adapter after its published compatibility catches up. Revocation nuance JWKS caching improves performance but means emergency signing-key revocation can have a cache window in external backend verifiers. Supabase documents this trade-off; incident-response plans should account for it. Debug by layer Authentication debugging order Does Next.js have a current session? Was Authorization header sent? Did CORS allow browser request? Did guard extract Bearer token? Level 1 - Follow Install the backend Supabase client, add API environment variables, create SupabaseAuthService, create the guard, add @CurrentUser(), and protect /auth/me. Level 2 - Modify Protect TasksController at controller level. Keep /health public. Verify the no-token and valid-token paths. Level 3 - Implement Build an authenticated GET /auth/me response that returns only safe verified identity fields. Add a frontend page that calls it from Next.js using the current access token. Level 4 - Engineer Design the production authentication policy for a payroll API containing public health checks, employee endpoints, HR endpoints, and internal automation endpoints. Decide whether auth should be global/default-deny and identify which endpoints truly need different credential types. Phase exit oral questions • Why is a userId query parameter not identity? • What exactly turns claims.sub into trusted identity? • Why is decode-only JWT handling unsafe? • Why does a 401 differ from a 403? • Why is CORS not authentication? • Why do we keep authorization out of AuthGuard? • When would direct JWKS verification be appropriate? Exit checklist • Valid Supabase token reaches NestJS as a Bearer token. • Missing/malformed/expired tokens return 401. • Verified sub is attached as request user.id. • Protected Tasks routes reject anonymous callers. • Health route remains public. • No access token or secret key is committed/logged. • You can explain the difference between authentication, authorization and business rules. Phase 18 is complete when NestJS can establish a trusted caller identity independently of the browser and independently of Next.js. text: authorization-mental-model-and-threats Authorization Mental Model and Threats Authorization Mental Model & Threats Separate identity from access and understand broken-access-control failure modes Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Authenticated subject v Action v Resource v Context v Decision Phase 19 transforms verified identity… Authorization Mental Model & Threats Separate identity from access and understand broken-access-control failure modes Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Authenticated subject v Action v Resource v Context v Decision Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions. Authentication and authorization solve different problems A valid bearer token proves the caller identity. It does not grant access to every row. Authorization evaluates the subject, action, resource, and context. OWASP recommends least privilege, deny-by-default, and validating access on every request. Question Layer Who is calling? SupabaseAuthGuard Which TaskFlow user is that subject linked to? AuthorizationService Which workspace membership exists? Membership relation What may this role generally do? Role -> permission mapping May this user act on this specific task? Object-level policy / service logic Broken access control is usually contextual A user may be allowed to read Task objects in one workspace and forbidden from reading an identical Task object in another. Type-level access alone is not enough. Four useful models • RBAC - role grants broad capabilities. • Permission/claims model - actions such as task.delete or member.manage. • ABAC - decisions include attributes such as project state or time. • ReBAC/ownership - decisions depend on relationships: member-of, assigned-to, manager-of. authorization Explain Authorization Mental Model and Threats in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: link-supabase-identity-to-taskflow-user Link Supabase Identity to TaskFlow User Link Supabase Identity to TaskFlow User Create a safe bridge between external identity and application-domain authorization data Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone claims.sub v User.authSubject v User.id v Membership Phase 19 transforms verified identity… Link Supabase Identity to TaskFlow User Create a safe bridge between external identity and application-domain authorization data Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone claims.sub v User.authSubject v User.id v Membership Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions. Debugging Workshop — Phase 19: Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. text: accessibility-keyboard-and-focus-architecture Accessibility Keyboard and Focus Architecture Accessibility, Keyboard & Focus Architecture Build WCAG 2.2 thinking into component behavior and semantics Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Semantic structure v Keyboard operation v Visible focus v Readable states v Usable targets Phase 20 turns the… Accessibility, Keyboard & Focus Architecture Build WCAG 2.2 thinking into component behavior and semantics Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Semantic structure v Keyboard operation v Visible focus v Readable states v Usable targets Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the browser. Accessibility is component architecture TaskFlow targets WCAG 2.2 AA thinking from the beginning. The goal is not a “compliance page” at the end; keyboard behavior, focus, labels, semantics, target size, reflow, and error communication influence how components are designed. Concern TaskFlow pattern Keyboard Every action is a link/button/form control, not clickable divs Focus Visible `:focus-visible`; no sticky UI fully hides focus Bypass Skip link to `#main-content` Target size Primary controls designed around >=44px comfort; never crowd tiny targets State Status uses text + color Tables caption, th, scope, labeled scroll region Zoom/reflow Test at narrow widths and 200% zoom Why 24px and 44px both appear in accessibility discussions WCAG 2.2 AA introduces a 24x24 CSS pixel minimum target-size criterion with exceptions. A 44x44 target is the stronger enhanced target and remains a practical design goal for primary controls, especially touch interfaces. Figure 1 - Keyboard path Skip link v Primary navigation v Page heading/actions v Filters/table links v Pagination/actions v Account controls Focus order should follow the visual and semantic reading order. Focus must stay visible Do not remove outlines without replacing them. WCAG 2.2 requires keyboard focus to be visible and adds requirements around focus not being obscured by authored content. ui Explain Accessibility Keyboard and Focus Architecture in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: responsive-and-adaptive-ui-design Responsive and Adaptive UI Design Responsive & Adaptive UI Design Adapt the application shell and domain surfaces across real viewport pressure points Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Wide shell v Collapsed shell v Stacked actions v Contained mobile overflow Phase 20 turns… Responsive & Adaptive UI Design Adapt the application shell and domain surfaces across real viewport pressure points Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Wide shell v Collapsed shell v Stacked actions v Contained mobile overflow Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the browser. Responsive design is not “desktop, then shrink everything” TaskFlow uses layout changes at pressure points rather than device-name breakpoints. The shell collapses when the sidebar and content can no longer coexist comfortably; page actions stack when horizontal space becomes constrained. Width / condition Expected behavior Wide desktop 260px sidebar + centered content area Laptop/tablet landscape Same shell with tighter padding <= 900px Desktop sidebar removed; mobile navigation available <= 640px Page header stacks; primary action becomes full width Narrow mobile Table remains inside contained horizontal-scroll region Use modern viewport units carefully The shell uses `100dvh` so mobile browser chrome changes are handled better than a hard `100vh` assumption. But content should still be allowed to grow; avoid locking pages to viewport height when they contain long data. Responsive test matrix • 320px narrow mobile • 390px common mobile • 768px tablet portrait • 900px shell breakpoint • 1024px laptop/tablet landscape • 1366px common desktop • 1920px wide desktop Horizontal overflow belongs to the component, not the whole page If a table needs horizontal scrolling, contain it in the table region. A page-level scrollbar often indicates a broken layout constraint. authentication Explain Responsive and Adaptive UI Design in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: server-and-client-component-composition Server and Client Component Composition Server & Client Component Composition Keep Server Components as the default and hydrate only interaction islands Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Server page/layout v Server-rendered UI v Client interaction island Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation… Server & Client Component Composition Keep Server Components as the default and hydrate only interaction islands Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Server page/layout v Server-rendered UI v Client interaction island Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the browser. Server Components remain the default Next.js App Router pages and layouts are Server Components by default. They are ideal for protected page composition and initial API fetching. Client Components enter only where browser state, event handlers, lifecycle hooks, or browser APIs are needed. Feature Server or Client? Why App protected layout Server Session gate + shell composition Tasks page initial list Server Fetch close to server/API boundary Sidebar static links Server No local interaction required Mobile menu toggle Client Local open/close state + click events Future dialog Client Focus management + interaction StatusBadge Server-compatible Pure presentation Figure 1 - Client island pattern Server layout/page v Mostly server-rendered UI v Small `use client` component v Hydrate only interactive island Once a module is marked `use client`, its imported subtree becomes part of the client bundle boundary. Serializable props Props crossing from Server Components into Client Components must be serializable. Do not pass server-only functions, database clients, or secrets into a client island. Client Component is not “bad” Interactive UI needs client JavaScript. The goal is not zero Client Components; it is deliberate boundaries so the browser receives only what interaction needs. ui Explain Server and Client Component Composition in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: permission-aware-ui-without-client-side-trust Permission Aware UI without Client Side Trust Permission-Aware UI Without Client-Side Trust Improve UX with capabilities while keeping authorization authoritative on the API Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Known capabilities v Conditional UI v User action v NestJS re-authorization Phase 20 turns the secure… Permission-Aware UI Without Client-Side Trust Improve UX with capabilities while keeping authorization authoritative on the API Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Known capabilities v Conditional UI v User action v NestJS re-authorization Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the browser. Permission-aware UI improves clarity but never replaces backend authorization Phase 19 owns the security decision. Phase 20 can use known permissions to hide or disable impossible actions, reducing user frustration, but callers can still construct HTTP requests manually. Figure 1 - UI permission flow Verified session v Fetch current-user/workspace capabilities v Render actions user can plausibly perform v User triggers operation v NestJS re-authorizes resource/action v Allow or 403 The browser optimizes experience; the API enforces security. UI pattern Use when Hide action Action is irrelevant/inappropriate for current capability Disable + explanation User benefits from knowing the action exists but why unavailable Show then handle 403 Capability may change or resource rule is only known server-side Never render secret data Unauthorized sensitive content should never be fetched into the browser Avoid role-name conditionals everywhere Instead of `if role === ADMIN` in dozens of components, prefer capability-oriented data such as `canCreateTask`, `canManageMembers`, or a normalized permission set supplied by a trusted server path. No “security by hidden button” DevTools can alter DOM and requests. Lab C - Route states • Create loading.tsx. • Create error.tsx with reset button. • Create not-found.tsx. • Verify errors do not remove the surrounding app shell unexpectedly. text: guided-build-lab Guided Build Lab Purpose Build a production application shell and reusable UI states instead of isolated demo components. Guided Build Lab — Phase 20: Production Application UI Purpose Build a production application shell and reusable UI states instead of isolated demo components. Deliverable TaskFlow responsive shell with navigation, workspace context, task screens, loading/empty/error states, and accessible interactions. Before you touch the code Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything. Architecture trace route/layout -> server data boundary -> page composition -> client interaction islands -> responsive/accessibility states Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization. Step 1 — Design the application shell first: sidebar/topbar/main content/mobile navigation. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 20: Production Application UI Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk route/layout -> server data boundary -> page composition -> client interaction islands -> responsive/accessibility states Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Only styling the success state Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Production Application UI Mission Rebuild the capability of Phase 20 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes? Required outcome Build a production application shell and reusable UI states instead of isolated demo components. Required artifact TaskFlow responsive shell with navigation, workspace context, task screens, loading/empty/error states, and accessible interactions. Constraints • Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch. • Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt. • Keep changes scoped to the capability. • Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases. • Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable. Acceptance criteria • Can compose a shell from reusable patterns. • Can model all UI states. • Can choose server/client boundaries. • Can verify basic accessibility and responsive behavior. Independent build sequence 1. Design the application shell first: sidebar/topbar/main content/mobile navigation. 2. Create reusable primitives for page header, panel/card, empty state, loading skeleton, and error state. 3. Build workspace/board/task navigation with active state derived from routing rather than duplicated local state. 4. Compose Server and Client Components so interactive islands remain small. 5. Test keyboard focus, labels, landmarks, reduced-motion expectations, and narrow widths. 6. Exercise all non-happy states by forcing no data, slow data, error, and forbidden responses. Self-review Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence. Stretch challenge Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly. It is a temporary client-side editing model that collects user intent. Until the server accepts the request, the form contains proposed data, not authoritative application state. FORM STATE SERVER STATE typed title stored Task selected priority authorization dirty fields business rules client errors database constraints Figure 1 - Form state and authoritative server state have different owners. The lifecycle User edits fields React Hook Form tracks values, touched/dirty state and errors Zod validates the client-side form shape Submit maps form values to API input NestJS validates the request again Business rules and authorization run Prisma persists accepted state UI refreshes from authoritative server result Why not plain useState for every field? You can build forms with useState, but large forms quickly accumulate repetitive value, touched, error, reset and pending logic. React Hook Form provides a focused form-state model and works especially well with native uncontrolled inputs. What stays local? text: zod-resolver-and-shared-validation-rules Zod Resolver and Shared Validation Rules Zod Resolver & Shared Validation Rules Reuse rules without confusing form, transport and persistence contracts Phase 21 - Forms with React Hook Form + Zod Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Why Zod appears again NestJS already validates transport input with Zod. The frontend also needs immediate validation feedback. This is the first time the same field-level rules are genuinely useful in two workspace packages, so a small shared validators package has now earned its place. packages/validators: reusable field primitives apps/api: HTTP transport schema apps/web: UI form schema Both use Zod 4.6.5 Shared field primitives // packages/validators/src/tasks.ts import { z } from "zod"; export const taskTitleSchema = z .string() .trim() .min(1, "Title is required.") .max(200, "Title must be 200 characters or fewer."); export const taskDescriptionSchema = z .string() .trim() .max(2000, "Description must be 2000 characters or fewer."); export const taskPrioritySchema = z.enum([ "LOW", "MEDIUM", "HIGH", ]); UI form schema // apps/web/src/components/tasks/task-form.schema.ts import { z } from "zod"; import { taskDescriptionSchema, taskPrioritySchema, taskTitleSchema, } from "@taskflow/validators/tasks"; export const taskFormSchema = z.object({ title: taskTitleSchema, description: taskDescriptionSchema, priority: taskPrioritySchema, dueAtLocal: z.string(), }); export type TaskFormValues = z.infer<typeof taskFormSchema>; Connect Zod to React Hook Form const form = useForm<TaskFormValues>({ resolver: zodResolver(taskFormSchema), defaultValues, mode: "onBlur", }); Important boundary The UI form schema is allowed to differ from the API transport schema. Debugging Workshop — Phase 21: Forms with React Hook Form + Zod Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk input controls -> React Hook Form state -> Zod resolver -> submit mutation -> API validation/business rules -> field/non-field feedback Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Duplicating server data into form state without reset strategy Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. title: Server State and Cache Mental Model
subtitle: TanStack Query
text: server-state-and-cache-mental-model Server State and Cache Mental Model Server State and Cache Mental Model Know what TanStack Query owns - and what it does not Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Four different kinds of frontend state A common React mistake is to place every changing value into component… Server State and Cache Mental Model Know what TanStack Query owns - and what it does not Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Four different kinds of frontend state A common React mistake is to place every changing value into component state. TaskFlow now has enough complexity that this becomes harmful. The important question is not “does this value change?” but “who owns the truth?” State Examples Owner Server state Task rows, total count, Task detail NestJS/PostgreSQL; cached by TanStack Query URL state page, search, status, sort URL/searchParams Form state title being edited, dirty fields, field errors React Hook Form UI state mobile menu open, local dialog tab React component Wrong mental model Better mental model fetch into useEffect query describes remote data copy response into useState cache stores last result manual loading flag URL describes collection view manual refresh everywhere form owns unsaved input Cache is not the database The query cache is a performance and synchronization layer. It can become stale. It can be cleared. It can be garbage collected. PostgreSQL remains authoritative. This means the application should be designed to tolerate refetching rather than treating cached objects as permanent local records. Queries versus mutations A query reads asynchronous data. A mutation performs a server-side effect such as create, update, delete, approve or assign. A POST can technically be used as a query if it is only a read transport, but TaskFlow follows HTTP semantics and uses mutations for writes. Do not duplicate server state Avoid copying query.data into useState just to render it. Doing so creates two sources of truth and makes refetches harder to reason about. query Explain Server State and Cache Mental Model in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Implement or reproduce the smallest TaskFlow slice that demonstrates this query concept. Diagnose one representative query failure using observable evidence instead of trial-and-error. The rest of the App Router tree does not become client-only merely because it is passed through this provider. // apps/web/src/lib/query/get-query-client.ts import { environmentManager, QueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query"; function makeQueryClient() { return new QueryClient({ defaultOptions: { queries: { staleTime: 30_000, retry: 2, }, mutations: { retry: 0 }, }, }); } let browserQueryClient: QueryClient | undefined; export function getQueryClient() { if (environmentManager.isServer()) return makeQueryClient(); if (!browserQueryClient) browserQueryClient = makeQueryClient(); return browserQueryClient; } // apps/web/src/app/providers.tsx "use client"; import { QueryClientProvider } from "@tanstack/react-query"; import { ReactQueryDevtools } from "@tanstack/react-query-devtools"; import { getQueryClient } from "@/lib/query/get-query-client"; export function Providers({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const queryClient = getQueryClient(); return ( <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}> {children} <ReactQueryDevtools initialIsOpen={false} /> </QueryClientProvider> ); } Why staleTime is not cache lifetime staleTime controls when data is considered fresh. gcTime controls how long inactive query data remains before garbage collection. They answer different questions. TaskFlow starts with a modest 30-second freshness window, then overrides it where the domain requires different behavior. Current v5 default to remember Cached query data is stale by default unless staleTime is configured. Inactive queries are garbage-collected after five minutes by default. Client queries retry failures three times by default, but TaskFlow deliberately starts with a smaller retry budget. A default is a policy decision Do not copy staleTime values from another application. A stock-price dashboard, an HR directory and a static country list have different freshness expectations. Global defaults are baselines; individual queries can override them when the domain requires it. text: query-keys-and-query-options Query Keys and Query Options Query Keys and Query Options Design cache identity before writing hooks Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend A query key is the identity of cached data If two requests can return different data, they must not accidentally share the same key.… Query Keys and Query Options Design cache identity before writing hooks Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend A query key is the identity of cached data If two requests can return different data, they must not accidentally share the same key. TanStack Query requires top-level array keys and hashes serializable key contents deterministically. export const taskKeys = { all: ["tasks"] as const, lists: () => [...taskKeys.all, "list"] as const, list: (query: TaskListQuery) => [...taskKeys.lists(), query] as const, details: () => [...taskKeys.all, "detail"] as const, detail: (id: string) => [...taskKeys.details(), id] as const, }; Variables used by queryFn belong in the key taskKeys.list({ page: 2, pageSize: 20, status: "IN_PROGRESS", search: "payroll", }) Page, search, status, priority and sort affect the returned collection, so they belong in the list key. If you omit one, the cache can return data produced under different inputs. Use queryOptions for reusable contracts import { queryOptions } from "@tanstack/react-query"; export function taskListOptions(query: TaskListQuery) { return queryOptions({ queryKey: taskKeys.list(query), queryFn: () => fetchTasks(query), staleTime: 30_000, }); } queryOptions keeps the key and fetch function together. The same definition can later be used by useQuery, prefetchQuery and cache operations. Do not put access tokens in query keys Keys are cache identifiers and debugging surfaces. Never include bearer tokens, refresh tokens, passwords or secrets. Authentication is transport context, not data identity. Prefix invalidation The key factory makes broad-but-targeted invalidation easy: invalidating taskKeys.lists() refreshes every cached Task collection without also invalidating unrelated resources. query Explain Query Keys and Query Options in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: usequery-freshness-retries-and-background-refetch useQuery Freshness Retries and Background Refetch useQuery, Freshness, Retries and Background Refetch Read server state without recreating fetch lifecycle by hand Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend useQuery is a state machine for one remote dependency const tasksQuery = useQuery(taskListOptions(query)); if (tasksQuery.isPending) return <TaskListSkeleton />; if (tasksQuery.isError)… useQuery, Freshness, Retries and Background Refetch Read server state without recreating fetch lifecycle by hand Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend useQuery is a state machine for one remote dependency const tasksQuery = useQuery(taskListOptions(query)); if (tasksQuery.isPending) return <TaskListSkeleton />; if (tasksQuery.isError) return <TaskListError error={tasksQuery.error} />; return <TaskTable tasks={tasksQuery.data.data} />; Pending is not the same as fetching Signal Meaning isPending No successful data is available yet isFetching A fetch is currently running, including background refetch isError The query reached an error result dataUpdatedAt When successful cached data last changed This lets the page keep showing useful data during a background refresh instead of replacing the whole table with a spinner. Cached successful Tasks Freshness window expires Window focus / mount / explicit invalidation Background refetch UI keeps old data until replacement succeeds Retry policy should understand HTTP semantics function shouldRetry(failureCount: number, error: unknown) { if (error instanceof ApiClientError) { if ([400, 401, 403, 404, 409].includes(error.status)) return false; } return failureCount < 2; } Retrying an authorization failure does not create permission. Retrying malformed input does not fix it. Transient network and server failures are better retry candidates. Background refresh is a feature Do not flash the whole page back to a first-load skeleton every time isFetching becomes true. A subtle refresh indicator can communicate activity while preserving the last successful result. Think in freshness transitions A successful query can be fresh, later become stale, remain visible while a refetch runs, and then receive a newer successful value. Stale does not mean unusable. It means TanStack Query may seek a newer answer according to its configured triggers. Situation What the user should usually see First visit, no cache Purposeful skeleton or pending state Fresh cache Immediate data, no unnecessary request Stale cache + refetch Existing table plus subtle refreshing feedback Refetch fails but old data exists Keep useful data and offer retry No data and final failure Dedicated error state query Explain useQuery Freshness Retries and Background Refetch in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. This keeps authentication, error parsing and HTTP semantics outside React components. export async function fetchTasks(query: TaskListQuery) { const params = new URLSearchParams(); params.set("page", String(query.page)); params.set("pageSize", String(query.pageSize)); if (query.search) params.set("search", query.search); if (query.status) params.set("status", query.status); if (query.priority) params.set("priority", query.priority); return authenticatedFetch( `/tasks?${params.toString()}`, ); } Client component reads cached server state "use client"; export function TasksScreen({ query }: { query: TaskListQuery }) { const result = useQuery(taskListOptions(query)); if (result.isPending) return ; if (result.isError) return ; if (result.data.data.length === 0) return ; return ( <> {result.isFetching ? Refreshing... : null} ); } Keep the response shape typed export type TaskPage = { data: Task[]; meta: { page: number; pageSize: number; totalItems: number; totalPages: number; hasPreviousPage: boolean; hasNextPage: boolean; }; }; One API client, many consumers Server Components, TanStack Query hooks and form mutations should reuse the same transport contract where practical. Preserve the Phase 13 error contract The API client should throw the structured ApiClientError created earlier, including status, stable error code and requestId when available. subtitle: TanStack Query
text: pagination-filters-and-url-state Pagination Filters and URL State Pagination, Filters and URL State Let URL state describe the collection while Query handles remote data Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend The URL still owns filters and page number TanStack Query should not replace the Phase 15/20 URL architecture. Search,… Pagination, Filters and URL State Let URL state describe the collection while Query handles remote data Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend The URL still owns filters and page number TanStack Query should not replace the Phase 15/20 URL architecture. Search, status, sort and page are navigational state. They belong in search parameters so the view remains refreshable, bookmarkable and shareable. URL: ?status=DONE&page=3 Next.js searchParams normalized TaskListQuery taskKeys.list(query) TanStack Query cache entry NestJS collection API Every page gets a separate cache entry ["tasks", "list", { page: 1, pageSize: 20, status: "DONE" }] ["tasks", "list", { page: 2, pageSize: 20, status: "DONE" }] Keep previous page visible during navigation import { keepPreviousData, useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query"; const result = useQuery({ ...taskListOptions(query), placeholderData: keepPreviousData, }); When the key changes from page 1 to page 2, the second page is a distinct query. keepPreviousData lets the previous successful result remain visible while the new page is fetched and exposes isPlaceholderData so Next can be disabled until the next page is known. Reset page when filter identity changes If a user is on page 8 and changes status or search, navigation should normally set page back to 1. That remains URL logic, not cache logic. Do not make the key enormous by accident Use a normalized query object containing only values that affect the API response. Do not insert router objects, functions, class instances or access tokens into a query key. Prefetch the likely next page - only when justified Once pagination is stable, TaskFlow can prefetch page N+1 when metadata says a next page exists. This can make navigation feel instant. It is an optimization, not a correctness requirement, and should not multiply requests for pages the user is unlikely to visit. if (result.data.meta.hasNextPage) { queryClient.prefetchQuery( taskListOptions({ ...query, page: query.page + 1 }), ); } Because the next page has its own query key, prefetching warms exactly that cache entry without replacing the currently displayed page. state Explain Pagination Filters and URL State in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. title: Mutations and Targeted Invalidation
subtitle: TanStack Query
text: mutations-and-targeted-invalidation Mutations and Targeted Invalidation Mutations and Targeted Invalidation Create and update remote state without manual refresh choreography Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Writes belong in mutations export function useCreateTask() { const queryClient = useQueryClient(); return useMutation({ mutationFn: createTask, onSuccess: async () => { await… Mutations and Targeted Invalidation Create and update remote state without manual refresh choreography Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Writes belong in mutations export function useCreateTask() { const queryClient = useQueryClient(); return useMutation({ mutationFn: createTask, onSuccess: async () => { await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: taskKeys.lists(), }); }, }); } A successful create means cached Task lists may now be stale. We do not need to manually discover every rendered list and call refetch on it. We invalidate the relevant key family. Update mutation export function useUpdateTask(taskId: string) { const queryClient = useQueryClient(); return useMutation({ mutationFn: (input: UpdateTaskInput) => updateTask(taskId, input), onSuccess: async (saved) => { queryClient.setQueryData(taskKeys.detail(taskId), saved); await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: taskKeys.lists() }); }, }); } Why invalidate instead of patching every list manually? TaskFlow lists can differ by status, priority, search, sort and page. A status update can move a record out of one list and into another. Manual patching is possible, but it is easy to create subtle cache inconsistencies. Phase 22 starts with targeted invalidation. Optimistic cache manipulation is intentionally deferred to Phase 25. Mutation retry Mutations default to zero retries, which is safer for writes because a retry can repeat a side effect unless the operation is known to be idempotent. TaskFlow keeps retry disabled until an operation explicitly earns it. Await invalidation when the UX depends on fresh data If onSuccess returns the invalidateQueries promise, the mutation remains pending until the related active queries have finished invalidation/refetch work. This can make “Save -> return to refreshed list” deterministic. Invalidation matrix Mutation Detail cache List caches Create Task Usually no existing detail key Invalidate Task lists Update Task Set saved Task into its detail key Invalidate lists because filters/sort membership may change Delete Task Remove or invalidate detail Invalidate lists Status transition Refresh detail if viewed Invalidate lists; record may enter or leave filtered pages This is deliberately conservative. Phase 25 can optimize perceived latency with optimistic updates after rollback and concurrency hazards are understood. validation Explain Mutations and Targeted Invalidation in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: next-js-app-router-prefetch-and-hydration Next.js App Router Prefetch and Hydration Next.js App Router Prefetch and Hydration Keep server rendering while gaining a live client cache Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Preserve Server Components with hydration A common migration mistake is adding useQuery directly to a page and converting the entire… Next.js App Router Prefetch and Hydration Keep server rendering while gaining a live client cache Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Preserve Server Components with hydration A common migration mistake is adding useQuery directly to a page and converting the entire route to a Client Component. Next.js App Router and TanStack Query can work together: the Server Component can prefetch, dehydrate the cache, and a smaller Client Component can subscribe to the same query. Next.js Server Component request-scoped QueryClient prefetchQuery(taskListOptions) dehydrate(queryClient) HydrationBoundary Client TasksScreen useQuery // app/(app)/tasks/page.tsx - Server Component import { dehydrate, HydrationBoundary } from "@tanstack/react-query"; import { getQueryClient } from "@/lib/query/get-query-client"; export default async function TasksPage({ searchParams }: PageProps) { const query = normalizeTaskSearchParams(await searchParams); const queryClient = getQueryClient(); await queryClient.prefetchQuery(taskListOptions(query)); return ( <HydrationBoundary state={dehydrate(queryClient)}> <TasksScreen query={query} /> </HydrationBoundary> ); } Server authentication context matters The server-side query function must be able to forward the current Supabase access token to NestJS. The browser query function can acquire the browser session token. Keep these transport details behind environment-appropriate API client helpers rather than making every component understand cookies and bearer headers. Set a non-zero staleTime for hydrated data Without a freshness window, the client can immediately consider the hydrated result stale and refetch as soon as it mounts. The official App Router guidance recommends a staleTime above zero for this pattern. Data ownership warning Avoid rendering the same mutable query data independently in a Server Component and a Client Component if the client can later refetch it. The two surfaces can drift. Prefer the Server Component as a preloader and the Client Component as the owner of data that will revalidate in the browser. Do not prefetch everything Server prefetch is most valuable for above-the-fold data that materially improves the first render. Low-priority panels can remain ordinary client queries. Prefetching every possible query increases server work and hydration payload without necessarily improving the experience. subtitle: TanStack Query
text: authentication-cache-isolation-and-privacy Authentication Cache Isolation and Privacy Authentication, Cache Isolation and Privacy Treat logout as a data-boundary event, not just a navigation action Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Cached data can be sensitive A browser QueryClient can outlive individual route components. If user A signs out and… Authentication, Cache Isolation and Privacy Treat logout as a data-boundary event, not just a navigation action Phase 22 - TanStack Query Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Cached data can be sensitive A browser QueryClient can outlive individual route components. If user A signs out and user B signs in without a full browser reload, stale cache entries must not become an accidental cross-account disclosure. User A loads authorized Tasks Tasks stored in browser QueryCache User A signs out queryClient.clear() Supabase session cleared User B starts with empty application cache export async function signOutTaskFlow(queryClient: QueryClient) { await supabase.auth.signOut({ scope: "local" }); queryClient.clear(); window.location.assign("/sign-in"); } Do query keys need the user ID? Sometimes tenant/user context belongs in a query key because it changes the requested resource. However, adding user IDs everywhere is not a substitute for clearing security-sensitive caches on auth transitions. TaskFlow treats logout as a cache lifecycle boundary. 401 handling A query that receives 401 should not retry repeatedly. The API client should surface an ApiClientError; retry policy returns false; the UI can start session recovery or redirect to sign-in. Authorization failures (403) should remain visible as permission outcomes, not auth-refresh loops. Never persist auth-bearing cache casually Phase 22 does not enable localStorage persistence for QueryCache. Persisting cached business data introduces privacy, staleness and logout-cleanup responsibilities that should be justified by a concrete offline requirement. Account-transition checklist Event Cache action Local sign-out Clear QueryClient before or with redirect Session becomes invalid Stop retries; recover auth; clear sensitive cache if identity is lost Switch tenant/workspace Scope request/key and invalidate obsolete scoped data Sign in as another account Start from a clean account-sensitive cache This is a privacy boundary as much as a correctness rule. A stale cache must never become an alternate way to view data the current identity could not retrieve from the API. query Explain Authentication Cache Isolation and Privacy in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. It is especially useful when a query “does not refetch” or “refetches too much.” Debug in this order Symptom First questions Wrong list appears Does queryKey include every input used by queryFn? Refetches constantly What is staleTime? Is focus refetch expected? Mutation succeeds but UI old Was the correct key family invalidated? Pagination flashes empty Use placeholderData / keepPreviousData? 401 repeats Is retry disabled for auth failures? Different user sees old data Was QueryClient cleared on auth transition? Test the contract, not the library Component tests should verify loading, success, error and mutation behavior. Query-option tests can verify key shape. End-to-end tests should prove a successful mutation eventually produces the correct server-backed UI. Trigger a create mutation and observe list queries become invalidated. Refocus the browser after staleTime expires and watch background fetching without losing the previous successful table. A cache bug usually starts as an identity bug When data looks unexpectedly shared or stale, inspect the query key before adding manual refetch calls. Debugging Workshop — Phase 22: TanStack Query Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk component -> query key/options -> cache -> HTTP fetch -> server -> cache update/invalidation -> render Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. If a value can be derived from props, query data, URL state, or another state variable during render,… Avoid Redundant, Duplicate and Synchronized State Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 The most expensive state is copied state Every duplicate introduces a synchronization problem. If a value can be derived from props, query data, URL state, or another state variable during render, storing another copy usually increases bug surface without adding capability. Classic TaskFlow anti-pattern const tasksQuery = useQuery(taskListOptions(query)) const [tasks, setTasks] = useState<Task[]>([]) useEffect(() => { if (tasksQuery.data) { setTasks(tasksQuery.data.data) } }, [tasksQuery.data]) Duplication creates synchronization work Query cache useEffect Local state Rendered UI tasks[] tasks[] copy table rows Better: render directly from the query result unless the user is intentionally editing a draft. Figure 23.1 - Classic TaskFlow anti-pattern Better const tasksQuery = useQuery(taskListOptions(query)) const tasks = tasksQuery.data?.data ?? [] When a copy is legitimate • The user is editing a draft that must diverge from server data. • You are taking a deliberate snapshot for undo/history. • An animation/intermediate interaction needs its own transient representation. • You have explicitly named the synchronization boundary and its conflict policy. Effect warning Do not use an effect merely to keep one state variable equal to another value you already have. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 23: Professional Frontend State Architecture Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk classify state -> choose authoritative owner -> derive values -> share only when necessary -> avoid synchronization loops Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — useEffect syncing query data into local state Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 2 — Global store used for all state categories Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Do not hide the evidence Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant. text: design-the-taskrepository-contract Design the TaskRepository Contract Design the TaskRepository Contract Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Design from the consumer inward Start from what TasksService actually needs. Do not start by reproducing every Prisma method. A repository contract is an application boundary, not an ORM compatibility layer. Feature-owned… Design the TaskRepository Contract Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Design from the consumer inward Start from what TasksService actually needs. Do not start by reproducing every Prisma method. A repository contract is an application boundary, not an ORM compatibility layer. Feature-owned contract export interface TaskRepository { findById(id: string): Promise<TaskRecord | null> findScopedById( taskId: string, userId: string, ): Promise<TaskRecord | null> listScoped( userId: string, query: TaskListQuery, ): Promise<PaginatedTasks> create(input: CreateTaskRecord): Promise<TaskRecord> update(id: string, input: UpdateTaskRecord): Promise<TaskRecord> delete(id: string): Promise<void> } Contract design rules • Return application-owned shapes when persistence independence is worth the mapping cost. • Keep HTTP request/response concerns out of the repository. • Do not put authorization decisions in the repository; it may enforce a caller-provided scope, while the service decides the policy. • Prefer methods that capture meaningful query intent over dozens of tiny ORM wrappers. • Keep the interface inside the feature until more features genuinely need a shared abstraction. authentication Explain Design the TaskRepository Contract in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: incremental-adoption-and-anti-patterns Incremental Adoption and Anti Patterns Incremental Adoption and Anti-Patterns Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Do not big-bang refactor TaskFlow migrates read/list and straightforward write paths first. Transaction-heavy or cross-feature persistence can remain direct Prisma temporarily if forcing it behind the new boundary would make correctness harder… Incremental Adoption and Anti-Patterns Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Do not big-bang refactor TaskFlow migrates read/list and straightforward write paths first. Transaction-heavy or cross-feature persistence can remain direct Prisma temporarily if forcing it behind the new boundary would make correctness harder to see. Migration path Step 1 identify repeated/complex persistence logic Step 2 define the smallest useful contract Step 3 implement Prisma adapter Step 4 bind with Nest DI token Step 5 move one service path at a time Step 6 add fake service tests Step 7 add repository integration tests Step 8 reassess remaining direct Prisma usage Anti-patterns • One repository interface per Prisma model by default. • A generic repository that only renames Prisma methods. • Repositories throwing HTTP exceptions. • Repositories deciding user permissions instead of receiving an already-decided scope. • Mapping every field through ceremonial classes with no boundary benefit. • Breaking transaction atomicity to keep repositories pure. • Assuming repository means the application is database-agnostic in practice. Success criterion The repository is successful when TasksService becomes easier to read and test while persistence correctness remains explicit. title: Debugging Workshop
subtitle: Repository Pattern
text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 24: Repository Pattern Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk service/use case -> repository interface -> Prisma implementation -> database -> mapped domain/application result Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — GenericRepository<T> mirroring ORM methods Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 2 — Repository wrapping every trivial Prisma call with no value Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 3 — Mocks proving an imaginary database behavior Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 4 — Mapping everything into duplicate types without a domain need Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Do not hide the evidence Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant. Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Repository Pattern Mission Rebuild the capability of Phase 24 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes? Required outcome Introduce repository boundaries only where they improve persistence isolation, domain language, testing, or future changeability. Required artifact One TaskFlow aggregate/use case refactored behind a purposeful repository interface with real database integration tests. Constraints • Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch. • Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt. • Keep changes scoped to the capability. • Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases. • Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable. Acceptance criteria • Can explain when not to use a repository. • Can design task-specific repository methods. • Can test both service and real persistence. • Can identify ORM leakage tradeoffs. Independent build sequence 1. Choose a service whose persistence queries are complex enough to justify a boundary. 2. Write repository methods in application language rather than generic findAll/create/update/delete. 3. Move Prisma-specific selection/query details into the implementation. 4. Decide whether persistence types may cross the boundary or need mapping and document the trade-off. 5. Unit-test service behavior with a fake only where it proves useful behavior. 6. Integration-test the real repository against PostgreSQL so fake and implementation do not drift. Self-review Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence. Stretch challenge Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly. text: mastery-capstone-lab Mastery Capstone Lab Integrate Phase 24 without following a transcript. Mastery Capstone Lab This is the transfer exercise for Phase 24: Repository Pattern. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.
