text: filtered-and-paginated-caches Filtered and Paginated Caches Filtered and Paginated Caches Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The hard part is list membership One mutation can affect several cached views differently All Tasks status=TODO status=DONE Task remains visible Task may disappear Task may appear Perfectly recreating every… Filtered and Paginated Caches Phase 25 - Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The hard part is list membership One mutation can affect several cached views differently All Tasks status=TODO status=DONE Task remains visible Task may disappear Task may appear Perfectly recreating every filtered + paginated server result on the client is expensive. Prefer a small local prediction, then invalidate and let the server reconcile authoritative lists. Why “patch every list” becomes fragile A status update can remove a Task from one filtered page, add it to another filter, shift page boundaries, change counts, and interact with search/sort order. Reproducing all backend query semantics in client cache code creates a second query engine that can drift from NestJS/Prisma behavior. TaskFlow strategy • Use UI optimism for the visible row when possible. • Optimistically patch the Task detail cache when several observers need the same pending value. • Avoid fabricating pagination metadata. • Invalidate list prefixes after settlement so the server reconstructs the authoritative collection. • Only implement filter-aware list patching for specific high-value interactions with strong tests. Important rule If an optimistic cache algorithm starts reimplementing filtering, authorization, search, sorting, and pagination, stop. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 25: Optimistic Updates Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk user action -> cancel/snapshot relevant queries -> optimistic cache write -> server mutation -> rollback on error -> invalidate/reconcile on settle Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Optimism without rollback Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 2 — Temporary IDs colliding with real IDs Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. text: realtime-mental-model-and-when-it-earns-its-place Realtime Mental Model and When It Earns Its Place Realtime Mental Model and When It Earns Its Place Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The problem Realtime solves • User A changes a Task while User B is looking at the same Workspace. • Without Realtime, User B sees the change only after manual… Realtime Mental Model and When It Earns Its Place Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The problem Realtime solves • User A changes a Task while User B is looking at the same Workspace. • Without Realtime, User B sees the change only after manual refresh, navigation, focus refetch, or polling. • Realtime reduces the time between committed server truth and another client learning that it changed. Do not confuse freshness with authority The event does not become the database. The browser uses the event as a hint that cached server state may now be stale. HTTP/API reads still reconstruct authoritative state. When Realtime earns its cost • Collaborative task boards where changes from coworkers should appear quickly. • Live operations consoles where stale state has real workflow cost. • Notifications or activity streams where delay matters. • Presence/typing/cursor indicators for collaborative experiences. When normal refetch is enough • Rarely changed settings pages. • Forms mostly edited by one person. • Admin reports where refresh every 30-60 seconds is acceptable. • Screens where realtime complexity would exceed UX value. text: realtime-with-optimistic-updates Realtime with Optimistic Updates Realtime with Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The same mutation can generate two signals User A clicks DONE -> optimistic UI predicts DONE -> HTTP PATCH /tasks/:id -> Postgres commits DONE -> Broadcast event arrives -> mutation response arrives -> onSettled invalidates… Realtime with Optimistic Updates Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture The same mutation can generate two signals User A clicks DONE -> optimistic UI predicts DONE -> HTTP PATCH /tasks/:id -> Postgres commits DONE -> Broadcast event arrives -> mutation response arrives -> onSettled invalidates too Is duplicate invalidation wrong? Usually no. Invalidation is idempotent from the application point of view: both signals say “the cache may be stale.” The cost is extra refetch work, not data corruption. Optimize only if measurements show meaningful churn. Do not suppress every self-originated event Trying to perfectly identify “my own” database broadcast adds correlation state and can accidentally ignore a server-side change you still need. TaskFlow first accepts harmless duplicate freshness signals. Conflict behavior • If another user changes the Task while your optimistic mutation is pending, the server remains the authority. • Serial mutation scopes from Phase 25 still protect same-Task mutation order in the local client. • Realtime invalidation helps surface remote commits quickly. • A 409/403 response still rolls back the local optimistic prediction. Rule Optimistic UI improves perceived latency. Realtime improves cross-client freshness. text: multi-tenant-channel-strategy Multi Tenant Channel Strategy Multi-Tenant Workspace Channel Strategy Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Topic design workspace:<workspaceId>:tasks Examples: workspace:11111111-...:tasks workspace:22222222-...:tasks Why Workspace scope • One channel can cover all Task changes visible within the current Workspace. • Changing Workspace naturally tears down the old channel and joins the new… Multi-Tenant Workspace Channel Strategy Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Topic design workspace:<workspaceId>:tasks Examples: workspace:11111111-...:tasks workspace:22222222-...:tasks Why Workspace scope • One channel can cover all Task changes visible within the current Workspace. • Changing Workspace naturally tears down the old channel and joins the new one. • The Realtime Authorization policy maps the JWT subject to TaskFlow Membership. • The topic itself contains no secret; authorization decides whether the subscriber may receive it. Avoid one global Task channel A global tasks channel would force every tenant event through one topic and make tenant isolation harder to reason about. Multi-tenant systems benefit from a topic boundary that mirrors authorization scope. Avoid one channel per row by default A channel for every Task can create excessive joins and cleanup pressure. Use fine-grained topics only when the interaction genuinely needs them, such as a deeply collaborative Task detail view. Reconnect means: rejoin + refetch… Reliability, Scaling and Troubleshooting Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Realtime is lossy from the app perspective Clients can sleep, lose Wi-Fi, change networks, suspend background tabs, or disconnect during token expiry. Therefore TaskFlow never assumes it observed every event. Reconnect means: rejoin + refetch authoritative state. Subscription statuses • SUBSCRIBED - channel is joined; refresh current data. • CHANNEL_ERROR - inspect the full error payload. • TIMED_OUT - connectivity/join problem. • CLOSED - channel ended; determine whether expected cleanup or unexpected disconnect. Built-in reconnection The Realtime protocol/client supports reconnection with backoff. Application code should still make recovery idempotent and refresh server state after re-subscription. Scaling lesson Supabase currently recommends Broadcast for database-change subscriptions because Postgres Changes can become costly under many subscribers; each database change can require authorization work across subscribers. Measure your own workload and plan limits. Troubleshooting order • Confirm the user has a valid Supabase session/JWT. • Confirm setAuth() occurs before joining a private channel. • Confirm topic string exactly matches the policy. • Confirm Membership/authSubject mapping. • Confirm Realtime public-access/private-channel setting. • Confirm trigger exists and fires. • Check Realtime logs and browser WebSocket frames. • Confirm removeChannel cleanup to avoid duplicate subscriptions. Observability Log channel topic (not token), status, Workspace id, reconnect count, error category and request/user correlation where policy allows. title: Hands On Lab and Phase Exit
subtitle: Realtime
text: hands-on-lab-and-phase-exit Hands On Lab and Phase Exit Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Lab A - Enable database-triggered Broadcast • Apply the Task trigger migration. • Create the Realtime authorization helper/policy. • Disable public channel access in a production-like project or ensure private channels are required by… Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture Lab A - Enable database-triggered Broadcast • Apply the Task trigger migration. • Create the Realtime authorization helper/policy. • Disable public channel access in a production-like project or ensure private channels are required by your policy. • Use two authenticated users who belong to the same Workspace. Lab B - Connect two browsers • Open User A and User B in separate browser profiles. • Both join the same Workspace Task channel. • User A changes a Task through NestJS. • Verify User B refetches and sees the committed change without manual refresh. Lab C - Prove tenant isolation • Create Workspace B. • Ensure User B is not a member. • Attempt to subscribe User B to Workspace B topic. • Verify the private channel cannot deliver Task broadcasts to the unauthorized user. Lab D - Disconnect recovery • Take User B offline. • Change several Tasks from User A. • Reconnect User B. • Verify SUBSCRIBED triggers an authoritative Task refetch so missed events do not matter. Lab E - Realtime + optimism • Make a status change from User A with optimistic UI. • Observe local optimistic update plus database Broadcast. • Verify final state equals the server response. • Force a 409 or 403 and verify rollback still works. Exit criteria You can explain Broadcast vs Postgres Changes vs Presence, secure a private Workspace channel, emit database-triggered events, clean up subscriptions, synchronize TanStack Query, recover after reconnect, and explain why Realtime is a freshness layer rather than the source of truth. TaskFlow instead lets the browser upload directly to Storage after… Signed Upload Intent Architecture TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Why not proxy every byte through NestJS A backend proxy can work, but it makes the API server carry file bandwidth, memory and timeout pressure. TaskFlow instead lets the browser upload directly to Storage after NestJS authorizes a narrowly scoped upload intent. End-to-end flow TaskFlow attachment upload - authorization stays in NestJS Browser NestJS Postgres Storage Browser file upload intent PENDING row signed token direct upload NestJS finalize Postgres verify object READY metadata Storage holds bytes. PostgreSQL holds application meaning and relationships. Trust boundary Signed upload intent - trust boundary Browser NestJS Signed token Storage untrusted filename auth + permission one object path enforces bucket MIME + size allowlist + limit time limited constraints service-role key remains server-only original filename is metadata - not the authoritative object path Two-step commit • Intent endpoint validates Task access, file policy and requested metadata, creates a PENDING row, then returns a signed upload token. • Browser transfers bytes directly to the exact object path. • Finalize endpoint checks the object exists and its Storage metadata matches the expected size/type, then marks the row READY. Why PENDING matters Direct object storage and PostgreSQL are separate systems. A PENDING state gives TaskFlow an explicit way to represent “intent exists but upload is not yet committed to the application”. authentication Explain Signed Upload Intent Architecture in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. Dependency pnpm --filter web add tus-js-client@4.3.1 Signed TUS upload sketch const upload = new tus.Upload(file, { endpoint: `https://${projectRef}.storage.supabase.co` + `/storage/v1/upload/resumable`, headers: { "x-signature": signedUploadToken, }, metadata: { bucketName: "task-attachments", objectName: objectPath, contentType: file.type, }, chunkSize: 6 * 1024 * 1024, retryDelays: [0, 3000, 5000, 10000, 20000], removeFingerprintOnSuccess: true, onProgress(bytesUploaded, bytesTotal) { onProgress(bytesUploaded / bytesTotal) }, onSuccess() { void completeAttachment(attachmentId) }, }) upload.start() Important implementation details • Use the direct project-ref.storage.supabase.co hostname for large uploads. • Supabase currently requires 6MB TUS chunks. • Signed upload tokens can be forwarded in the x-signature header. • Progress is a transfer-progress signal; the attachment is not READY until NestJS finalizes it. Verification flow async complete(id: string, user: AuthenticatedUser) { const attachment = await this.attachments.findPendingScoped(id, user.id) if (!attachment) { throw new AttachmentNotFoundException(id) } const info = await this.storage.info( attachment.bucket, attachment.objectPath, ) if (info.size !== attachment.sizeBytes) { throw new AttachmentUploadMismatchException() } if (normalizeMime(info.contentType) !== attachment.mimeType) { throw new AttachmentUploadMismatchException() } return this.attachments.markReady(id, new Date()) } What info() provides Supabase Storage currently exposes an info(path) API that returns object details such as size, content type and timestamps. Upload a new UUID-named object, verify it, update the application metadata/reference, then clean up the old object. This avoids stale-caching behavior and gives… Replacement, Deletion and Orphan Cleanup TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Replacement strategy Do not overwrite the same object path by default. Upload a new UUID-named object, verify it, update the application metadata/reference, then clean up the old object. This avoids stale-caching behavior and gives rollback options. Deletion is a distributed workflow Deletion across database + object storage is not one ACID transaction READY DELETING Storage.remove DB delete metadata mark row delete bytes remove row If a step fails, keep enough state to retry cleanup safely. Recommended delete flow • Authorize attachment deletion in NestJS. • Mark metadata DELETING so concurrent UI actions stop treating it as normal. • Call storage.remove([objectPath]). • After successful object deletion, remove the TaskAttachment row. • If Storage deletion fails, retain DELETING (or restore READY) and retry operationally. Orphan cleanup • PENDING rows older than the signed-upload lifetime may indicate abandoned intents. • Cleanup job checks whether an object exists; remove any abandoned bytes and delete stale metadata. • Object without TaskAttachment metadata is an orphan and still consumes storage. • Do not delete directly from storage.objects; use the Storage API. Why this is not one database transaction PostgreSQL and object storage cannot share the same local Prisma transaction. Correctness comes from explicit workflow states, idempotent operations and compensating cleanup. storage Explain Replacement Deletion and Orphan Cleanup in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: testing-security-troubleshooting-and-phase-exit Testing Security Troubleshooting and Phase Exit Testing, Security, Troubleshooting and Phase Exit TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Security test matrix • Unauthenticated intent request -> 401. • Authenticated non-member attaches to another Workspace Task -> 404/403 according to policy. • Disallowed MIME or >20MB -> rejected before signed token issuance.… Testing, Security, Troubleshooting and Phase Exit TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Security test matrix • Unauthenticated intent request -> 401. • Authenticated non-member attaches to another Workspace Task -> 404/403 according to policy. • Disallowed MIME or >20MB -> rejected before signed token issuance. • Path sent by browser is ignored; server generates objectPath. • Service-role key never appears in web bundle or API response. • Finalize without an object -> failure; row remains non-READY. • Finalize with size/type mismatch -> failure. • Download for unauthorized caller -> denied. • Expired signed download -> no permanent access. • Delete failure leaves recoverable state for retry. Common failures • 400 Asset Already Exists: path collision or unintended reuse; unique UUID paths avoid this. • 413/size error: global or bucket limits are lower than the application policy. • TUS stalls/retries: verify direct storage hostname, 6MB chunks, token header and network conditions. • Signed upload works but finalize fails: inspect info() result and expected metadata. • Object remains after business deletion: run orphan/deletion retry workflow; do not manipulate storage tables directly. Phase exit checklist • Private bucket configured with allowed MIME types and 20MB limit. • TaskAttachment migration applied. • Signed upload intent is authorized by NestJS. • Small-file upload works; TUS path understood/tested if enabled. • Finalize verifies object metadata and marks READY. • Download uses short-lived signed URL. • Delete/replacement have explicit failure recovery. • Tests prove cross-Workspace file access is denied. Status transition example export function assertTaskStatusTransition( from: TaskStatus, to: TaskStatus, ) { const allowed = ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS[from] if (!allowed.includes(to)) { throw new TaskStatusTransitionNotAllowed(from, to) } } describe("assertTaskStatusTransition", () => { it.each([ ["TODO", "IN_PROGRESS"], ["TODO", "CANCELED"], ["IN_PROGRESS", "DONE"], ["DONE", "IN_PROGRESS"], ])("allows %s -> %s", (from, to) => { expect(() => assertTaskStatusTransition(from, to)).not.toThrow() }) it("rejects DONE -> TODO", () => { expect(() => assertTaskStatusTransition("DONE", "TODO")) .toThrow(TaskStatusTransitionNotAllowed) }) }) Time should be injectable • Avoid new Date() buried inside a rule if the rule needs deterministic testing. • Pass now into the policy or inject a Clock abstraction only when multiple services genuinely need it. • Use fake timers for code that is actually timer-driven, not as a default for ordinary date comparisons. testing Explain Pure Business Logic Unit Tests in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 28: Testing Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk risk/question -> choose boundary -> arrange controlled state -> execute behavior -> assert outcome/contract -> cleanup Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Mocking the thing the test is supposed to prove Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 2 — Huge number of brittle snapshot/UI implementation tests Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 3 — Shared mutable test data causing order-dependent failures Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 4 — E2E used for every rule, making feedback too slow Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Do not hide the evidence Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant. text: file-upload-and-storage-hardening File Upload and Storage Hardening File Upload and Storage Hardening TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Phase 27 gets an adversarial review • Keep private bucket default. • Authorize before issuing an upload intent or signed download. • Server generates object paths; original filename is display metadata only. • Allowlist… File Upload and Storage Hardening TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Phase 27 gets an adversarial review • Keep private bucket default. • Authorize before issuing an upload intent or signed download. • Server generates object paths; original filename is display metadata only. • Allowlist business-required MIME/extensions; enforce maximum size at multiple layers. • Do not trust browser Content-Type alone; add content/signature scanning when business risk requires it. • Use PENDING/READY/DELETING states to recover cross-system failures. • Consider antivirus/CDR for documents in higher-risk deployments. text: hands-on-lab-and-phase-exit Hands On Lab and Phase Exit Hands-On Security Hardening Lab and Phase Exit TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Lab 1 - Headers • Install @fastify/helmet 13.1.1 and inspect API response headers. • Add a conservative Next.js header baseline and verify using browser DevTools/curl. • Document a CSP plan instead of… Hands-On Security Hardening Lab and Phase Exit TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Lab 1 - Headers • Install @fastify/helmet 13.1.1 and inspect API response headers. • Add a conservative Next.js header baseline and verify using browser DevTools/curl. • Document a CSP plan instead of enabling an untested permissive policy. Lab 2 - Abuse controls • Install/configure @nestjs/throttler 6.5.0. • Create a tighter policy for an expensive endpoint. • Test 429 behavior and confirm proxy IP handling in the deployment topology. Lab 3 - Attack-oriented tests • Cross-workspace Task ID -> never returns foreign data. • Unknown write fields / oversized strings -> rejected. • Forbidden role escalation -> denied. • Unsafe upload type/oversize -> rejected before READY. • Public 500 response -> no stack/secret leakage. • Logout -> QueryClient private data cleared. Debugging Workshop — Phase 29: Security Hardening Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk asset/trust boundary -> abuse case -> preventive control -> detection/logging -> test -> residual risk Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. text: observability-mental-model Observability Mental Model Observability Mental Model Full Stack Developer 2026 Complete - TaskFlow Monitoring asks known questions such as “is error rate above 5%?” Observability is broader: it lets engineers investigate unfamiliar failures by correlating multiple signals. TaskFlow uses logs for discrete events, metrics for aggregate trends, traces… Observability Mental Model Monitoring asks known questions such as “is error rate above 5%?” Observability is broader: it lets engineers investigate unfamiliar failures by correlating multiple signals. TaskFlow uses logs for discrete events, metrics for aggregate trends, traces for request paths, and error monitoring for grouped exceptions with release context. METRICS: how often/how TRACES: where time ERRORS: which failures LOGS: what happened much flowed need action → → → Figure 2. Four complementary signals Questions each signal answers Signal Best questions Logs What happened on request 7fd2? Which business decision failed? Metrics What is p95 latency? Is 5xx rate rising? How many requests are active? Traces Which dependency/span consumed 1.8 seconds? Error monitoring Which exception regressed after release X? How many users/requests were affected? No signal replaces the others. A metric may show a latency spike but not the exact failing request. A log may explain one request but not reveal whether the problem affects 1% or 80% of traffic. Production caution: Do not turn user IDs, task IDs, raw URLs, emails, or arbitrary search text into metric labels. High-cardinality attributes can create unbounded time-series growth and cost. observability Explain Observability Mental Model in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 30: Logging & Observability Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk request/user action -> correlation ID -> structured events -> error monitor/metrics -> dashboard/alert -> diagnosis Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — console.log strings with no searchable structure Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Phase 31 teaches evidence-first index design: observe a slow query, capture its plan,… PostgreSQL EXPLAIN, Indexes, and Pagination Indexes are workload-specific. PostgreSQL can only choose well when statistics describe the data and the index matches real predicates/order patterns. Phase 31 teaches evidence-first index design: observe a slow query, capture its plan, change one thing, and compare. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, title, status, priority, "createdAt" FROM "Task" WHERE "projectId" = $1 AND status = $2 ORDER BY "createdAt" DESC, id ASC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0; Plan signal Question Seq Scan Is table small, predicate unselective, or useful index missing? Index Scan / Bitmap Does chosen index align with actual filter/order? Rows estimate vs actual Are planner statistics inaccurate? Buffers Is query reading far more pages than expected? Sort Could ordering be supported by a useful index, or is sort cheap enough already? PostgreSQL 18 documents that multicolumn B-tree indexes are most effective when constraints apply to leading columns and recommends using multicolumn indexes sparingly. For the TaskFlow query above, an index such as (projectId, status, createdAt DESC, id) is a candidate to measure, not a rule to apply blindly. Deep pagination Offset pagination is excellent for page-number navigation, but very deep OFFSET values require PostgreSQL to walk past earlier rows. If TaskFlow evolves into an infinite activity feed, cursor/keyset pagination becomes a better candidate. Production caution: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Layer Good candidates Browser / Next.js immutable assets, route output where semantics permit, optimized images/fonts TanStack Query authenticated server state with intentional staleTime API/application expensive repeatable public/reference reads only after measurement Database buffer cache is automatic; optimize query/index before inventing app cache CDN/Storage public/static content; private files require correct signed-access semantics Compression and payload size Compression helps large textual payloads, but reducing payload size at the source is better: paginate, project only required fields, avoid repeated metadata, and do not return large nested graphs the UI never renders. Keep offset pagination for ordinary admin tables, but use cursor/keyset pagination for deep sequential feeds where jumping to arbitrary page numbers is not required. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 31: Performance Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk measure baseline -> locate bottleneck -> form hypothesis -> change one thing -> remeasure -> add regression guard Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Optimizing from intuition only Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 2 — Caching incorrect data or bypassing authorization Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 3 — Adding indexes that slow writes without helping real queries Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Failure drill 4 — Benchmarking development mode and assuming production behavior Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Do not hide the evidence Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant. Debugging Workshop — Phase 32: Docker Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Deployment platforms should route traffic only after the new version is ready, and the old version should have time to finish work during termination. Start new version → /health/ready 2xx → Switch traffic → SIGTERM old → Graceful exit Figure 8 - Health-gated promotion Endpoints • /health/live: process is alive; avoid making it fail because PostgreSQL is briefly unavailable. • /health/ready: operation-critical dependencies such as PostgreSQL are available. • Never require user authentication for platform health probes. text: rollback-recovery-and-incident-decisions Rollback Recovery and Incident Decisions Rollback, Recovery, and Incident Decisions A rollback plan must exist before the release. Roll back application code quickly when code/config is the cause; treat database/schema incidents separately because destructive migrations may not be reversible by restoring an old image. Investigate root Bad release Stop promotion… Rollback, Recovery, and Incident Decisions A rollback plan must exist before the release. Roll back application code quickly when code/config is the cause; treat database/schema incidents separately because destructive migrations may not be reversible by restoring an old image. Investigate root Bad release Stop promotion Rollback app Verify health → → → → cause Figure 10 - Recovery path API rollback • Railway can roll back to a previous successful deployment while restoring that deployment's image and custom variables within the platform retention window. • Use the last known-good immutable SHA, then rerun smoke checks. Web rollback • Promote a known-good previous Vercel deployment or redeploy the known-good commit according to team policy. • Keep production environment variables version/change-controlled operationally even though they live outside Git. Database incident • Do not assume an application rollback fixes a destructive migration. • Use backup/PITR or a forward-fix migration according to the incident runbook. • This is why expand-contract and tested migrations are part of deployment design. Rollback is a capability, not a strategy. Recovery decisions depend on whether the failure is code, configuration, data, migration, dependency, or infrastructure. Debugging Workshop — Phase 34: Production Deployment Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk verified commit/artifact -> migration gate -> Vercel web + API host -> Supabase prod services -> DNS/TLS -> smoke test -> monitor/rollback Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Coupling smells • A UI component imports generated Prisma enums directly. • A repository throws NestJS HTTP exceptions. • A shared package imports from apps/web or apps/api. • A service accepts Fastify Request/Reply objects. • Infrastructure credentials become arguments to domain/business helpers. # Review question for every import Who owns this contract? If A imports B: - Does A genuinely depend on B's responsibility? - Or did a convenient type/location create accidental coupling? Do not chase zero coupling. Every abstraction has carrying cost: naming, navigation, indirection, tests, documentation, and onboarding. - Identify - - Keep / merge / Find abstraction Measure value > consumers > > delete Figure 7 - Architecture can improve by removing layers Candidate smells • A repository method used once that exactly mirrors one Prisma call and adds no policy/query value. • A Context provider with one nearby consumer. • A mapper that copies identical fields between structurally identical objects. • A utility package created for one function and no independent ownership. • A generic interface introduced to support hypothetical future databases with no actual migration pressure. Delete carefully • Prove behavior with tests before simplification. • Prefer a smaller explicit design over a generic framework built inside the application. • Keep abstractions that protect valuable boundaries even when their implementation is currently simple. The simplest architecture is not the one with the fewest files; it is the one with the fewest unnecessary concepts. Refactor one bounded pressure point at a time, record consequential decisions, and use the existing testing/deployment system to keep changes reversible. Problem - - - - - Continue / Decision… Refactoring Strategy, ADRs, and Change Safety Architecture review produces a backlog, not a giant rewrite. Refactor one bounded pressure point at a time, record consequential decisions, and use the existing testing/deployment system to keep changes reversible. Problem - - - - - Continue / Decision Small change Tests Observe evidence > > > > > revert Figure 8 - Safe refactoring loop Prioritization model • P0: correctness/security/data-loss risk. • P1: blocks frequent change or causes repeated incidents. • P2: meaningful maintainability/testing/performance debt. • P3: cosmetic consistency with little practical impact. ADR discipline • Record context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and revisit trigger. • Use ADRs for meaningful architecture decisions, not every small refactor. • A decision can be superseded later; the historical reasoning remains useful. Change safety • One conceptual refactor per pull request when practical. • No opportunistic behavior change hidden inside structural cleanup. • Use feature flags or compatibility layers when migration cannot be atomic. Refactoring should reduce uncertainty. A giant rewrite multiplies it. text: debugging-workshop Debugging Workshop Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. Debugging Workshop — Phase 35: Architecture Review & Refactoring Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk observe architecture -> identify smell/risk -> establish tests -> small refactor -> verify behavior -> document decision Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next. Failure drill 1 — Big-bang rewrite Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails. Model the workflow explicitly instead of scattering booleans such as approved=true across controllers. - - - - DRAFT SUBMITTED REVIEW APPROVED EXECUTED > > > > Figure 3 -… Approval Workflows and Long-Running Processes Enterprise systems contain processes that live longer than one HTTP request. Model the workflow explicitly instead of scattering booleans such as approved=true across controllers. - - - - DRAFT SUBMITTED REVIEW APPROVED EXECUTED > > > > Figure 3 - A workflow is a state machine with actors, transitions, and evidence Workflow design checklist • Define states, allowed transitions, actor/permission requirements, transition preconditions, timestamps, reason/comments, and terminal states. • Put transition rules in one authoritative backend policy/service; the UI only presents actions that may be available. • Use explicit actions such as submit(), approve(), reject(), cancel(), finalize() instead of generic update({status}). Long-running workflow • An approval may wait hours or days. Persist workflow state; do not keep it in memory or an HTTP connection. • For multi-step asynchronous work, store progress and make each step restartable. Background workers can continue after process restarts. approvePurchaseOrder(poId, actor) { assertPermission(actor, "po.approve") assertState(po, "SUBMITTED") assertApprovalThreshold(actor, po.total) return transition(po, "APPROVED") } An approval is a business transition, not merely a status field edit. Business - - - - Investigation / Transaction Domain row Audit record command > > > > report Figure 4 - Audit evidence is durable business data Audit record • Capture actor identity, action, entity type/id, timestamp, relevant before/after or structured change data, reason, requestId/correlation, and business context. • Write critical audit evidence in the same transaction as the business change when atomicity is required. • Do not treat console/Sentry logs as the authoritative business audit ledger; operational telemetry can expire or be sampled. Effective-dated data • HR salary, employment status, tax settings, and organization assignments often change "effective from" a date rather than by overwriting history. • Prefer explicit effectiveFrom/effectiveTo or versioned records when historical reconstruction is a business requirement. Logs explain system behavior; audit records explain business accountability. They overlap, but they are not interchangeable. text: background-jobs-idempotency-and-retries Background Jobs Idempotency and Retries Background Jobs, Idempotency, and Retries Payroll calculation, report generation, imports, email batches, document generation, and integrations should not turn user-facing HTTP requests into long-running processes. - - - - - Notify / query HTTP command Persist intent Enqueue job Worker Persist result > > >… Background Jobs, Idempotency, and Retries Payroll calculation, report generation, imports, email batches, document generation, and integrations should not turn user-facing HTTP requests into long-running processes. - - - - - Notify / query HTTP command Persist intent Enqueue job Worker Persist result > > > > > status Figure 5 - Long work moves to durable workers while the API remains responsive 2026 course line • @nestjs/bullmq 12.0.0 integrates BullMQ with NestJS 12; BullMQ 6.x is the current major queue line. • Jobs must be designed for retries. BullMQ explicitly recommends idempotent jobs so retrying a failed job leads to the same final state as a successful first attempt. • Use stable business idempotency keys/job IDs where duplicate execution would be harmful, but remember queue de-duplication alone is not a complete business idempotency strategy. Examples • Generate payroll PDF, import attendance CSV, synchronize government contribution tables, send approved PO to supplier integration, rebuild reporting projection. • Recurring work should use the current BullMQ Job Scheduler API rather than removed legacy repeatable-job APIs in BullMQ 6. job key: payroll-run:<runId>:calculate Worker checks database: - already COMPLETED? return existing result - PROCESSING stale? recover according to policy - otherwise claim work and continue Retry is safe only when the operation is designed to survive duplicate delivery and partial failure. Monetary arithmetic, finalization, periods, rounding, and reproducibility must be explicit business rules. Money rules • Never use binary floating-point for authoritative monetary amounts. PostgreSQL numeric/decimal is exact and selectable in precision; PostgreSQL also warns against floating point for money because of rounding risk. • Define currency, scale, rounding mode, and when rounding occurs. Do not let UI formatting decide accounting behavior. • Persist calculation inputs/version references needed to reproduce a finalized payroll or journal result. Finalize means something • DRAFT calculations may be recomputed. FINALIZED payroll/journal results should normally be immutable; corrections are new adjustment/reversal records, not silent edits. • Accounting journal entries require balanced debits and credits before posting; closed periods reject ordinary postings. • PayrollRun should have a deterministic lifecycle: DRAFT -> CALCULATING -> REVIEW -> FINALIZED -> PAID/ARCHIVED as appropriate. model MoneyExample { amount Decimal @db.Decimal(18, 2) currency String @db.VarChar(3) } # Never store authoritative payroll money in float/double. Financial correctness is a domain invariant, not a formatting concern. text: procurement-inventory-and-stock-consistency Procurement Inventory and Stock Consistency Procurement, Inventory, and Stock Consistency Procurement and inventory illustrate why enterprise systems need ledgers, reservations, and transaction boundaries rather than one mutable “quantity” field. - - - - - Accounting Requisition PO Receive Stock movement Available stock > > > > > impact Figure 6… Procurement, Inventory, and Stock Consistency Procurement and inventory illustrate why enterprise systems need ledgers, reservations, and transaction boundaries rather than one mutable “quantity” field. - - - - - Accounting Requisition PO Receive Stock movement Available stock > > > > > impact Figure 6 - Physical and financial consequences cross module boundaries Stock model • Use StockMovement as durable evidence: RECEIPT, ISSUE, TRANSFER, ADJUSTMENT, RETURN. Current balance can be derived/materialized from movement history. • If reservations exist, distinguish onHand, reserved, and available rather than subtracting arbitrary UI values. • Validate source/destination, item status, quantity sign, authorization, and sufficient stock under a transaction/concurrency strategy. Procurement consistency • Received quantity cannot exceed the allowed ordered quantity without an explicit variance policy. • PO approval authority may depend on amount, department, budget, category, and segregation-of-duties rules. • Goods receipt should be linked to its PO lines and later accounting/payables process, not represented as an unrelated stock edit. A stock balance is the result of controlled movements; the movement ledger is the evidence. text: integration-boundaries-events-and-outbox Integration Boundaries Events and Outbox Integration Boundaries, Events, and the Outbox Pattern Enterprise systems integrate with banks, biometrics, email/SMS, government services, accounting systems, suppliers, and identity providers. External side effects cannot participate in the same database transaction. Business - - - - Inbox/idempoten Outbox row Publisher/worker External system transaction >… Integration Boundaries, Events, and the Outbox Pattern Enterprise systems integrate with banks, biometrics, email/SMS, government services, accounting systems, suppliers, and identity providers. External side effects cannot participate in the same database transaction. Business - - - - Inbox/idempoten Outbox row Publisher/worker External system transaction > > > > cy Figure 7 - Persist intent before performing unreliable external side effects Boundary rule • Do not call an external provider halfway through a database transaction and assume both systems commit atomically. • Persist the business change and an outbox/integration intent atomically; a worker publishes/sends after commit and records delivery state. • Inbound webhooks should verify authenticity, store a stable provider/event ID, and process idempotently so duplicate delivery cannot duplicate business effects. Event design • Use business events such as PurchaseOrderApproved or PayrollRunFinalized, not low-level "row updated" messages as the default integration contract. • Keep event payloads versionable and avoid leaking internal ORM row shapes to external consumers. BEGIN TRANSACTION update purchase_order set status = 'APPROVED' insert audit_event (...) insert integration_outbox (event_type, aggregate_id, payload) COMMIT worker -> supplier/accounting integration The outbox solves "database committed but message was never sent" by making publish intent durable. text: scaling-migration-and-service-extraction Scaling Migration and Service Extraction Scaling and Migration Without a Rewrite The TaskFlow architecture is intentionally replaceable. Scale the constrained boundary first, then extract only where independent operation creates more value than distributed-system cost. - - - Selective - Cloud/on-prem Modular monolith Workers Read models > > > services > options Figure 9 - Evolution is incremental and evidence-driven Typical evolution • Vercel web can remain independent while NestJS API/workers scale separately. • Move long work to BullMQ workers before splitting business modules into network services. • Supabase PostgreSQL can migrate to self-hosted/AWS PostgreSQL because Prisma/application services do not depend on dashboard-only business logic. • Supabase Storage can migrate behind an application-owned storage adapter to S3-compatible storage; Redis/Upstash can move to self-hosted/managed Redis. text: guided-build-lab Guided Build Lab Purpose Generalize TaskFlow patterns into larger enterprise systems while preserving modular boundaries, workflows, auditability, integration reliability, and migration paths. Guided Build Lab — Phase 36: TaskFlow -> Enterprise Systems Purpose Generalize TaskFlow patterns into larger enterprise systems while preserving modular boundaries, workflows, auditability, integration reliability, and migration paths. Deliverable Enterprise expansion blueprint for an HRIS/procurement/inventory/payroll-style system with modules, workflows, events, audit, and scaling triggers. Before you touch the code Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything. Architecture trace business capabilities -> modular monolith -> workflow/state machines -> transactional boundaries -> outbox/events -> background workers -> reporting/integrations -> scale-out only when earned Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. Debugging Workshop — Phase 36: TaskFlow -> Enterprise Systems Goal Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it. The debugging loop 1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action. 2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state. 3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior. 4. Form one hypothesis. 5. Change one variable. 6. Re-run the same reproduction. 7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis. Boundary walk business capabilities -> modular monolith -> workflow/state machines -> transactional boundaries -> outbox/events -> background workers -> reporting/integrations -> scale-out only when earned Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.
